card.headline: Curly tail, bright eyes, eager eater
card.look: A healthy pig is alert and curious, comes quickly to the trough at feeding time, and carries its tail curled or swinging. Its skin is clean, its breathing is quiet and its droppings are firm.
card.action: Check every pig at morning feeding, and write down any pig that does not rush to eat, lies apart or carries its tail limp.

detail.summary: This page describes what a normal, healthy pig looks, sounds and behaves like, so you can spot trouble early. Pigs often hide illness until it is serious, and many pig diseases, including African swine fever, spread fast through a herd. A farmer who knows what normal looks like will notice the first small change, such as a pig that eats slowly or lies alone. That farmer can then isolate the pig and call the vet a day or two earlier, which often makes the difference between losing one pig and losing the whole pen.
detail.cause: Good health in pigs rests on five things working together: feed, water, housing, hygiene and disease protection. Pigs grow very fast, so they need a balanced ration with enough energy, protein (especially the amino acid lysine, a building block of muscle), minerals such as calcium and phosphorus for bones, and vitamins. Clean water must be available all the time. Pigs drink far more than many farmers expect, and a lactating sow needs a great deal, because milk is mostly water. Pigs cannot sweat properly, so they depend on shade, airflow and wet floors or wallows to stay cool. Heat stress cuts their appetite, fertility and growth. A dry, draught-free sleeping area with clean bedding protects piglets, which chill easily. Regular cleaning breaks the cycle of worms, mange mites and gut germs. Good biosecurity protects the herd from outside infections. Biosecurity means the habits that keep disease out, such as controlling visitors, footbaths, and never feeding uncooked swill. When all these are right, the pig's immune system copes with the everyday germs around it, and the pig stays active, eats well and grows steadily.
spread: Health is lost most often when a new pig is brought in without a quarantine period and carries an infection such as African swine fever, mange or worms into the herd.
Feeding uncooked kitchen waste, hotel swill or pork scraps can bring in serious viruses, including African swine fever, which survives for a long time in pork products.
Visitors, traders, butchers and vehicles moving between farms can carry germs on boots, clothes, crates and tyres.
Dirty, wet pens, blocked drains and dung left lying around allow worm eggs, mange mites and diarrhoea-causing germs to build up.
Mouldy maize, maize bran or other feeds can contain aflatoxins. These are poisons made by moulds that damage the liver and weaken immunity even when the feed looks fairly normal.
Sudden changes in feed, overcrowding, mixing unfamiliar pigs, hot afternoons and cold, wet nights all stress pigs and make them more likely to fall sick.
Free-ranging pigs that roam can pick up worms, pork tapeworm cysts and infections from other herds, and may eat rubbish or human faeces.
detail.atRisk: Every pig benefits from a daily check, but some groups need closer watching. Newborn piglets in their first weeks chill easily, can be crushed by the sow, and can become anaemic (short of iron in the blood) if raised on concrete with no soil. Weaners, the young pigs taken off the sow, face stress from separation, a new diet and mixing, and often show the first signs of diarrhoea or poor growth. Sows around farrowing and during milk production need extra feed, water and attention. Boars and heavy finishers suffer more in heat. In Kenya, the hot dry months before the long rains bring heat stress. The long and short rains bring wet, muddy pens, more worms and mange, and more mouldy feed. Backyard and free-range systems face more parasite and disease contact. Zero-grazing and commercial units face crowding and faster spread once a disease gets in.

early: Bright, alert and curious: a healthy pig lifts its head, grunts and comes to investigate when you enter the pen.
Eats eagerly: all pigs rush to the trough at feeding time and finish their ration in a reasonable time without leaving feed behind.
Tail curled, wagging or swinging when the pig is active. Many pigs relax the tail when asleep, which is normal.
Normal body temperature is about 38.5–39.5 °C. Young piglets may run slightly higher, and readings rise a little after exercise or on hot afternoons.
Breathing is quiet, even and done with the chest, without heaving flanks. Pigs breathe faster in heat and young piglets breathe faster than adults.
Droppings are firm, formed and moist, shaped like soft balls or logs. Suckling piglets normally pass softer, pasty yellowish droppings.
Urine is clear to pale yellow, and the pig passes it easily without straining.
Lies stretched out on its side or on its belly, close to its pen mates but not piled on top of them. It gets up easily when disturbed.
Skin is clean, smooth and free of scabs, crusts or blotches. The coat lies flat and the ears are clean inside.
Walks freely on all four legs with no limping, and keeps the dunging area separate from the sleeping area.
advanced: Leaves feed, eats slowly, or does not get up at feeding time. This is often the very first sign of illness.
Temperature above about 40 °C in a pig that has been resting in the shade suggests fever. A low temperature in a weak pig is also serious.
Lies apart from the group, hides in the bedding, or pigs pile on top of each other when the weather is not cold, which suggests chill or fever.
Tail hangs straight and limp while the pig is awake, or the pig looks dull with its head down and ears drooping.
Red, purple or bluish patches on the ears, belly, legs or tail are a warning sign of serious disease, including African swine fever. Isolate the pig and call the vet at once.
Diarrhoea, blood in the droppings, hard dry droppings with straining, or vomiting.
Coughing, sneezing, discharge from the nose or eyes, or fast heaving breathing at rest in cool weather.
Constant scratching and rubbing on walls, crusty skin, or bitten tails and ears, which can point to mange, lice or stress.
Limping, swollen joints, trembling, staggering, or walking in circles.
Sudden death of one or more pigs. Do not open or sell the carcass, and call the vet immediately.

lookalikes.name: Normal panting and wallowing in hot weather
lookalikes.howToTell: Pigs breathe faster and lie in water, mud or their own wet dung on hot afternoons to cool down, because they cannot sweat. A healthy pig that is just hot still gets up, eats when feed comes, and breathes normally again in the cool evening. A sick pig breathes hard even in cool weather, has a fever when rested, and refuses feed.

lookalikes.name: Sow off feed around farrowing
lookalikes.howToTell: Many sows eat less in the day before farrowing (giving birth) and may be restless and build a nest. Appetite usually returns within a day or so after farrowing. Call the vet if she stays off feed after this time, or has a fever, a hard, hot or red udder, a foul discharge, or piglets that are hungry and squealing.

lookalikes.name: Swollen red vulva in a gilt or sow on heat
lookalikes.howToTell: A gilt is a young female that has not yet farrowed. When a gilt or sow is on heat (ready to mate), the vulva becomes swollen and pink. She may be restless, mount others and stand still when pressed on the back. This lasts a couple of days and returns about every three weeks. Swelling with pus, a foul smell or bleeding is not normal.

lookalikes.name: Sunburn or rough skin in white pigs
lookalikes.howToTell: White or pink pigs kept in the sun can redden on the back and ears, which then peel. The redness is on the parts that face the sun, and the pig is otherwise bright and eating. Blotchy red or purple patches on the belly, ear tips and legs, together with fever and dullness, are a disease warning and need the vet.

detail.diagnosis: You can do a simple home health check every day. Stand quietly at the pen before feeding and watch for a minute. Does every pig get up, grunt and come forward? Count them. Then feed, and watch who eats eagerly and who hangs back. Look at the droppings in the dunging area, the skin, the eyes, the tail and the way each pig walks. Listen for coughing. To take a temperature, use a digital thermometer from the agrovet. Clean it, lubricate the tip with a little petroleum jelly or cooking oil, and gently insert it into the rectum (back passage) about 3–5 cm. Angle it slightly so the tip touches the rectal wall. Hold it until it beeps, usually about a minute. Take readings while the pig is calm and eating or resting, not after chasing it or in the hottest part of the day. Clean and disinfect the thermometer between pigs. If one pig looks unwell, take the temperature of a healthy pen mate too, so you can compare. To check breathing, count flank movements for 30 seconds while the pig rests, then double the number. To track growth, weigh pigs on a scale or use a pig weigh band (a measuring tape that estimates weight from chest size) once a month. Keep a notebook with dates, weights, temperatures, feed changes, deworming, vaccinations and any sick pigs. When you call the vet, this record helps them reach a diagnosis faster. If a pig dies, the vet may do a post-mortem (an examination of the body after death) and take samples for a laboratory.
firstSteps: Do your pen check every morning at feeding time, when changes in appetite are easiest to see. Do a quick second look in the evening.
If any pig is off feed, dull or has a fever, move it to a separate sick pen and use separate boots and buckets for it. Handle it last.
Make sure every pig has clean drinking water at all times. Check that nipple drinkers actually release water, and that water troughs are clean.
Give shade, airflow and a way to cool off in hot weather. In cold, wet weather, give dry bedding and a draught-free sleeping area, especially for piglets.
Stop buying in, selling or moving pigs if any are unwell. Keep visitors, traders and butchers out of the pens until the vet has seen them.
Write down what you see: which pig, its temperature, its signs and when they started. Take a photo of any skin changes to show the vet.
Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer early. Do not give leftover or borrowed drugs, because the wrong treatment can hide the problem or leave residues in the pork.
detail.vetTreatment: Routine vet care keeps healthy pigs healthy. A good plan, agreed with your vet or animal health officer, usually includes several things. Piglets raised on concrete get iron in their first days of life to prevent anaemia, and your vet will advise on the product and how to give it. Deworming follows a regular schedule, especially for sows before farrowing and for weaners and growers, using a dewormer the vet recommends. Mange and lice are controlled by treating sows before farrowing and treating new arrivals. Castration of male piglets not kept for breeding should be done young, cleanly and with pain relief where possible. Vaccination needs vary by area and farm. Ask your vet which vaccines are available and worth using locally. There is currently no approved vaccine for African swine fever in Kenya, so biosecurity is the main protection. The vet can also check your feed ration, inspect breeding stock, advise on farrowing pens, and examine any pig that dies unexpectedly. Any drug a vet prescribes, including dewormers, antibiotics and mange treatments, has a withdrawal period. This is the time you must wait after treatment before the pig can be slaughtered for meat. Always follow it. Antibiotics should only be used when a vet has prescribed them for a bacterial infection, and the full course should be given. Routine use of antibiotics as 'growth boosters' or 'just in case' breeds resistant germs. These germs make treatment fail for both pigs and people.
prevention: Quarantine every new pig for at least two to three weeks in a separate pen away from the herd. Watch it daily, and deworm and treat it for mange on the vet's advice before mixing.

Never feed uncooked swill, hotel waste or pork scraps. Kitchen waste should only be fed if it is boiled thoroughly, and pork products should be left out completely, because they can carry African swine fever.
Keep a footbath with fresh disinfectant at the pen entrance, limit visitors, and keep traders, butchers and their vehicles away from the pens.
Feed a balanced ration suited to each stage: creep feed for piglets, then weaner, grower, finisher, and sow and boar meals. Make feed changes gradually over several days.
Store maize, bran and pig meal dry, off the floor and away from leaking roofs. Do not feed mouldy or musty-smelling feed, as it may contain aflatoxins.
Provide clean water all day. Check drinkers daily and clean troughs often.
Clean the pens daily and remove dung. Keep floors sloped and drains clear, and disinfect and rest pens between batches.
Avoid overcrowding, give shade and cooling in the dry season, and keep sleeping areas dry and draught-free in the rains.
Keep free-range pigs confined or tethered, build and use latrines for people, and deworm regularly to cut worm and pork tapeworm cycles.
detail.impact: Healthy pigs make money; sick pigs quietly lose it. A pig that eats well and grows steadily reaches market weight sooner and costs less to feed per kilogram of pork. A healthy sow comes back on heat on time, farrows regularly and raises strong litters. On a Kenyan smallholding, a few weeks of poor growth from worms, mange or low-grade illness can wipe out the profit on a batch of finishers. A disease outbreak can do far worse. African swine fever can kill most of an infected herd and lead to movement restrictions in the area. Catching problems early through a daily check means lower vet and drug costs, fewer deaths, and pork that is free of drug residues and sells well to butchers and processors.
detail.humanHealth: Pigs that look healthy can still carry germs that infect people, so good hygiene always matters. Pork tapeworm is a real risk in East Africa, especially with free-range pigs. Pigs pick up tapeworm cysts by eating human faeces, and people get the tapeworm by eating undercooked pork. Tapeworm eggs from a human carrier can also cause cysts in people, including in the brain, which can lead to epilepsy. Use latrines, keep pigs confined, have pigs slaughtered where meat is inspected, and cook pork thoroughly. Pigs can also pass on Streptococcus suis, Salmonella, brucellosis and influenza viruses. Wash your hands after handling pigs or dung, cover cuts, and wear boots and overalls in the pens. Do not let children play in pig pens. Always respect drug withdrawal periods so that pork reaching your family and customers is free of residues.
detail.outlook: A herd that is fed well, housed well, kept clean and protected from outside disease will usually stay productive with only occasional minor problems. When something does go wrong, the outlook depends heavily on how early it is noticed. A pig that is spotted on the first morning it leaves feed, isolated and seen by a vet has a much better chance of recovery than one found after days of illness. Early action also gives the rest of the herd a better chance of staying healthy. Farmers who keep simple daily records and know their pigs' normal behaviour catch problems sooner and lose fewer animals.

faqs.q: What is the normal temperature of a pig?
faqs.a: A healthy pig's temperature is usually about 38.5–39.5 °C. Young piglets can be slightly higher. Temperatures also rise a little after the pig has been chased or excited, or on a hot afternoon. Take the temperature when the pig is calm, using a digital rectal thermometer. If a resting pig reads above about 40 °C and is also dull or off feed, it likely has a fever and you should call the vet. Comparing with a healthy pen mate helps you judge.

faqs.q: Why is my pig's tail straight? Is it sick?
faqs.a: A curly or wagging tail is a good sign of a happy, healthy pig. A pig's tail often relaxes and straightens when it is asleep or resting quietly, and that is normal. Worry when the tail hangs limp and straight while the pig is awake, especially if the pig is also dull, off feed or lying apart. Then check its temperature and watch it closely. Also look for tail biting, which usually points to crowding, boredom, heat or a diet problem.

faqs.q: How often should I check my pigs?
faqs.a: Look at every pig at least once a day, ideally at morning feeding, when a pig that does not come to eat stands out at once. A short evening check is also useful, especially for sows about to farrow and young piglets. Weigh or use a weigh band monthly to make sure growth is on track. Keep a simple notebook so you can see changes over time.

faqs.q: How much water does a pig need?
faqs.a: Pigs need far more water than many farmers think, and they need it all day, not just at feeding times. Needs rise with body size, hot weather and milk production, and a lactating sow drinks a great deal. A sow short of water produces less milk, and her piglets suffer. Check that nipple drinkers actually flow when pressed and that troughs are clean and full. If pigs crowd around the water or eat less, check the water supply first.

faqs.q: Is it normal for my pigs to lie in mud or their own dung?
faqs.a: Pigs cannot sweat, so in hot weather they lie in water, mud or wet patches to cool their skin. This is normal cooling behaviour, not dirtiness. If they are lying in dung, it usually means they have no better way to cool off. Give them shade, airflow, a clean wet area or a sprinkler, so they can cool without dirtying themselves. Given space, a healthy pig keeps its sleeping area dry and dungs in one corner.

faqs.q: Do I need to give vitamins or supplements to healthy pigs?
faqs.a: Pigs fed a good, balanced commercial meal or a well-formulated home mix usually get most of what they need. Extra support can still help in some situations, such as breeding sows, pigs fed mostly home-grown maize and bran, or times of heat or stress. Ask your vet or animal nutrition adviser before adding supplements, so you fix real gaps rather than waste money. Supplements support good feeding and management; they do not replace them.

products.role: Mixed into pig meal or home rations based on maize and maize bran, this mycotoxin binder helps protect pigs from aflatoxin and ochratoxin in feed that may carry hidden mould poisons. This supports normal liver function, appetite and growth. It is an aid alongside proper dry feed storage and never a reason to feed visibly mouldy feed.

For breeding sows and gilts, this supplement helps meet the extra nutritional needs of fertility and milk production when added to a balanced sow ration. It supports regular breeding and strong litters as part of good feeding, water supply and vet-guided herd care.

healthy.imagePrompt: A healthy pink pig with a tightly curled tail and bright eyes eating eagerly from a clean feed trough in a tidy, well-lit smallholder pig pen in rural Kenya, with dry bedding and a water nipple visible.
healthy.seoDescription: Learn what a healthy pig looks like: normal temperature 38.5–39.5 °C, curly tail, eager eating, firm droppings, and a daily pen check for Kenyan farmers.

card.headline: Red-purple ears, belly and legs
card.look: Pigs run a high fever, stop eating and huddle together, with dark red to purple blotches on the ears, belly, tail and legs. Several pigs may die suddenly within a few days, sometimes before any other sign is seen.
card.action: Stop all pig movement and sales at once and report to your County Veterinary Officer immediately, because ASF is a notifiable disease.

detail.summary: African swine fever (ASF) is a severe viral disease of pigs that often kills nearly all infected animals within days. There is no approved vaccine available in Kenya and no cure. It spreads easily through live pigs, pork, kitchen leftovers (swill), and dirty boots, vehicles and equipment. Because it can wipe out a whole herd and a whole neighbourhood's pigs, it is a notifiable disease in Kenya and must be reported to the veterinary authorities straight away.
detail.cause: ASF is caused by the African swine fever virus, a large and very tough virus. It only infects pigs and their wild relatives. In Africa, warthogs and bushpigs can carry the virus without getting sick, and soft ticks that live in warthog burrows can carry it for a long time. When the virus enters a domestic pig, usually through the mouth or nose, it attacks the white blood cells that normally defend the body. It then damages the lining of the blood vessels, so blood leaks into the skin and organs. This is why the ears, belly and legs turn red or purple, why the spleen and lymph nodes (glands that filter blood) swell and darken, and why pigs bleed internally. The body's defences collapse, the fever climbs, and most pigs with the severe form die within about a week of showing signs. The virus survives for a long time in blood, meat and the environment: it can stay alive for weeks to months in raw, frozen, salted or smoked pork, and in pig dung and contaminated pens, which is why it travels so easily from farm to farm.
spread: Direct contact between sick or carrier pigs and healthy pigs, for example when new pigs are bought, boars are borrowed for mating, or pigs roam freely and mix with neighbours' pigs.
Feeding swill, kitchen leftovers, hotel or school waste that contains pork or pork products, including sausages, smokies, bacon and ham, even if they looked fine to eat.
Pork and pig products moved from infected areas, including meat bought cheaply during an outbreak when farmers rush to sell sick pigs.
Contaminated boots, clothes, hands, buckets, feeding troughs, castration tools and knives carried between farms by farmers, traders, butchers, boar keepers and even helpful neighbours.
Vehicles, motorbikes and handcarts that carried pigs or pork and were not cleaned and disinfected.
Blood, dung, urine and saliva from sick pigs, and carcasses dumped in rivers, bush or open pits where dogs, other pigs or people can reach them.
Soft ticks (Ornithodoros) and contact with warthogs or bushpigs in areas near wildlife, especially where pigs scavenge near game areas.
detail.atRisk: All domestic pigs of every breed, age and sex can catch ASF, and local breeds are not protected. Piglets, growers, fatteners and pregnant sows are all affected; pregnant sows often abort. The highest risk is on free-range and scavenging systems, small backyard units that feed swill, and farms close to markets, slaughter slabs, roads used by pig traders or areas with warthogs and bushpigs. In Kenya outbreaks have been reported in several pig-keeping areas, including western Kenya near the Uganda border and central Kenya. Risk often rises when pigs are moved a lot, for example around festive seasons when trade and pork demand increase, and when farmers panic-sell during an outbreak nearby. Commercial zero-grazing units with poor fencing, shared boars, or many visitors are also at serious risk.

early: Sudden high fever: the pig feels very hot to touch, especially behind the ears and on the belly.
Loss of appetite: the pig stops coming to the trough or eats very little.
Dullness and weakness: pigs lie down most of the time and are slow to get up when you enter the pen.
Huddling together or burying themselves in bedding, even when the weather is warm.
Redness of the skin, especially the ears, belly, tail and inner legs, which may be the first thing you notice on white or light-coloured pigs.
One or two pigs found dead suddenly without having looked very sick.
advanced: Dark red, purple or bluish blotches on the ears, snout, belly, tail and legs, which do not fade.
Staggering, wobbly walking, weakness of the back legs, and sometimes fits or paddling.
Breathing difficulty, coughing and froth or a bloody discharge from the nose.
Vomiting and diarrhoea, which may be bloody, or constipation with hard dark dung.
Discharge from the eyes and redness around them.
Abortions in pregnant sows, often at any stage of pregnancy.
Many pigs dying over a few days, with deaths spreading from pen to pen and to neighbouring farms.

lookalikes.name: Swine erysipelas
lookalikes.howToTell: Erysipelas often causes raised, diamond- or square-shaped red patches on the skin, and fewer pigs usually die. Affected pigs often respond quickly to antibiotics given by a vet, while ASF does not respond to any treatment. Only a laboratory test can safely rule out ASF, so never assume it is erysipelas during deaths.

lookalikes.name: Classical swine fever (hog cholera)
lookalikes.howToTell: Classical swine fever looks almost identical to ASF in the field, with fever, red-purple skin and deaths. It is caused by a different virus and can only be told apart by laboratory tests. Both are serious and must be reported.

lookalikes.name: Salmonellosis and other bacterial blood infections
lookalikes.howToTell: Salmonella can cause fever, purple ears and diarrhoea, often in weaners and growers, but usually spreads more slowly and often fewer pigs die. Some cases improve with vet treatment. A vet and laboratory are needed to confirm.

lookalikes.name: Heat stroke
lookalikes.howToTell: Heat stroke happens on very hot days, often after pigs are moved or crowded without shade or water. Pigs pant heavily and skin may redden, but they usually recover when cooled. It does not spread from farm to farm and does not keep killing pigs over days.

detail.diagnosis: ASF cannot be confirmed by looking alone, because several diseases cause fever and red skin. The vet or County Veterinary Officer will examine the live pigs, take temperatures, and ask about recent pig purchases, swill feeding, deaths and contacts with other farms. They will collect blood samples from sick pigs and tissue samples (often spleen and lymph nodes) from dead pigs. On post-mortem, ASF typically shows a greatly enlarged, dark, soft spleen, swollen and bloody lymph nodes, and bleeding in the kidneys, heart and other organs, but the final answer comes from the laboratory. Samples are sent to a government or approved laboratory, such as the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete, where tests like PCR (which detects the virus itself) and antibody tests are used. Do not open carcasses yourself, because this spreads the virus. To help the vet, prepare a written record of when signs started, how many pigs are sick and dead, their ages, any pigs bought, sold or borrowed in the last three weeks, what you have been feeding, and who has visited the farm. Keep dead pigs covered and in one place until the vet advises how to dispose of them.
firstSteps: Report immediately to your County Veterinary Officer, local veterinary office, or your nearest vet or animal health assistant; this is required by law for ASF in Kenya.
Stop all movement of pigs, pork, manure and equipment on and off the farm, and do not sell, give away or slaughter any pig, even ones that look healthy.
Confine all pigs in their pens so none roam, and keep visibly sick pigs apart from the others if you can do so safely.
Close the farm gate to visitors, traders, butchers and boar keepers, and keep dogs and other animals away from the pigs and any carcasses.
Use one set of boots and clothes only for the pig unit, wash hands well after handling pigs, and do not visit other pig farms, markets or slaughter slabs.
Give sick pigs clean drinking water, shade, and dry bedding to keep them as comfortable as possible, but do not give any injections or drugs without a vet.
Do not throw dead pigs into rivers, the bush or latrines, and do not eat or sell their meat; cover the carcasses and wait for the vet's instructions on burial or burning.
Write down the number of pigs sick and dead each day, the dates signs began, and all recent pig movements and feed sources to help the investigation.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no cure for African swine fever and no approved vaccine available in Kenya. Antibiotics do not kill the virus, and injecting pigs with antibiotics or other drugs will not save them; it only wastes money, risks drug residues in pork, and helps antimicrobial resistance (germs becoming resistant to medicines) to develop. Any medicine for pigs must be prescribed by a vet, and the milk and meat withdrawal periods on any drug must always be respected before pork is eaten or sold. When ASF is suspected, the veterinary authorities focus on control rather than treatment. This usually includes placing the farm under quarantine, restricting pig and pork movement in the surrounding area, humane killing of infected and exposed pigs under official supervision where this is ordered, safe disposal of carcasses by deep burial or burning, and thorough cleaning and disinfection of pens, equipment and vehicles. Neighbouring farms are inspected and monitored. Whether farmers receive compensation for pigs killed varies and depends on government decisions at the time, so ask your County Veterinary Officer. After cleaning, the farm must stay empty of pigs for a period set by the vet before restocking.
prevention: Never feed swill, kitchen leftovers or hotel and school waste to pigs unless it contains no pork at all; if waste is used, it must be thoroughly boiled first, but avoiding pork-containing waste completely is the safest choice.
Keep pigs confined in a fenced or walled unit instead of letting them roam, so they cannot mix with other pigs, scavenge pork waste, or meet warthogs and bushpigs.
Buy new pigs only from known, healthy farms, avoid buying cheap pigs during or near an outbreak, and keep newcomers separate for at least three weeks while watching for signs.
Avoid sharing boars; use artificial insemination where possible, or bring the sow to a trusted boar only after checking that farm is disease-free.

Set up a footbath with a vet-recommended disinfectant at the pig unit entrance, keep dedicated boots and clothes for the piggery, and limit visitors, especially traders, butchers and other pig farmers.
Clean and disinfect feeding troughs, water containers, tools, and any vehicles or handcarts that come into contact with pigs or pork.
Stay informed through your County Veterinary Officer and local farmer groups about outbreaks in your area, and tighten all measures immediately when ASF is reported nearby.
Report any sudden deaths or sick pigs quickly, and never sell or slaughter sick pigs, as panic-selling is one of the main ways ASF spreads across whole regions.
detail.impact: ASF is one of the most costly pig diseases for Kenyan farmers because it can kill nearly every pig on a farm within one to two weeks. A smallholder can lose all their savings in pigs, which are often kept as a 'bank' to pay school fees or emergencies. Breeding sows abort, so future litters are lost as well. Quarantine and movement restrictions stop pig and pork sales in the area, hurting healthy farms, butchers and traders too. Restocking takes time and money, and farms must stay empty for a period before new pigs come in. Outbreaks also shake buyer confidence, lower pork prices locally, and can discourage farmers from continuing pig keeping.
detail.outlook: The outlook for pigs with acute ASF is very poor: most die, often within a week of first showing signs, and there is no treatment that changes this. A small number of pigs, especially with milder forms of the disease, may survive, but survivors can remain carriers and spread the virus to other pigs, which is why authorities usually do not allow them to be kept or sold. For the farm, the outlook depends on how quickly the disease is reported, how strictly movement is stopped, and how well carcasses are disposed of and pens are cleaned. Farms that report early, follow the vet's instructions, clean thoroughly and improve biosecurity can successfully restart pig keeping after the period advised by the veterinary authorities.

faqs.q: Can people catch African swine fever from pigs or pork?
faqs.a: No. ASF does not infect people, and it is not a danger to human health. However, people are one of the main ways the virus moves between farms, on boots, clothes, hands, vehicles and in pork products. So even though you cannot get sick, you can carry the virus to your pigs or a neighbour's pigs. Meat from sick or dead pigs should never be sold or moved, because it spreads the disease to other pigs.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine or injection I can buy at the agrovet to protect my pigs?
faqs.a: No vaccine for ASF is approved or available in Kenya at present, and no injection from the agrovet can prevent or cure it. Be careful of anyone selling a so-called ASF cure or vaccine. The only protection is good biosecurity: confining pigs, not feeding pork-containing swill, controlling visitors, buying pigs from safe sources, and reporting sick pigs quickly.

faqs.q: My neighbour's pigs are dying. Should I sell my pigs quickly before they get sick?
faqs.a: No. Selling pigs during an outbreak is one of the biggest ways ASF spreads to new areas, and your pigs may already be carrying the virus without showing signs. Moving them can also break the law if movement restrictions are in place. Instead, lock down your farm: keep pigs confined, stop visitors, use separate boots, do not share equipment, and inform the County Veterinary Officer. This gives your pigs the best chance of staying free.

faqs.q: What does it mean when the vet says my farm is under quarantine?
faqs.a: Quarantine means no pigs, pork, pig manure or pig equipment may leave or enter the farm without permission from the veterinary authorities. Often the restrictions cover an area around the farm too, and pig markets and slaughter may be closed for a time. These rules are legal requirements under Kenya's animal disease laws, and breaking them can lead to penalties. They exist to stop the virus spreading. The restrictions are lifted only when the vet is satisfied the disease is under control.

faqs.q: How long should I wait before bringing new pigs after an outbreak?
faqs.a: The waiting time is set by the veterinary authorities and depends on how well the farm has been cleaned and disinfected. The virus can survive for a long time in dung, blood and pens, so everything must be cleaned, disinfected, and left empty. Your vet may suggest bringing in a few pigs first and watching them closely before restocking fully. Never restock without the vet's advice, and fix the biosecurity gaps that let the disease in.

faqs.q: Will boiling or cooking pork make swill safe for my pigs?
faqs.a: Thorough boiling can kill the ASF virus, but in practice swill is often not heated long or evenly enough, and it can be contaminated again after cooking. Cured, smoked or frozen pork can still carry live virus for months. The safest rule is not to feed any kitchen waste that contains pork or pork products. Use commercial feeds, home-mixed rations from clean ingredients, or vegetable waste that has never been in contact with meat.

african-swine-fever.imagePrompt: A realistic farm photo of a light-skinned grower pig lying weakly on straw in a simple Kenyan pig pen, with clearly visible dark red to purple blotches on its ears, belly and legs, other pigs huddled behind it.
african-swine-fever.seoDescription: African swine fever in pigs: spot red-purple ears, high fever and sudden deaths, report to your County Vet, and protect your herd with strict biosecurity.

card.headline: Blisters on snout and feet, severe lameness
card.look: Pigs lie down, squeal when made to stand and walk on their knees or tiptoes, with pale fluid-filled blisters or raw patches on the snout, mouth and along the top of the hooves. Young piglets may die suddenly without showing any blisters at all.
card.action: Stop all movement of animals, people and products off and onto your farm and report immediately to your County Veterinary Officer, because foot-and-mouth disease is notifiable by law.

detail.summary: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) is a highly contagious viral disease of cloven-hoofed animals, including pigs, cattle, sheep, goats and wild animals such as buffalo. In pigs it causes painful blisters on the snout, mouth, feet and teats, severe lameness, hooves that can come loose, abortions, and sudden deaths in young piglets. It is a notifiable disease in Kenya, so every suspected case must be reported to the County Veterinary Officer. Outbreaks lead to quarantines, closed markets and heavy losses for the whole community, not just the affected farm.
detail.cause: FMD is caused by a virus from the picornavirus family (genus Aphthovirus). There are seven main types of the virus, called serotypes: O, A, C, SAT1, SAT2, SAT3 and Asia1. Several of these, especially O, A, SAT1 and SAT2, have been found in Kenya and East Africa. Immunity to one serotype does not protect against the others, which is why animals can get FMD more than once. Once the virus enters the pig, usually through the mouth, nose or a small break in the skin, it multiplies quickly and spreads through the blood. It then attacks the skin cells in places that rub or carry weight: the snout, lips, tongue, the coronary band (the soft band of skin where the hoof meets the leg), the heels, between the claws and the teats of nursing sows. Fluid collects under the skin and forms blisters, called vesicles. These burst within a day or two, leaving raw, painful sores. On the feet, the damage can separate the hoof horn from the tissue underneath, so the claw may partly or completely come off (sloughing). In very young piglets the virus often attacks the heart muscle instead, causing heart failure and sudden death, sometimes before any blisters appear. Pigs are especially dangerous spreaders because they breathe out very large amounts of virus into the air, far more than cattle, which is why they are called 'amplifier' hosts.
spread: Direct contact with infected pigs, cattle, sheep or goats, for example at markets, shared boar services, communal grazing or when animals are bought and mixed with the herd.

Feeding swill (kitchen or hotel waste) that contains raw or undercooked meat, bones or offal from infected animals; the virus can survive for a long time in chilled, frozen and some cured meats, bone marrow and lymph nodes.
Breathing in virus carried in the air from infected animals nearby; pigs exhale huge amounts of virus, which can then infect cattle and other animals on neighbouring plots.
People carrying the virus on their boots, clothes, hands and even in their nose after visiting an infected farm, market or slaughter slab.
Contaminated vehicles, crates, feed bags, tools, water and bedding moved from one farm to another.
Contact with infected cattle or wildlife, especially African buffalo, which can carry SAT-type viruses without looking sick and pass them to cattle that then infect pigs.
Manure, urine, saliva, blister fluid and milk from infected animals, which all contain virus and can contaminate pens, paths and shared water points.
detail.atRisk: All pigs of any age, breed or sex can catch FMD. Young piglets, especially those under a few weeks old, are most likely to die because the virus damages their heart. Pregnant sows may abort, and nursing sows with sore teats may refuse to let piglets suckle. Pigs kept close to cattle, sheep or goats, as on many mixed smallholder farms in Central, Western and Rift Valley regions, face extra risk, as do herds that are fed hotel or kitchen swill. Free-range and village pigs that roam, share water points or mix with neighbours' stock are exposed more often than pigs in closed, well-run units. Risk rises when animals are moved a lot, such as during dry-season grazing movements, festive-season trading and around livestock markets, and when outbreaks are already being reported in cattle in the county. Farms near wildlife areas where buffalo live also face a higher background risk.

early: Sudden lameness in several pigs at once, with pigs lying down, refusing to get up, squealing loudly when forced to stand, or shifting weight from foot to foot.
Fever, dullness and reduced appetite; pigs may stop coming to the feed trough or eat only a little.
Pigs walking on their knees or on the tips of their claws, or arching their back to avoid putting weight on painful feet.
Pale, white or slightly raised areas, or small fluid-filled blisters, on the snout, lips and tongue.
Redness, heat and small blisters along the coronary band at the top of the hooves, on the heels and between the claws.
Blisters on the teats of nursing sows, and sows unwilling to let piglets suckle.
Sudden, unexplained deaths of young piglets, sometimes before any adult pigs look sick.
advanced: Burst blisters leaving raw, red, painful sores on the snout, mouth and feet, often with flaps of dead skin.
Hoof horn separating from the foot, with claws partly or completely coming off (sloughing) in severe cases.
Pigs lying down most of the time, becoming thin and losing condition because pain stops them feeding and drinking.
Secondary infection of the foot sores, with swelling, bad smell and pus, and long-lasting lameness.
Abortions in pregnant sows and poor milk supply, leading to weak, starving piglets.
High death rates in piglets in affected litters, while most adult pigs survive but recover slowly.

lookalikes.name: Other vesicular (blister) diseases such as swine vesicular disease, vesicular stomatitis and Senecavirus A infection
lookalikes.howToTell: These diseases cause blisters on the snout and feet that look exactly like FMD, and no farmer or vet can tell them apart by eye. Only laboratory tests on blister samples can separate them. Because they look the same, any pig with blisters on the snout or feet must be treated as suspected FMD and reported.

lookalikes.name: Foot injuries, foot rot or rough, wet floors
lookalikes.howToTell: Injuries and foot infections usually affect one or a few pigs, often on one foot, and there are no blisters on the snout, mouth or teats. FMD affects many pigs quickly, causes fever, and produces blisters in several places at once, including the snout.

lookalikes.name: Swine erysipelas
lookalikes.howToTell: Erysipelas can cause fever, lameness and swollen joints, and often raised, diamond-shaped red or purple patches on the skin of the body. It does not cause fluid-filled blisters on the snout, tongue or coronary band, and a vet may see a response to the right treatment.

lookalikes.name: African swine fever
lookalikes.howToTell: African swine fever causes high fever, red or purple skin on the ears, belly and legs, weakness and very high deaths in pigs of all ages, but not blisters on the snout and feet. Both are emergencies and both must be reported to the County Veterinary Officer, so call the vet either way.

detail.diagnosis: A vet cannot confirm FMD by looking alone, because other blister diseases look identical. When you report a suspected case, a government or private vet will visit, examine the pigs, check their temperature, look closely at the snout, mouth, feet and teats, and ask about recent purchases, swill feeding, visitors and sick cattle nearby. The vet will collect samples, usually pieces of blister skin and blister fluid, and sometimes blood or swabs, in a special transport solution. These are sent to the national FMD laboratory at Embakasi, Nairobi, or another approved laboratory, where tests such as ELISA and PCR (a test that detects the virus's genetic material) confirm FMD and identify the serotype. Knowing the serotype helps the authorities choose the right vaccine for cattle and other animals in the area. If piglets have died, the vet may do a post-mortem; pale streaks in the heart muscle (sometimes called 'tiger heart') strongly suggest FMD in young piglets. To help, keep the sick pigs penned in one place, do not move or sell any animals, write down when signs started, how many pigs are sick or dead, any recent purchases, visitors and feed sources, and keep dead piglets covered and away from dogs until the vet advises how to dispose of them. Do not cut open dead pigs yourself.
firstSteps: Report the suspected outbreak immediately to your County Veterinary Officer, the nearest government veterinary office or your local vet; this is required by law in Kenya and is the fastest way to get help and protect your neighbours.
Stop all movement on and off the farm: do not sell, buy, lend or move any pigs, cattle, sheep or goats, and do not send meat, manure or feed off the farm until the vet says it is safe.
Keep sick pigs in their pen and separate them from healthy pigs and from other livestock as far as possible, without herding or chasing them, as stress and walking worsen foot damage.
Give sick pigs a clean, dry, soft bed such as dry straw or grass, and keep the pen shaded, quiet and draught-free, because standing on hard or wet floors is very painful.
Provide plenty of fresh, clean water within easy reach, and offer soft, wet feed such as moistened mash or porridge, since sore mouths and feet make eating and drinking difficult.
Keep piglets warm and close to the sow, and watch them closely; if the sow refuses to suckle because of sore teats, ask the vet how best to keep piglets fed.

Limit visitors to the farm, set up a footbath or boot-washing point at the gate, and make sure anyone handling sick pigs changes clothes, washes and avoids contact with other livestock for several days.
Record the date signs started, the number of pigs affected and any deaths, and keep feed and medicine records ready for the vet; do not give any drugs unless the vet has prescribed them.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no medicine that kills the FMD virus, and antibiotics do not cure it, because antibiotics work only against bacteria. Most adult pigs recover on their own over a few weeks if they are kept comfortable and well cared for, while young piglets often die despite care. Treatment is supportive, meaning it helps the pig cope while its own immune system fights the virus. A vet may prescribe pain relief and anti-inflammatory drugs (for example from the NSAID group) to reduce pain so pigs can stand, eat and drink. Where foot or mouth sores have become infected with bacteria, the vet may prescribe an antibiotic or apply antiseptic dressings and sprays to the wounds; these must be used only as prescribed, for the full course and at the correct dose, because careless antibiotic use breeds resistant bacteria that make future infections harder to treat. All drugs must be prescribed by a vet, and you must respect the meat withdrawal period on the label, which is the time after treatment before the pig can be slaughtered for food. Because FMD is notifiable, the Directorate of Veterinary Services and the County Veterinary Officer will also manage the outbreak itself. This usually means placing your farm, and possibly the surrounding area, under quarantine. Quarantine and movement restrictions mean that no animals, meat, milk, hides or manure may leave or enter the area without official permission, markets and slaughter slabs may be closed, and checkpoints may be set up. The authorities may order vaccination of cattle and other animals around the outbreak and, in some situations, other control measures. Restrictions are lifted only after the vets are satisfied that no new cases are appearing. Follow all instructions; breaking quarantine is illegal and spreads the disease to other farmers.
prevention: Never feed raw swill: if you use kitchen or hotel waste, it must be boiled thoroughly, kept at a rolling boil for at least an hour and then cooled before feeding, and waste containing meat from unknown sources is best avoided altogether.

Buy pigs only from known, healthy farms with no recent disease, ask for movement permits, and keep new pigs in a separate pen away from the herd for about two to three weeks while you watch for any signs.
Keep pigs housed or fenced so they do not mix with neighbours' pigs, cattle, goats, sheep or wildlife, and avoid sharing boars, water points and grazing areas during outbreaks.

Control visitors: limit who enters the pig pens, provide a footbath and boot-washing point at the entrance, and ask people who have been to markets, slaughterhouses or other farms to change boots and clothes first.

Clean and disinfect pens, tools, crates and vehicles regularly with a disinfectant your vet recommends; FMD virus is killed by suitable acid or alkaline disinfectants such as washing soda (sodium carbonate) solution or approved commercial products.

Support FMD vaccination of cattle in your area, which reduces the amount of virus around pigs; vaccination of pigs is not routine in Kenya, and vaccines must match the serotype, so ask your County Veterinary Officer whether vaccinating your pigs is advised.
Listen for outbreak reports on local radio and from extension officers and agrovets; during an outbreak in your county, stop buying animals, avoid markets and tighten all biosecurity measures.
Keep pigs well fed, dewormed and in clean, dry housing so they are in good condition and recover better if disease does strike.
detail.impact: FMD can be very costly for a Kenyan pig farmer. Litters of piglets may be lost, sows may abort, and sick pigs stop eating and lose weight for weeks, so they take longer to reach market weight and the feed spent on them earns less. Pigs with damaged or lost claws may stay lame for a long time and may have to be culled, and breeding sows and boars may be out of production. The biggest losses often come from quarantine: you may not be able to sell pigs or pork for weeks or longer, while you still have to feed them, and local markets, butcheries and slaughter slabs may close. Because pigs spread the virus so efficiently, one infected herd can trigger an outbreak in cattle across a whole area, hitting dairy farmers' milk income, livestock trade and even exports. Farmers should not assume they will receive compensation for losses, so prevention and early reporting are the best protection.
detail.humanHealth: Foot-and-mouth disease is not considered a public health threat; human infection is extremely rare, and meat from animals in an FMD-affected area is not normally a direct danger to people. It is a completely different disease from 'hand, foot and mouth disease' in children, which is caused by a different virus and does not come from animals. The main human role in FMD is spreading it: people can carry the virus on their clothes, boots and hands and even in their nose for a short time after handling infected animals. Anyone working with sick pigs should wear separate clothes and boots, wash hands well, and avoid contact with other livestock for several days. Do not slaughter or sell sick animals or their meat, as this breaks the law during quarantine and spreads the virus. If any drugs are given, observe the meat withdrawal period so that no residues reach consumers.
detail.outlook: Most adult and growing pigs survive FMD and recover within a few weeks, although lameness and weight loss can last longer, especially where claws have come off or foot sores have become infected. Recovery is better when pigs are kept on soft, dry bedding, have easy access to water and soft feed, and receive vet care for pain and secondary infection. Young piglets have a poor outlook because the virus often damages their heart, and deaths in affected litters can be high. Recovered pigs are protected only against the serotype that infected them, not against other types. The outlook for the whole area depends on how quickly the outbreak is reported and how well movement restrictions are followed.

faqs.q: Can I sell or slaughter my pigs quickly before the vet comes, to avoid losses?
faqs.a: No. FMD is notifiable in Kenya, and moving, selling or slaughtering animals from a suspected FMD farm is against the law. It also spreads the virus to markets, butcheries and other farms, causing far bigger losses for everyone, including you if restrictions are extended. Keep the pigs at home, report the case and follow the vet's instructions.

faqs.q: Will antibiotics from the agrovet cure my pigs?
faqs.a: No. FMD is caused by a virus, and antibiotics do not kill viruses. A vet may prescribe antibiotics only if foot or mouth sores become infected with bacteria, and pain relief to help pigs stand and eat. Using antibiotics without a vet wastes money, leaves residues in meat, and helps create resistant bacteria that are harder to treat in future.

faqs.q: My pigs got sick but my cows look fine. Is it really FMD?
faqs.a: It can be. Pigs are often infected first, for example through swill containing infected meat, and then they breathe out large amounts of virus that can infect cattle and other animals nearby within days. Only a laboratory test can confirm FMD, so report it and keep your cattle, goats and sheep away from the pigs. Watch your cattle for drooling, lameness and blisters in the mouth.

faqs.q: Can my pigs be vaccinated against FMD?
faqs.a: FMD vaccines exist, and in Kenya vaccination is mainly done in cattle. Pig vaccination is not routine here, and any vaccine must match the serotypes circulating in your area and needs repeat doses to keep protection. Ask your County Veterinary Officer whether vaccinating your pigs is advised, especially during an outbreak. Good biosecurity and not feeding raw swill remain the most important protection for pigs.

faqs.q: Is it safe for my family to eat pork from a farm with FMD?
faqs.a: FMD is not considered a danger to human health, and people almost never catch it. However, during an outbreak you must not slaughter, sell or move meat from the quarantined farm without official permission, because the meat can carry the virus to other animals, especially if scraps end up in swill. Follow the vet's instructions on what may be done with animals and meat.

faqs.q: How long will the quarantine last?
faqs.a: There is no fixed length. The Directorate of Veterinary Services and County Veterinary Officer will keep restrictions in place until they are satisfied no new cases are appearing in the farm or area, which often takes several weeks or longer. Reporting early, cleaning and disinfecting as advised, and strictly following movement rules all help restrictions to be lifted sooner.

foot-and-mouth-disease.seoDescription: Foot-and-mouth disease in pigs: spot blisters on snout and feet, severe lameness and piglet deaths. Notifiable in Kenya – report, isolate, prevent.

card.headline: Raised red diamond-shaped patches on skin
card.look: A feverish, dull pig that is off its feed, may lie apart and walk stiffly, and often shows raised pink-to-purple, square or diamond-shaped patches on the back, sides or belly. Some pigs die suddenly before any skin signs appear.
card.action: Separate the sick pig, wear gloves, and call your vet today, because early treatment often works well.

aka: Ugonjwa wa almasi (descriptive Swahili for diamond skin disease)
detail.summary: Swine erysipelas is a bacterial disease of pigs that causes high fever, raised red diamond-shaped skin patches, painful joints and sometimes sudden death. It appears in three forms: sudden and severe (acute), milder (subacute), and long-lasting (chronic), which damages joints and heart valves. It matters because it kills growing pigs, causes abortions in sows, leaves survivors lame and slow-growing, and can infect the people who handle pigs and pork. The good news is that early treatment by a vet often works well, and vaccines exist.
detail.cause: The disease is caused by a bacterium called Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae. It is a tough germ that can survive for weeks to months in soil, manure, slurry and damp, dirty pens, especially in cool, wet conditions. Many healthy-looking pigs carry it in their tonsils (the glands at the back of the throat) and pass it in their dung and saliva without showing illness. When a pig's defences drop, for example after stress, a change of feed, hot weather or mixing with new pigs, the bacteria multiply and enter the bloodstream. This is called septicaemia (blood poisoning). In the blood the germ damages the small blood vessels, which causes fever and the raised red or purple patches on the skin, and it can kill quickly. In pigs that survive or have a slower infection, the bacteria settle in the joints, causing swollen, painful arthritis, and on the heart valves, where they form cauliflower-like growths that make the heart fail, sometimes leading to sudden collapse when the pig is exerted. In pregnant sows the fever and infection can cause abortion or weak litters.
spread: Healthy carrier pigs shed the bacteria in dung, urine, saliva and nose discharge, contaminating pens, troughs and water for other pigs.
Pigs swallow the germ by eating contaminated feed, soil, manure or swill, or by drinking dirty water.
Bacteria can enter through skin wounds, cuts from fighting, rough floors, tail biting or navel infections in piglets.
Soil and muddy pig runs can stay contaminated for long periods, so outbreaks can return to the same plot season after season.
Buying in pigs from markets or other farms without knowing their health or vaccination status brings carriers onto the farm.
Stress triggers disease in carrier pigs: sudden feed changes, transport, mixing groups, overcrowding, hot weather and sudden temperature swings.
Biting flies, rodents, birds and other animals such as sheep and poultry can also carry the germ and help move it around a farm.
Feeding uncooked kitchen waste or pork scraps can introduce the bacteria, as well as far more dangerous diseases like African swine fever.
detail.atRisk: Growing and finishing pigs from about three months to a year old are most commonly affected, along with unvaccinated breeding sows and boars. Young piglets are usually protected for a few weeks by antibodies from the sow's first milk (colostrum), if the sow herself is immune. Outbreaks are often seen during hot weather and at changes of season, for example during the warm dry months or the humid start of the long and short rains, when stress and dampness combine. Pigs kept on bare soil, in muddy runs, or in dirty, poorly drained pens are at higher risk, as are herds that buy pigs from markets without quarantine. Both commercial units and smallholder or backyard pigs can be affected; unvaccinated herds in areas where the disease has occurred before carry the greatest risk.

early: High fever: the pig feels hot, often lies apart from the group and may shiver or pile up despite warm weather.
Loss of appetite, with the pig ignoring its feed or eating only a little, while some still drink.
Dullness and reluctance to get up; when forced to move the pig walks stiffly, as if walking on eggshells, and squeals when touched.
Pink, red or purple raised patches appearing on the back, flanks, belly, neck or ears, often one to three days into the illness; they are firm and can be felt with your fingers.
Patches that are square, rectangular or diamond-shaped, from the size of a coin to the palm of your hand, sometimes joining together.
Constipation, or sometimes vomiting, in a pig that was eating well the day before.
One or more pigs found dead suddenly with no warning, sometimes with a purplish tinge to the skin of the ears and belly.
advanced: Skin patches that darken to purple, then dry out, harden and may peel off in pieces; in severe cases the tips of the ears or tail die and fall away.
Swollen, hot and painful joints, especially the knees, hocks and fetlocks, with lameness that lasts weeks or months.
Chronic poor growth, with pigs that stay thin, rough-coated and much smaller than their pen mates.
Breathing difficulty, tiring easily, a bluish tinge to the skin and sudden collapse or death, especially when the pig is chased or exerted, due to damaged heart valves.
Abortion, stillborn piglets, small weak litters or returns to heat in sows that had a fever during pregnancy.
Poor milk production in sick sows, leading to hungry, weak piglets.
Deaths in a pen of growers that continue over several days if no treatment is given.

lookalikes.name: African swine fever (ASF)
lookalikes.howToTell: ASF is a deadly, notifiable viral disease present in Kenya. It causes blotchy red to purple discolouration, mainly of the ears, belly and legs, which is usually flat and not raised in neat diamonds, with very high fever and many deaths across the herd, often within days. Pigs with ASF do not respond to antibiotics. If several pigs are dying quickly, especially with purple ears and bloody diarrhoea or nose bleeding, treat it as suspected ASF, stop all movement and report to your County Veterinary Officer immediately.

lookalikes.name: Streptococcus suis or Glässer's disease (bacterial joint and brain infections)
lookalikes.howToTell: These also cause fever, swollen joints and sudden death, mainly in younger weaned piglets. Look for nervous signs such as paddling, shaking, tilting of the head or lying on the side, which are not typical of erysipelas, and the absence of raised diamond skin patches. A vet often needs laboratory tests to separate them.

lookalikes.name: Sunburn, bruising or skin irritation
lookalikes.howToTell: Sunburn affects pale pigs on the back and ears after time in strong sun and the pig is otherwise bright and eating. Bruises and bite marks from fighting are irregular, follow scratches or wounds, and come without fever. Erysipelas patches are raised, shaped like squares or diamonds and come with fever and dullness.

lookalikes.name: Foot injuries and mycoplasma arthritis
lookalikes.howToTell: Lameness from a cracked hoof, stone or rough floor usually affects one foot, with a visible wound or heat in the claw, and no fever. Mycoplasma joint infections cause lameness in growers, often without high fever or skin patches. A vet can check joints and may take samples to tell them apart.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will usually suspect erysipelas from the combination of fever, raised diamond-shaped skin patches and stiff walking, and by checking the herd's vaccination history. A quick improvement within a day or so of correct antibiotic treatment strongly supports the diagnosis. To confirm it, the vet may take blood, swabs from affected joints or tissue from dead pigs and send them to a laboratory, such as a county veterinary laboratory or the Central Veterinary Laboratories in Kabete, where the germ can be grown (cultured) or detected by PCR, a test that finds the germ's genetic material. A post-mortem (examining a dead pig) is very useful: the vet may find an enlarged spleen, small bleeding spots on the kidneys and heart, swollen joints, or cauliflower-like growths on the heart valves in chronic cases. Because African swine fever can look similar, your vet may also take samples to rule it out. To help, have ready: how many pigs are sick and dead and when it started, ages affected, any recent purchases, feed changes or mixing, vaccination records, and any treatments already given. Keep a fresh carcass cool and covered, away from dogs and other animals, until the vet sees it, and do not open it yourself.
firstSteps: Move sick pigs to a clean, dry, shaded pen away from the healthy ones, and look after the healthy pigs first each day before handling the sick ones.
Call your vet or animal health assistant the same day, because erysipelas usually responds well when treated early, and the vet needs to rule out African swine fever.
Protect yourself: wear gloves, cover any cuts on your hands and wash thoroughly with soap and water after touching pigs, pens, carcasses or meat.
Give constant access to clean, cool drinking water in a trough the pig can reach easily without walking far, as feverish pigs lose water quickly.

Keep the sick pigs cool and comfortable on soft, dry bedding such as wood shavings or dry grass, out of direct sun and draughts, and avoid chasing or forcing them to move, as pigs with heart damage can collapse.
Stop selling, buying, mixing or moving pigs until the vet has seen them, and do not sell sick pigs for slaughter.
Check every pig in the herd twice a day for fever, dullness, skin patches and lameness, and write down the date, pig, signs and any deaths.
Clean out manure and wet bedding from the pens, and keep dead pigs covered and away from dogs until the vet advises how to dispose of them, usually by deep burial with lime or burning.
detail.vetTreatment: Swine erysipelas is one of the pig diseases that usually responds well to antibiotics when treatment starts early. Penicillin is generally the drug of choice, given by injection, and pigs in the acute stage often improve within a day or two; other antibiotic classes may be used depending on the vet's judgement and laboratory results. The vet may treat the whole pen or group, not just the sick pigs, because others are likely to be incubating the disease. Anti-inflammatory drugs may be given to bring down fever and ease joint pain so pigs get up to eat and drink. The vet will often also recommend vaccinating the rest of the herd once the outbreak is under control. Chronic cases with badly damaged joints or heart valves respond poorly, and the vet may advise culling pigs that will not recover or grow well. All treatment must be prescribed and supervised by a vet; do not guess doses or buy antibiotics to use on your own. Every drug has a withdrawal period, the time you must wait after the last treatment before a pig can be slaughtered for meat; follow it exactly and keep records, so that drug residues do not reach consumers. Use antibiotics only when prescribed, complete the full course, and never use them as a substitute for vaccination and hygiene, because overuse breeds antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to drugs on your farm and in people.
prevention: Vaccinate breeding sows and boars regularly and vaccinate growing pigs according to your vet's advice; both inactivated (killed) and live vaccines exist, and availability in Kenya varies, so ask your vet or agrovet which product and timing suit your herd.
Vaccinate sows before farrowing so piglets get protective antibodies through colostrum, and make sure every newborn piglet suckles well in its first hours of life.
Buy pigs only from known, healthy herds with vaccination records, and keep new arrivals in a separate pen for at least two to four weeks, watching for fever and skin patches before mixing.
Keep pens clean and dry: remove manure daily, fix leaking drinkers, improve drainage, and use concrete floors that can be washed and disinfected between batches.
Avoid keeping pigs on the same muddy soil runs year after year, because the germ survives in soil; rest and lime contaminated ground where possible.
Reduce stress by avoiding sudden feed changes, overcrowding and unnecessary mixing of groups, and give shade, good ventilation and plenty of water during hot weather.
Feed a balanced ration with correct protein, vitamins and minerals so pigs keep strong immunity, and store feed dry to avoid mouldy feed that weakens pigs.
Control rodents, birds and flies around the piggery, do not feed raw kitchen waste or pork scraps, and dispose of dead pigs safely by deep burial or burning.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan farm, erysipelas can cause sudden deaths of growers and finishers that are close to market weight, which is a heavy loss after months of feed costs. Pigs that survive may stay lame or stunted, take much longer to reach slaughter weight and fetch lower prices. Chronic heart damage can cause unexpected deaths later, even during loading for market. In breeding herds, abortions, stillbirths, small litters and sows returning to heat reduce the number of piglets sold or raised. Meat inspectors at the slaughterhouse may condemn parts or whole carcasses with skin lesions, swollen joints or signs of infection, cutting income further. There are also costs for vet visits, drugs and vaccines, plus lost sales during the time pigs cannot be sold because of treatment withdrawal periods. Because the germ lingers in soil, a farm that does not change its management may face repeat outbreaks.
detail.humanHealth: Swine erysipelas can infect people, so it is a zoonosis (a disease that passes from animals to people). Farmers, butchers, meat handlers, vets and cooks get infected mainly through small cuts or scratches on the hands when touching infected pigs, carcasses, raw pork, manure or contaminated equipment. In people it usually causes erysipeloid: a painful, itchy, red-to-purple swelling on a finger or hand that spreads slowly, sometimes with mild fever and stiffness of nearby joints. It usually heals with treatment, but rarely it can spread to the blood and heart, which is serious. To protect yourself, wear gloves when handling sick or dead pigs and raw meat, cover cuts with a waterproof plaster, wash hands well with soap after work, and clean knives and boards thoroughly. Cook pork thoroughly. If you develop a painful, spreading purple swelling on your hand after handling pigs or pork, see a doctor or visit a health centre and tell them you work with pigs. Also follow drug withdrawal periods strictly so antibiotic residues do not end up in pork.
detail.outlook: For pigs with the acute form, the outlook is usually good if a vet starts treatment early, and many recover fully within days. Delay worsens the chances, as pigs can die within a day of first signs, especially in unvaccinated herds. Pigs whose skin patches turn to dead, dark areas, or whose ear tips and tail die, recover more slowly. The chronic form is much harder: damaged joints often stay stiff and swollen, and heart valve damage usually cannot be reversed, so these pigs may grow poorly or die suddenly and are often better culled. Herds that vaccinate, keep pens clean and dry, and reduce stress usually see outbreaks stop and rarely return.

faqs.q: How can I tell erysipelas from African swine fever?
faqs.a: Erysipelas typically causes raised, firm, square or diamond-shaped patches you can feel with your fingers, affects some pigs rather than wiping out the herd, and responds quickly to treatment by a vet. African swine fever causes flat, blotchy purple skin especially on the ears and belly, very high death rates in a short time, and does not respond to antibiotics. You cannot always tell by eye, so if many pigs are dying fast, stop all movement, do not sell or slaughter any pigs, and report to your County Veterinary Officer immediately, because ASF is notifiable.

faqs.q: Can I eat or sell meat from a pig that had erysipelas?
faqs.a: Do not slaughter or sell sick pigs. Meat from pigs with active infection may be condemned by the meat inspector and can infect people who handle it. After a pig has recovered and been treated, you must wait for the full withdrawal period of every drug used before slaughter, and the pig should go through an inspected slaughterhouse. Ask your vet when the pig is safe to sell.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine, and where do I get it?
faqs.a: Yes, vaccines against swine erysipelas exist and are widely used around the world, both killed and live types. Supply in Kenya can vary, so ask your vet, County Veterinary Office or a reputable agrovet which vaccine is available and when to give it. Breeding pigs usually need regular boosters, and your vet will advise a schedule for growers and sows based on your herd.

faqs.q: Why did my pigs get sick when I have never bought new pigs?
faqs.a: Many healthy pigs carry the germ in their throats without showing signs, and it can also survive in soil, manure and damp pens for a long time. Stress such as hot weather, feed changes, overcrowding or mixing groups can trigger disease in pigs that were already carrying it. Birds, rodents and contaminated feed or swill can also bring it in. That is why vaccination and clean, dry housing matter even in closed herds.

faqs.q: My pig recovered but is still lame. Will it get better?
faqs.a: Some lameness improves over weeks with rest, soft bedding and good feeding, but if the germ has damaged the joints badly, the stiffness may be permanent. Pigs with chronic erysipelas may also have damaged heart valves and can die suddenly. Ask your vet to examine the pig; if it is not growing or walking well, culling under the vet's advice may make more economic sense than keeping it.

faqs.q: Can my family catch this from our pigs?
faqs.a: Yes. People usually get a painful, purplish swelling on the hand or finger after the germ enters a cut while handling pigs, pork or manure. Wear gloves, cover cuts, wash hands with soap after work and cook pork well. Keep children away from sick pigs. Anyone with a spreading painful swelling on the hand after pig work should see a doctor and mention contact with pigs.

products.role: An oral rehydration and heat-stress relief solution that can be added to drinking water to help feverish pigs, which eat little and lose fluids, stay hydrated and keep drinking during recovery; it supports comfort alongside the vet's antibiotic treatment and does not treat the infection.
