card.headline: Yellow watery diarrhoea in young piglets
card.look: Piglets have wet, yellow, white or grey droppings smeared around the tail and back legs, and the pen floor is wet and smelly. Affected piglets look hollow-flanked, shiver, huddle together and may stop suckling.
card.action: Move the litter and sow to a clean, dry, warm pen, make sure every piglet can reach water and the sow's milk, and call your vet the same day.

detail.summary: Piglet scours is diarrhoea in suckling piglets, usually in the first three weeks of life. It is not one disease but a group of infections, mainly E. coli bacteria, clostridia bacteria, rotavirus and coccidia parasites, often made worse by cold, dirt and too little colostrum. Young piglets have very small body reserves, so they dehydrate and die quickly, sometimes within a day. It is one of the most common reasons smallholder pig farmers in Kenya lose whole litters.
detail.cause: Most scours starts when germs that live in the farm environment, in sow dung or on the sow's skin get into a piglet's gut before its defences are ready. Enterotoxigenic E. coli (a type of E. coli that makes toxins) sticks to the gut lining and releases poisons that pull water and salts out of the body into the gut, giving watery yellow diarrhoea, often in the first few days of life. Clostridium perfringens, especially type C, is a bacterium that damages and kills the gut lining, causing bloody diarrhoea and sudden death in the first week; type A causes milder, creamy diarrhoea. Rotavirus is a virus that destroys the tiny finger-like projections (villi) that absorb milk, so milk passes through undigested, usually in piglets from about one to five weeks old. Coccidia, mainly Cystoisospora suis, are tiny single-celled parasites that invade the gut wall, typically causing pasty to watery, yellow-grey, sour-smelling diarrhoea from around five to fifteen days of age. Often more than one of these causes is present at the same time. In every case the result is the same: the piglet loses water, salts and energy faster than it can replace them, its blood becomes thick and acidic, its body temperature drops, and without help it collapses and dies. Poor colostrum intake, chilling and a dirty farrowing pen are the biggest factors that turn a few germs into a serious outbreak.
spread: Piglets swallow germs from the sow's dung, teats and skin, and from dirty floors, bedding and walls in the farrowing pen.
Scouring piglets pass huge numbers of germs in their droppings, which quickly contaminate the whole pen and infect littermates.
Germs and coccidia eggs (oocysts) survive for a long time in cracked floors, wet bedding and dung left between litters, so the next litter is infected if the pen is not properly cleaned and dried.
Boots, hands, buckets, brooms and wheelbarrows carry dung from a sick pen to a clean one.
Bought-in pigs, especially gilts and sows from other farms, can bring new strains of E. coli or rotavirus onto your farm.
Chilling from cold floors, draughts or wet pens weakens piglets and slows their gut, making infection much more likely, especially on cold nights during the long and short rains.
Too little colostrum, from a sow with poor milk, mastitis, a very large litter or weak piglets that cannot compete for teats, leaves piglets without the antibodies they need.
Sudden changes such as moving the sow, mixing litters or feed changes in the sow can trigger outbreaks.
detail.atRisk: Piglets from birth to about three weeks of age are most at risk, with E. coli and clostridia striking mainly in the first week, coccidia from around the end of the first week to the third week, and rotavirus anywhere from one to several weeks, including around weaning. Litters from gilts (first-time mothers) suffer more because gilts have less experience of the farm's germs and so pass fewer protective antibodies in their colostrum. Small, weak or late-born piglets in large litters miss out on colostrum and are hit hardest. Risk is higher in cold, damp, draughty housing without a warm creep area, in pens with cracked concrete or earth floors that cannot be cleaned, and where farrowing pens are used back-to-back without cleaning and resting. Outbreaks are common during the long and short rains and on cold highland nights in places like Kiambu, Nyeri and Nakuru. Both zero-grazing style indoor pig units and backyard sties are affected; free-range piglets that wallow in muddy, dung-soaked ground are also at risk.

early: Wet, pasty or watery droppings, often yellow, creamy-white or grey, sticking to the tail and back legs.
A wet, shiny pen floor and a sour or unpleasant smell in the farrowing pen.
Piglets huddling together, lying on top of each other or under the heat lamp, and shivering.
Some piglets suckling less, or wandering away from the udder and standing with heads down.
Rough, dull hair coat and slightly sunken flanks.
Dung-stained, reddened skin around the anus and tail.
advanced: Very watery diarrhoea that may run straight through, sometimes with blood or a reddish-brown colour (a warning sign for clostridia).
Sunken eyes, wrinkled skin that stays tented when gently pinched, and a thin, bony appearance from dehydration.
Cold ears, legs and body to the touch, weakness and wobbling when walking.
Vomiting in some piglets, particularly with viral causes.
Piglets lying flat on their side, unable to stand or suckle, sometimes paddling their legs.
Sudden deaths, sometimes before diarrhoea is even seen, and several piglets in a litter dying over a few days.
Survivors that stay stunted, pot-bellied and slow-growing for weeks.

lookalikes.name: African swine fever (ASF)
lookalikes.howToTell: ASF can cause diarrhoea, often bloody, but pigs of all ages including sows and growers fall sick, with high fever, red or purple blotches on ears, belly and legs, loss of appetite and very high deaths across the herd. Scours usually affects only young piglets while the sow stays bright. ASF is notifiable in Kenya: if older pigs are sick or dying, stop all movement and report to your County Veterinary Officer immediately.

lookalikes.name: Transmissible gastroenteritis or porcine epidemic diarrhoea (viral)
lookalikes.howToTell: These viruses spread very fast through the whole farm, causing vomiting and watery diarrhoea in pigs of all ages, with very high deaths in piglets under a week old. Ordinary scours tends to affect individual litters. If many litters and older pigs develop diarrhoea and vomiting at once, call the vet urgently for laboratory testing.

lookalikes.name: Starvation and chilling (sow milk failure)
lookalikes.howToTell: When the sow has little milk, for example from mastitis, fever or poor feeding, piglets become thin, squeal, fight at the udder and get weak and cold, but droppings may be normal or scanty rather than watery. Check the sow's udder for hard, hot or swollen quarters and whether milk comes when you gently squeeze a teat.

lookalikes.name: Iron-deficiency anaemia
lookalikes.howToTell: Indoor piglets not given iron become pale (white ears and gums), breathe fast after exertion and grow poorly at around two to four weeks. They may have mild diarrhoea but the main sign is paleness. Anaemic piglets also catch scours more easily, so both can occur together; ask your vet about iron injections soon after birth.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will look at the age of the affected piglets, the colour and smell of the diarrhoea, how many litters are affected, whether the sows are sick, and your housing, cleaning and colostrum management. The age when scours starts is a very useful clue: first few days points to E. coli or clostridia, around one to two weeks points to coccidia, and later ages to rotavirus or E. coli. To confirm the cause, the vet may collect fresh droppings or rectal swabs from untreated piglets for laboratory testing, such as bacterial culture, antibiotic sensitivity testing, virus tests and examination for coccidia oocysts. A post-mortem of a freshly dead or a sick piglet chosen by the vet is often the most useful test, because the gut damage from clostridia, coccidia and viruses looks different, and samples can be sent to a county or national veterinary laboratory. Before the vet arrives, keep a freshly dead piglet cool (not frozen) in a sealed bag, avoid giving any medicines so tests are accurate, and write down the date each piglet fell sick, its age, the litter, sow parity (first litter or not), any deaths, and any treatments or vaccines already used.
firstSteps: Call your vet or County Veterinary Office the same day; piglets dehydrate within hours, so do not wait to see if it passes.

Keep the piglets warm: provide a dry, draught-free creep corner with clean dry bedding and a safe heat source such as a covered lamp or brooder, and check that piglets lie spread out comfortably rather than piled up.
Clean out wet bedding and dung at least twice a day, keep the floor as dry as possible and put down fresh dry bedding such as wood shavings or dry grass.
Make sure every piglet can suckle; help weak piglets onto a teat and check the sow is eating, drinking and has milk.
Offer clean, fresh drinking water and an oral rehydration solution in a clean, shallow drinker the piglets can reach, as advised by your vet, without stopping access to the sow's milk.
Keep the affected litter separate, and use a dedicated pair of boots, broom and bucket for that pen, or clean and disinfect them before going to other pigs.
Wash your hands with soap after handling sick piglets or their dung, and wear gloves if you can.
Record which piglets are sick, their ages, deaths and anything you have done, and do not give antibiotics or other drugs unless your vet prescribes them.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on the cause, so it must be prescribed by a vet. The most important part of treatment for every type of scours is replacing lost water, salts and energy, usually with oral rehydration solutions and keeping piglets warm; very weak piglets may need fluids given by the vet. For bacterial scours caused by E. coli or clostridia, the vet may prescribe an antibiotic, ideally chosen after a sensitivity test, because E. coli on many farms has become resistant to commonly used drugs. Classes sometimes used include penicillins such as amoxicillin, and other classes your vet judges suitable. For coccidiosis, antibiotics do not work; the vet may prescribe an anticoccidial drug such as toltrazuril, which works best when given to piglets early, before signs appear, in litters at risk. Rotavirus and other viruses cannot be cured by antibiotics; treatment is supportive with fluids, warmth and hygiene, though the vet may sometimes treat secondary bacterial infections. The whole litter is often treated, not just the sick piglets, because littermates are usually already infected. Follow the vet's instructions exactly, finish the full course and never share leftover drugs between farms; using antibiotics carelessly breeds resistant germs that will make future outbreaks harder to control. Every drug has a meat withdrawal period, the time that must pass before the pig can be slaughtered for food; ask your vet and follow the label. Most piglets that are treated early improve within a few days, but badly dehydrated ones may still die.
prevention: Colostrum first: make sure every piglet suckles within the first few hours of birth, because piglets can only absorb protective antibodies from colostrum well during the first day; split-suckle large litters by closing the first-born, stronger piglets in a warm box for an hour or two so weaker ones can feed.
Warmth: give piglets a dry, draught-free creep area with bedding and a safe heat source, since newborn piglets need much more warmth than the sow, especially at night and during the rains.

All-in, all-out farrowing hygiene: before each sow farrows, remove all dung and bedding, scrub the pen with water and detergent, apply a disinfectant recommended by your vet or agrovet, and leave the pen empty and dry for several days.
Wash the sow, especially her udder, belly and legs, with warm water and mild soap before she enters the clean farrowing pen, and treat her for worms and mange as advised by your vet.

Vaccinate sows and gilts before farrowing against E. coli and Clostridium perfringens where vaccines are available; this protects piglets through colostrum, so ask your vet what is available in your area and the right timing.

Feed the pregnant and nursing sow a balanced diet with enough energy, protein, minerals and clean water so she produces plenty of good-quality milk, and avoid mouldy feed, which can reduce milk and weaken immunity.
Repair cracked floors and use concrete or slatted floors that can be cleaned; avoid earth floors in farrowing pens where possible.

Give piglets iron as recommended by your vet, ask about preventive anticoccidial treatment if coccidiosis has been confirmed on your farm, and quarantine bought-in pigs for at least two to three weeks before mixing them with your herd.
detail.impact: Scours costs Kenyan pig farmers money in several ways. The most obvious loss is dead piglets: a sow that farrowed ten piglets but weans only five has eaten the same feed for nearly four months for half the income. Survivors often stay stunted, take longer to reach market weight and eat more feed per kilo of gain, cutting profit when they are sold as weaners or porkers. There are also costs for vet visits, drugs, extra labour and bedding. On farms where scours keeps returning, farmers lose trust in their breeding sows and may cull good animals. Because many smallholders rely on selling weaners to raise school fees or other household needs, losing a litter can be a serious blow.
detail.humanHealth: Most germs that cause piglet scours mainly affect pigs, but some types of E. coli, Clostridium, rotavirus and other gut germs such as Cryptosporidium and Salmonella found in pig dung can make people sick, especially children, older people and anyone with a weak immune system. Wash hands with soap and clean water after handling piglets, dung or bedding, keep children from playing in pig pens, and do not eat, drink or smoke while working with sick pigs. Keep pig dung away from household water sources and vegetable gardens unless it has been properly composted. If piglets or pigs have been treated with antibiotics or other drugs, do not slaughter them for meat until the withdrawal period given by your vet has passed, because drug residues in pork can harm people and add to antimicrobial resistance.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends on how early the problem is spotted, the cause, the age of the piglets and how dehydrated they are. Piglets that are caught early, kept warm and given fluids and the right vet treatment usually recover within a few days, although some may grow more slowly afterwards. Very young piglets, especially those under a week old, and those with clostridial or bloody diarrhoea, can die quickly even with treatment. Piglets already lying flat, cold and unable to suckle have a poor chance. On a farm level, outbreaks usually stop returning once colostrum, warmth, hygiene and sow vaccination are put right, but if the pens stay dirty and cold the problem will come back with the next litters.

faqs.q: My piglets have yellow scours but they still suckle. Should I still call the vet?
faqs.a: Yes. Piglets can go from mild diarrhoea to dangerous dehydration within a day, and the whole litter is often infected even if only a few show signs. Your vet can help find the cause and stop it spreading to other litters. Meanwhile keep them warm, dry and suckling, and provide clean water and rehydration solution.

faqs.q: Can I just buy an antibiotic from the agrovet and treat the piglets myself?
faqs.a: It is better not to. Antibiotics do nothing against rotavirus or coccidia, two very common causes of scours, and the wrong antibiotic or the wrong amount can fail, waste money and breed resistant germs. Some drugs are also unsafe for very young piglets. Let your vet decide the cause and prescribe the right treatment, and always respect the meat withdrawal period.

faqs.q: Why do my gilts' litters get scours more than my older sows' litters?
faqs.a: Gilts have not yet been exposed to all the germs on your farm, so their colostrum contains fewer protective antibodies. Their milk supply may also be lower. Bring gilts onto the farm well before breeding so they adapt, ask your vet about vaccinating them before farrowing, and pay extra attention to colostrum intake, warmth and hygiene for their litters.

faqs.q: Should I stop the piglets from suckling while they have diarrhoea?
faqs.a: No. The sow's milk gives piglets energy, water and antibodies that help them fight infection. Keep them suckling and offer an oral rehydration solution and clean water alongside the milk. Only your vet should advise any change in feeding.

faqs.q: How warm should the piglets be?
faqs.a: Newborn piglets need a much warmer spot than the sow, especially in the first week. A good guide is their behaviour: if they pile on top of each other or shiver, they are too cold; if they lie spread out and away from the heat, they are too hot; if they lie side by side comfortably, the temperature is right. Block draughts, use dry bedding and a safely covered heat lamp or brooder in the creep corner.

faqs.q: I cleaned the pen with water but scours came back. What am I missing?
faqs.a: Water alone does not kill germs or coccidia eggs. Remove all dung and bedding, scrub with detergent, rinse, then apply a disinfectant suitable for pig houses and let the pen dry completely and rest empty for several days before the next sow moves in. Coccidia eggs are very tough, so drying and resting matter a lot. Also check that boots, brooms and buckets are not carrying dung from other pens.

products.role: An oral rehydration solution that helps replace the water and salts piglets lose through diarrhoea; offer it in clean, shallow drinkers alongside the sow's milk and the treatment your vet prescribes, to support hydration while the cause is being dealt with. It does not kill the germs causing scours.

A breeding sow supplement that supports lactation, helping the sow produce good milk for her piglets as part of a balanced diet; good milk and colostrum supply is one of the foundations of scours prevention, alongside sow vaccination, warmth and farrowing hygiene.

card.headline: Dry cough when pigs get up
card.look: Growing pigs give a dry, hacking cough, especially when they first stand up or are moved. Some pigs breathe with a heaving, thumping movement of the belly and flanks, eat less and grow slower than their penmates.
card.action: Separate the coughing pigs into a clean, dry, draught-free but well-aired pen and call your vet to examine them before any treatment is given.

aka: Homa ya mapafu / nimonia ya nguruwe (Swahili)
detail.summary: Pneumonia means infection and swelling of the lungs. In pigs it is most often caused by a germ called Mycoplasma hyopneumoniae (enzootic pneumonia), which is then made worse by a second bacterium, Pasteurella multocida (pasteurellosis). It is one of the most common and costly diseases in growing pigs worldwide, including in Kenya. Few pigs die from mild enzootic pneumonia alone, but pigs that cough grow slowly, eat more feed per kilo gained and take longer to reach market weight, and the disease can turn severe and deadly when other germs, poor air or stress join in.
detail.cause: Enzootic pneumonia starts with Mycoplasma hyopneumoniae, a very small bacterium without a normal cell wall. It sticks to the tiny hairs (cilia) that line the windpipe and airways. These hairs normally sweep dust and germs up and out of the lungs like a broom. When the mycoplasma damages them, dust, ammonia and other germs reach deep into the lungs. The pig's lungs become swollen and firm, usually in the front and lower parts, and the pig coughs to try to clear them. On its own, this causes a long-lasting dry cough and slower growth. The real damage often comes when a second bacterium, most commonly Pasteurella multocida, takes advantage of the weakened lungs. Pasteurella causes a more serious bacterial pneumonia with fever, pus in the airways, heavy breathing and sometimes death. Other germs such as Actinobacillus, Streptococcus, Glaesserella (Haemophilus) and viruses like swine influenza can join in too, which is why vets talk of a 'respiratory disease complex'. Poor air is a big part of the cause: high ammonia from dung and urine, dust from dry feed, overcrowding, and sudden temperature changes all irritate the lungs and lower the pig's defences.
spread: The mycoplasma spreads mainly by close nose-to-nose contact and by droplets coughed into the air between pigs sharing the same airspace.
Sows that carry the germ can pass it to their piglets during suckling, so piglets may be infected early but often only start coughing weeks later, after weaning or when mixed.
Buying in pigs from other farms or markets is a very common way to bring the disease onto a clean farm, because carrier pigs can look healthy.
Mixing litters or pigs of different ages in one pen or one house allows older carrier pigs to infect younger ones.
Crowded, poorly ventilated houses with strong ammonia smell, dust and damp bedding greatly increase spread and make disease more severe.
Pasteurella multocida lives in the nose and throat of many healthy pigs and causes disease when stress, poor air or mycoplasma damage give it the chance.
Triggers that often set off an outbreak include weaning, moving and mixing, transport, cold nights and draughts, sudden weather changes at the start of the rains, and heat stress in the dry season.
Wild birds, rodents and other animals are not major spreaders of enzootic pneumonia, but people, vehicles and equipment moving between pig farms can carry germs and should be controlled.
detail.atRisk: Growing and finishing pigs, roughly from weaning to market age, are most affected, with coughing often seen from about two to six months of age. Weaners that have just been mixed or moved are especially at risk. Sows usually show few signs but can carry and pass on the germ. All breeds can be affected, including exotic Large White and Landrace crosses and local pigs. Risk is highest in closed, crowded houses with poor airflow, damp floors and strong ammonia, and in farms that keep pigs of many ages together or keep buying pigs from different sources and markets. In Kenya, outbreaks often worsen during the cold, wet months of the long and short rains when farmers close up houses and air goes stale, and during cold highland nights. Free-range and tethered pigs have fresher air but may also face lungworm and roundworm problems that damage the lungs and make pneumonia worse.

early: A dry, non-productive cough, often heard when pigs first get up in the morning, after feeding or when they are chased or moved.
Coughing in several pigs in the same pen or house rather than just one animal.
Some pigs looking slightly rough-coated and growing slower than their littermates, giving an uneven pen of big and small pigs.
Pigs still eating and generally alert, with normal temperature, in mild enzootic pneumonia.
Slightly faster breathing at rest, which you can count by watching the flank for one minute while the pig lies quietly.
Feed intake dropping a little and pigs taking longer to finish their ration.
advanced: Heavy, laboured breathing with a strong pumping or 'thumping' movement of the belly and flanks, sometimes with open-mouth breathing.
Fever: pigs feel hot behind the ears, lie huddled together, and may be dull and slow to get up.
Loss of appetite, weight loss and a hollow, tucked-up belly.
A wetter, more frequent cough and sometimes discharge from the nose.
Bluish or purplish tinge to the ears, snout or belly in pigs struggling to get enough oxygen.
Pigs sitting like a dog or standing with the head stretched forward to ease breathing.
Some pigs becoming permanently stunted ('runts'), and occasional deaths, especially when Pasteurella or other germs are involved.

lookalikes.name: African swine fever (ASF)
lookalikes.howToTell: ASF is a deadly viral disease present in Kenya and is notifiable. It can cause breathing difficulty, but pigs usually also have high fever, reddish-purple skin on the ears, belly and legs, refuse feed, may have bloody diarrhoea or vomiting, and many pigs of all ages die quickly within days. If you see sudden deaths, red or purple skin and high fever, stop all pig movement and report immediately to your County Veterinary Officer.

lookalikes.name: Actinobacillus pleuropneumonia (APP)
lookalikes.howToTell: This bacterial pneumonia is much more sudden and severe. Pigs may be found dead, or have very high fever, severe open-mouth breathing and blood-stained froth at the nose and mouth. Enzootic pneumonia is usually slow, with a lasting dry cough and few deaths.

lookalikes.name: Lungworm and roundworm migration
lookalikes.howToTell: Lungworms (Metastrongylus), picked up from eating earthworms, and young roundworms (Ascaris) travelling through the lungs cause coughing mainly in young pigs with access to soil or dirty pens. There may be pot-bellied, poorly growing pigs and worms in dung. Your vet can check dung samples and at slaughter may find worms in the airways or white 'milk spots' on the liver.

lookalikes.name: Swine influenza
lookalikes.howToTell: Flu spreads very fast, so most pigs in a house start coughing and have fever within a few days, then most recover within about a week. Enzootic pneumonia spreads more slowly and the cough lasts for weeks.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will look at the whole group, listen to the coughing, count breathing rates, take temperatures and listen to the chest. The pattern of a dry cough in growing pigs, slow spread and uneven growth strongly suggests enzootic pneumonia, but other diseases must be ruled out, especially African swine fever. The most useful evidence often comes from post-mortem examination of a pig that has died or been culled, or from checking lungs at the slaughter slab: enzootic pneumonia leaves typical purple to grey, firm areas in the front and lower parts of the lungs. Laboratory tests can confirm the germs: swabs or lung samples can be tested (for example by PCR, a test that detects the germ's genetic material), and bacteria such as Pasteurella can be grown and tested to see which antibiotics will work. Blood tests can show whether a herd has been exposed. To help your vet, write down when coughing started, how many pigs are affected, their ages, any deaths, feed and water intake, recent purchases, mixing or moves, and any treatments already given. Keep a fresh carcass cool (not frozen) for post-mortem, and ask the slaughterhouse to tell you about lung damage in your pigs.
firstSteps: Separate coughing or heavy-breathing pigs into a clean, dry pen with good fresh air but no cold draughts at pig level, and handle them gently and slowly because chasing makes breathing worse.
Make sure all pigs have constant access to clean, fresh water, as feverish pigs drink more and may stop eating first.
Improve air in the house straight away: open vents or curtains on the side away from the wind, remove wet dung and soiled bedding to cut ammonia, and dampen very dusty feed or floors lightly.
Reduce crowding if you can by moving some pigs out, and give sick pigs dry bedding such as wood shavings or straw so they can rest warmly at night.
Offer fresh, palatable feed in small amounts and check feed for mould, throwing away any that smells musty or looks caked.
Record which pigs are affected, their temperatures if you have a thermometer, appetite and breathing, and note any deaths.
Stop buying in, selling or moving pigs until a vet has examined the herd, especially if any pigs have high fever, red or purple skin or have died suddenly, as this could be African swine fever.
Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer, and do not give antibiotics or other drugs left over from earlier or bought without a prescription.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on which germs are involved and how sick the pigs are, and must be prescribed by a vet. Because Mycoplasma has no normal cell wall, some common antibiotics such as penicillin do not work against it. Vets commonly choose from drug groups such as tetracyclines (for example oxytetracycline), macrolides (such as tylosin, tilmicosin or tulathromycin), pleuromutilins (such as tiamulin) or lincosamides, while Pasteurella infections are often treated with drugs such as tetracyclines, florfenicol, penicillin or ceftiofur depending on laboratory results. Very sick pigs are usually given individual injections, while the rest of the group may be treated through water or feed under veterinary direction. Anti-inflammatory drugs may be used to bring down fever and help pigs eat again. Antibiotics help control the bacteria and reduce suffering, but they do not remove enzootic pneumonia from a herd, and damaged lungs heal slowly, so coughing may continue for some time. Treatment works best when combined with better ventilation, less crowding and less mixing. Every antibiotic has a meat withdrawal period, the time you must wait after the last dose before a pig can be slaughtered for food; follow it strictly and record treatment dates. Use antibiotics only when prescribed, complete the full course and avoid routine in-feed use without a vet's advice, because overuse breeds antibiotic-resistant germs that harm both animal and human health.
prevention: Ventilation is the single most important control: design or adapt houses so stale air and ammonia can escape, for example with adjustable side curtains, open ridges or eaves, while keeping cold draughts off pigs at floor level.
Avoid overcrowding by giving each growing pig enough floor and lying space, and plan pen numbers so you are not forced to squeeze pigs together as they grow.
Practise all-in, all-out management where possible: fill a pen or house with pigs of the same age, empty it completely when they leave, then clean, disinfect and let it dry before the next batch.
Do not mix pigs of different ages or from different litters more than necessary, and keep weaners away from older coughing pigs.

Buy replacement pigs only from known, healthy farms with no history of coughing, never from mixed markets if you can avoid it, and keep new pigs isolated for at least three to four weeks before joining the herd.

Ask your vet whether Mycoplasma hyopneumoniae vaccine is available and worthwhile for your farm; vaccines are widely used in commercial herds elsewhere and reduce lung damage, though they do not fully stop infection and availability in Kenya varies.
Keep floors dry and clean, remove dung daily, use dry bedding, and keep feed dust down to protect the airways.
Control worms with a deworming plan from your vet, especially for free-range or soil-kept pigs, as roundworms and lungworms damage the lungs.
Feed a balanced ration with adequate protein, vitamins and minerals, and keep feed dry and free of mould, because mycotoxins (poisons from moulds) weaken the immune system.

Reduce stress at weaning and transport, protect pigs from cold nights in the rains and from heat in the dry season, and keep strict farm biosecurity, including limiting visitors and cleaning boots and equipment.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan pig farm, pneumonia mostly costs money through slow growth rather than deaths. Coughing pigs eat feed but turn less of it into meat, so they take longer to reach market weight and each kilo of pork costs more to produce. Pens become uneven, with runts that must be kept longer or sold cheaply. Treatment, vet visits and labour add to costs, and severe outbreaks with Pasteurella or other germs can cause deaths and condemned lungs at slaughter. Because feed is the biggest cost in pig keeping, even a small drop in growth across a whole batch can wipe out much of the profit. Herds with ongoing pneumonia may also struggle to sell breeding stock to other farmers.
detail.humanHealth: Mycoplasma hyopneumoniae, the main cause of enzootic pneumonia, does not infect people. Pasteurella multocida can occasionally infect people, mostly through pig bites, scratches or cuts, so wash and disinfect any wounds and see a health worker if a wound becomes red, swollen or painful. The dust and ammonia that make pig pneumonia worse also irritate farmers' own lungs, so improve ventilation and consider a dust mask when cleaning. Antibiotics used to treat pigs can leave residues in meat, so always respect the withdrawal period before slaughter or sale, and never sell or eat pork from pigs still under treatment.
detail.outlook: Most pigs with mild enzootic pneumonia recover enough to keep eating and growing, although they often grow more slowly and some lung scarring remains. Pigs with severe secondary infection, high fever and laboured breathing have a more guarded outlook; quick vet treatment improves their chances, but some may die or stay stunted. The disease tends to stay in a herd once present, flaring up with poor air, crowding and stress, so long-term success depends far more on ventilation, stocking, all-in all-out management and careful buying than on medicines alone. Herds that improve their housing and management usually see far less coughing and better growth.

faqs.q: My pigs cough a little every morning but still eat well. Should I worry?
faqs.a: A morning cough in several growing pigs is a classic early sign of enzootic pneumonia. They may seem fine, but they are probably growing slower than they should. Ask your vet to check the herd, and start improving ventilation, cleaning out ammonia and reducing crowding now. Early action is cheaper than treating a severe outbreak later.

faqs.q: Can I just buy an antibiotic from the agrovet and put it in the water?
faqs.a: It is not safe to treat without a vet. Some common antibiotics, such as penicillin, do not work against Mycoplasma at all, and the wrong drug or wrong amount wastes money, leaves residues in meat and breeds resistant germs. A vet can identify what is causing the problem, choose an effective drug and tell you the correct withdrawal period before slaughter.

faqs.q: Should I close the pig house completely to keep my sick pigs warm during the rains?
faqs.a: No. Closing the house traps ammonia, dust and germs, which makes pneumonia worse. Pigs need fresh air moving above them, but no cold draughts at floor level. Keep them warm with dry bedding, a solid lower wall or boards to block wind at pig height, and openings higher up for stale air to escape.

faqs.q: Will the cough go away once I treat my pigs?
faqs.a: Treatment usually reduces fever and heavy breathing and helps pigs eat again, but the dry cough can continue for weeks because damaged airways heal slowly. Antibiotics also do not remove the mycoplasma from the herd, so coughing may return with new batches unless you fix ventilation, crowding and mixing.

faqs.q: How can I tell pneumonia from African swine fever?
faqs.a: Pneumonia usually spreads slowly, causes coughing and slow growth, and few pigs die. African swine fever often causes high fever, red or purple skin, pigs refusing feed and many sudden deaths across ages within days. If you see these signs, stop all pig movement, do not sell or slaughter pigs, and report immediately to your County Veterinary Officer.

faqs.q: Is pork from a pig that had pneumonia safe to eat?
faqs.a: Pork from a pig that has recovered and has completed the full withdrawal period after any treatment is generally considered safe after normal meat inspection. Badly affected lungs are usually condemned at slaughter. Never slaughter or sell a pig that is sick, feverish or still within its drug withdrawal period.

products.role: An oral rehydration and heat-stress relief solution that can be offered in drinking water to help feverish, off-feed pigs stay hydrated and cope with hot weather while they recover under vet treatment; it supports comfort and fluid intake but does not treat the lung infection.

A mycotoxin binder added to feed to reduce the effect of aflatoxin and ochratoxin from mouldy feed, which can weaken pigs' immunity; it supports good feed safety as part of prevention alongside ventilation, good stocking and vet advice, and is not a treatment for pneumonia.

card.headline: Pale, slow-growing piglets that pant easily
card.look: Piglets around 2–4 weeks old look pale white or yellowish instead of pink, with rough hair and wrinkled skin. They tire quickly, breathe in jerky gasps after running or suckling, and often have scours.
card.action: Call your vet or animal health assistant to examine the litter, and keep the piglets warm, calm and suckling until help arrives.

aka: Upungufu wa damu kwa nguruwe wachanga
detail.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia is a shortage of red blood cells in young piglets because they do not get enough iron in the first weeks of life. Piglets are born with only small iron stores, and sow milk contains very little iron, so without extra iron most fast-growing piglets become anaemic within two to three weeks. Anaemic piglets grow slowly, catch scours and pneumonia easily, and some die suddenly. It is one of the most common and most preventable problems in piglets kept indoors on concrete floors, which is how most Kenyan piggeries are built.
detail.cause: Iron is the mineral the body uses to make haemoglobin, the red substance inside red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to every part of the body. A newborn piglet has only a small store of iron in its liver. It then grows extremely fast, often doubling its birth weight within the first week, and every gram of new body needs more blood. Sow milk is rich in energy and protein but naturally very low in iron, and feeding the sow more iron does not meaningfully raise the iron in her milk. In the wild, or on free range, piglets top up their iron by rooting in soil. On a clean concrete floor there is no soil, so the small birth store runs out quickly. When iron runs short, the piglet cannot make enough haemoglobin, its red blood cells become fewer and paler, and its body receives less oxygen. The heart works harder to pump the thin blood, breathing becomes fast and laboured after any effort, growth slows, and the immune system weakens. This is why anaemic piglets so often pick up scours, joint infections and pneumonia. In severe cases the heart is overworked, fluid builds up in the body, and the piglet can collapse and die, sometimes the strongest, fastest-growing one in the litter.
spread: It is not infectious and does not pass from pig to pig; it is a nutritional shortage caused by how piglets are raised.
The main trigger is not giving piglets an iron injection or other reliable iron source in the first few days of life.
Housing on concrete or raised slatted floors with no access to soil removes the piglet's natural way of picking up iron.
Large litters and fast-growing improved breeds use up their iron stores faster, so they show signs sooner.
Delaying creep feed (the early starter feed offered to piglets while still suckling) or using a creep feed low in iron keeps piglets dependent on milk for too long.
Injecting iron too late, giving a poor-quality or expired product, or injecting into fat instead of muscle means the piglet does not absorb enough.
Blood loss from lice, mange or rough handling, and diarrhoea that damages the gut, can make an existing shortage worse.
detail.atRisk: Piglets between about one and four weeks of age are most at risk, with signs usually showing from the second or third week. Fast-growing improved breeds such as Large White, Landrace and their crosses are affected more than slower-growing local pigs, and the biggest, quickest-growing piglets in a litter can be hit hardest. Piglets in zero-grazing style indoor pens with concrete floors, which is the common system in Kenyan smallholder and commercial piggeries, are at much higher risk than piglets raised outdoors on soil. Litters born to young gilts, very large litters, and piglets that are weaned late without good creep feed are also at higher risk. The problem happens in any season, but cold, wet weather during the long and short rains adds stress and makes scours and pneumonia in anaemic piglets more common.

early: Skin and ears look pale white or slightly yellow instead of a healthy pink; this is easiest to see on white breeds.
The inside of the eyelids and the gums look pale pink or almost white when you gently open them.
Piglets grow more slowly than expected and look smaller or thinner than litter-mates that are doing well.
The hair coat becomes rough and dull, and the skin may look wrinkled.
Piglets tire quickly, lie down more and are slower to come to the teat.
Breathing becomes fast or jerky after short bursts of activity such as suckling or running, then settles when they rest.
advanced: Marked laboured breathing with a jerky, thumping movement of the flanks, which is why the condition is called 'thumps'.
Scours (diarrhoea), often yellowish or pasty, that keeps coming back or does not respond well to treatment.
Swelling around the head, neck or belly caused by fluid building up under the skin.
Weakness, staggering or collapse, especially after being chased or handled.
Frequent secondary infections such as swollen joints, coughing or pneumonia.
Sudden death of a piglet that seemed to be growing well, often one of the heaviest in the litter.
Survivors that stay stunted and never catch up with healthy pigs of the same age.

lookalikes.name: Piglet scours from E. coli or coccidiosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Infectious scours can appear in piglets that are pink and well coloured, and E. coli scours often starts in the first days of life before anaemia normally develops. Anaemic piglets are pale first, and the scours comes alongside slow growth and jerky breathing. Both can happen together, so a vet may need to check dung samples and blood.

lookalikes.name: Pneumonia
lookalikes.howToTell: Pneumonia usually brings coughing, sneezing, fever and breathing that is hard even at rest. The jerky breathing of anaemia mostly appears after exertion and settles with rest, and the piglet is pale rather than feverish.

lookalikes.name: Vitamin E and selenium deficiency (mulberry heart disease, white muscle disease)
lookalikes.howToTell: This can also cause sudden deaths and weakness in fast-growing piglets, but the skin is not necessarily pale, and some piglets show stiffness or trembling. It matters because piglets low in vitamin E and selenium can react badly or even die after an iron injection, so the vet may check for both.

lookalikes.name: African swine fever
lookalikes.howToTell: African swine fever affects pigs of all ages at once, causes high fever, red or purple blotches on the ears and belly, loss of appetite and many rapid deaths across the farm. Anaemia affects only young piglets, does not cause fever or skin blotches, and does not spread to older pigs. If you see fever and deaths in older pigs, call the County Veterinary Officer immediately, because African swine fever is notifiable.

detail.diagnosis: A vet or animal health assistant usually suspects iron deficiency from the age of the piglets, the pale skin and eyelids, the jerky breathing and, most importantly, the farm history of whether and when the piglets received iron. A simple blood test can measure haemoglobin or packed cell volume (the proportion of blood made up of red cells), which confirms anaemia and shows how severe it is; some vets carry a quick handheld haemoglobin meter. If a piglet has died, a post-mortem examination typically shows very pale tissues, thin watery blood, an enlarged soft heart, fluid in the chest and belly, and a pale or swollen liver. The vet will also look for secondary problems such as scours or pneumonia and may check the sow and diet for vitamin E and selenium shortage. To help, prepare the farrowing date, litter size, birth and current weights if you have them, the name and date of any iron product given and where it was injected, any treatments already given, and the number of piglets sick or dead.
firstSteps: Look at every piglet in the litter and in other litters of a similar age, check skin and eyelid colour, and write down which piglets are pale, scouring, breathing badly or have died.
Keep the piglets with the sow so they continue to suckle; milk is still their main food and source of energy even though it is low in iron.
Keep the creep area warm, dry and draught-free using a heat lamp, a covered corner or dry bedding, because anaemic piglets chill easily and cold makes scours and pneumonia worse.
Handle the piglets as little and as gently as possible, and avoid chasing them, because exertion can make an anaemic piglet collapse.
Make sure clean drinking water is available in a shallow container they can reach, and offer a fresh, good-quality creep feed if they are old enough to start nibbling.
If piglets have scours, clean the pen often, keep bedding dry and ask your vet about oral rehydration to replace lost fluids.
Do not give iron injections, antibiotics or other drugs to sick piglets on your own; let the vet examine them first, because some sick piglets react badly to iron and the dose must be right.
Wash your hands and boots after handling scouring piglets to avoid carrying germs to other litters, and call your vet or animal health assistant as soon as possible.
detail.vetTreatment: The main treatment is replacing the missing iron, usually with an injectable iron product such as iron dextran or gleptoferron given into the neck muscle; in some cases oral iron is used instead. The vet decides the product, the amount, the route and whether a repeat dose is needed based on the piglet's age, weight and condition, so this must be prescribed and given or supervised by a vet. Very weak piglets may first need warmth, fluids and supportive care, and the vet may check or treat for vitamin E and selenium shortage, because iron given to deficient piglets can cause severe reactions. Secondary infections such as bacterial scours, joint infection or pneumonia may need antibiotics, which only work against bacteria and do nothing for the anaemia itself. Use antibiotics only when a vet prescribes them, finish the full course, and never use them as a routine substitute for iron and good management, because overuse breeds resistant germs (antimicrobial resistance) that make future treatment harder for pigs and people. Any drug used carries a meat withdrawal period, the time after treatment before the pig can be slaughtered for food, so record the product and date and follow the label and vet advice. Most piglets improve in colour, energy and appetite within days of iron treatment, though catching up on lost growth takes longer.
prevention: Give every piglet a reliable iron source in the first days of life; an iron injection into the neck muscle around day 1 to day 3 is the standard method, so plan this with your vet or a trained animal health assistant who can show you the correct technique.
Inject into the neck muscle behind the ear rather than the ham, using a clean, sharp needle for each litter, so the iron is absorbed well and the valuable ham meat is not damaged or stained.
Buy iron products only from licensed agrovets, check the expiry date, store them as the label says, and record the date and product used for every litter.
Ask your vet whether a second iron dose is needed for very fast-growing piglets, large litters or piglets that will be weaned late.
Offer a good-quality creep feed from about the first or second week so piglets start eating solid feed that supplies iron and other nutrients before milk alone becomes too little.

Feed the sow a balanced diet with proper vitamins and minerals, especially vitamin E and selenium, during pregnancy and lactation, so piglets are born strong and are less likely to react badly to iron.

Some farmers give piglets a tray of clean soil; only use soil from a place where pigs have never been kept, because soil from pig areas can carry worms and germs, and do not rely on soil as the only iron source.
Control lice and mange on the sow, keep farrowing pens clean and dry, and prevent scours, because blood loss and damaged guts make anaemia worse.
detail.impact: Iron deficiency anaemia quietly eats into piggery profits. Anaemic piglets grow slowly, so weaners are lighter at sale or take longer to reach market weight, which means more feed and labour per pig. More piglets die before weaning, and every lost piglet is lost income from a sow you have already fed for months. The weak immunity of anaemic piglets leads to more scours and pneumonia, which means extra vet visits and drug costs and the risk of meat withdrawal delays. Stunted survivors may never reach their genetic potential, making the whole batch uneven and harder to sell at a good price. Because prevention is simple and inexpensive compared to these losses, routine iron for every litter is one of the best-value practices on a Kenyan pig farm.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good when anaemia is spotted early and the vet treats it promptly; most piglets regain their pink colour and energy within days and start growing again. Recovery is slower and less certain when the anaemia is severe, when piglets already have serious scours or pneumonia, or when they are also short of vitamin E and selenium. Some badly affected piglets die despite treatment, and some survivors stay smaller than their litter-mates. Litters that get iron on time rarely develop the problem at all.

faqs.q: Why can't the sow's milk give the piglets enough iron? Can I feed the sow more iron instead?
faqs.a: Sow milk is naturally very low in iron, and giving the sow extra iron in her feed does not raise the iron in her milk enough to protect fast-growing piglets. Iron also does not pass well from the sow to the unborn piglets. That is why the piglets themselves need their own iron source in the first days of life. Feeding the sow well still matters, because it produces strong piglets and plenty of milk, but it cannot replace iron for the piglets.

faqs.q: My piglets are kept outside and root in the soil. Do they still need iron?
faqs.a: Piglets that root freely in clean soil from early in life pick up some iron naturally, so anaemia is less common in outdoor and free-range systems. However, improved breeds grow so fast that soil alone may not be enough, and piglets in the first days often stay close to the sow before they start rooting. Ask your vet whether your system needs routine iron. For most farms with improved breeds, giving iron is the safer choice.

faqs.q: I heard some piglets died after the iron injection. Why does that happen?
faqs.a: Deaths after iron injection are uncommon but do happen. The most common reason is that the piglets were short of vitamin E and selenium, which protect the body from damage when iron is given. Other causes are giving the wrong amount, using a poor or expired product, or injecting very weak or sick piglets. This is why the sow's diet should contain enough vitamin E and selenium, and why iron should be given correctly under guidance from a vet or trained animal health assistant.

faqs.q: Which day is best to give the iron, and where do I inject it?
faqs.a: Iron is usually given within the first three days of life, often around day 3 once the piglet has suckled well and is settled. It is normally injected deep into the muscle of the neck, just behind the ear, not into the ham. Your vet or animal health assistant can show you the right product, amount and technique, and you should record the date for every litter.

faqs.q: Can I use iron by mouth instead of an injection?
faqs.a: Oral iron pastes and drenches exist and are used on some farms, but how much the piglet absorbs can vary, and it must be given at the right time to work. Injection is the most widely used and reliable method. If you prefer oral iron, discuss it with your vet so the product and timing suit your piglets.

faqs.q: My piglets are pale and scouring. Will antibiotics fix it?
faqs.a: Antibiotics do not cure anaemia; they only help if a bacterial infection is also present, and only a vet should decide that. The pale skin and jerky breathing come from lack of iron, which needs iron treatment. Giving antibiotics without a vet wastes money, can leave drug residues in meat, and helps germs become resistant. Call your vet so the cause of the scours and the anaemia can both be treated properly.

products.role: An oral rehydration solution that can help replace fluids and salts lost when anaemic piglets also have scours, used alongside the vet's iron treatment and good warmth and hygiene. It does not supply iron and does not treat the anaemia itself.

card.headline: Constant rubbing and crusty ears
card.look: The pig scratches and rubs against walls, posts and feeders almost non-stop, and the skin inside the ears shows grey-brown crusts. In long-standing cases the skin on the neck, shoulders and flanks becomes thick, wrinkled and hairless.
card.action: Separate the itchiest pigs, stop moving pigs in or out, and ask your vet to confirm mange and plan treatment for the whole herd at once.

aka: Upele (Swahili, general word for itchy skin disease)
detail.summary: Mange is an itchy skin disease caused by a tiny mite that burrows into the pig's skin. It rarely kills pigs, but it makes them restless, slows their growth, wastes feed and damages the skin. Once it is in a herd it tends to stay for years, passing from sows to every new litter, unless the whole herd is treated in a planned way. The good news is that it can be controlled, and on many farms fully removed.
detail.cause: Mange in pigs is caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. suis. A mite is a very small relative of ticks and spiders, too small to see clearly without a microscope. The female mite digs tunnels in the top layer of the skin, lays her eggs there, and the young mites hatch and mature in about two weeks, so numbers build quickly. The digging, the mites' droppings and their saliva irritate the skin and, after a few weeks, the pig's immune system reacts strongly against them. This reaction is an allergy (hypersensitivity), and it causes the intense itch and the small red pimples seen especially on the belly, flanks and back. The pig scratches and rubs, breaking the skin and letting germs in. In some pigs, usually older sows and boars, the skin reacts by becoming very thick, grey, wrinkled and crusty, especially inside the ears and around the head and neck. These chronic carriers may not even itch much, but they are full of mites and keep infecting other pigs. Energy that should go into growth and milk is spent on scratching and fighting the skin damage, which is why mangy pigs grow slowly.
spread: Direct skin-to-skin contact between pigs is the main route, especially when pigs sleep packed together in a pen.
Sows with crusty ears pass mites to their piglets while suckling and sleeping together, so the disease carries on from litter to litter.
Boars that move between farms for service, or between sows on one farm, can spread mites widely because they are often heavily infested.
Buying in pigs from markets or other farms without checking or treating them is a common way mange first enters a clean herd.
Mites can survive off the pig for a short time, usually a few days and longer in cool, damp conditions, so dirty bedding, rubbing posts, walls and transport crates can pass them on.
Crowding, poor hygiene, poor nutrition and stress make it easier for mite numbers to rise and spread.
detail.atRisk: Any pig can get mange, but it shows most clearly in weaners and growing pigs from about two months of age, which develop the itchy allergic rash. Adult sows and boars are the main hidden carriers, often with thick crusts inside the ears. Herds that share boars, buy pigs from markets, or mix pigs from different sources are at higher risk. In Kenya this includes many smallholder units in places like Kiambu, Murang'a, Nakuru, Busia and Western Kenya, where pigs are kept in small wooden or mud pens, often crowded and with little bedding change. Free-range and tethered pigs that mix with neighbours' pigs are also exposed. Mange can occur all year, but crowding during the cool, damp long and short rains, when pigs huddle together for warmth, favours spread. Pigs that are thin, wormy or poorly fed tend to suffer more severely.

early: Frequent scratching with the hind legs, and rubbing of the head, neck and sides against walls, posts, feeders and other pigs.
Repeated head shaking and flapping of the ears, because the inside of the ear is usually where mites first settle.
Small red pimples or spots on the belly, flanks, back and inside the thighs, often seen best on white or light-skinned pigs.
Light grey or brown scaly crusts starting on the inner surface of the ears.
Restlessness, with pigs getting up and lying down often instead of resting quietly after feeding.
Shiny, polished patches on pen walls and posts where pigs rub regularly.
advanced: Thick, grey, asbestos-like crusts filling the inside of the ears that can be peeled away as flakes.
Thick, wrinkled, leathery skin, especially on the neck, shoulders, flanks and around the eyes, sometimes with deep cracks.
Patchy or widespread hair loss, with rough, dry, scurfy skin.
Scratch wounds, scabs and small bleeding areas from constant rubbing, which may become infected and smell bad.
Slow growth, poor body condition and uneven pen mates, with some pigs clearly smaller than others of the same age.
Sows that are restless while nursing and may lie on and crush piglets, and boars that lose interest in serving.

lookalikes.name: Lice (Haematopinus suis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Pig lice are large enough to see with the naked eye, grey-brown and about the size of a grain of rice, crawling on the skin behind the ears, on the neck and inside the legs. Their white eggs (nits) are glued to the hairs. Lice also cause itching, but you can see the parasite itself. A pig can have lice and mange at the same time.

lookalikes.name: Greasy pig disease (exudative epidermitis)
lookalikes.howToTell: This is a bacterial skin infection mostly of young piglets, from a few days to a few weeks old. The skin becomes covered in a brown, greasy, sticky layer that starts on the face and spreads over the body. Affected piglets are usually dull and may die, and they do not scratch much. Mange is very itchy and is seen mainly in older weaners, growers and adults.

lookalikes.name: Parakeratosis (zinc deficiency)
lookalikes.howToTell: This causes thick, dry, brown-grey crusts in growing pigs, usually in an even pattern on both sides, on the legs, belly and back. It is not itchy, the pigs do not rub, and it is linked to diets low in zinc or very high in calcium. It improves when the diet is corrected.

lookalikes.name: Ringworm (fungal skin infection)
lookalikes.howToTell: Ringworm shows as round, slowly spreading patches of brown or reddish scaly skin, often behind the ears or on the back and flanks. It causes little or no itch. Mange causes strong itching and crusts inside the ears, which ringworm does not.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will first look at the herd as a whole: how many pigs are scratching, where the crusts are, and how growth looks across pens. Some vets count how often pigs scratch over a few minutes of watching, which gives a useful picture of how bad the problem is. To confirm it, the vet takes deep skin scrapings, usually from the inner surface of the ear where crusts are thickest, and examines them under a microscope for mites and eggs. Mites can be hard to find in pigs with the allergic rash, so a negative scraping does not always rule mange out; scrapings from older sows and boars with ear crusts are more likely to show mites. In some laboratories a blood test can show whether a herd has been exposed. At slaughter, inspectors may notice the typical pimply skin on carcasses, which tells you the herd is affected. To help the vet, note which pigs are scratching, when it started, whether you bought pigs or used an outside boar recently, what treatments you have already tried and when, and keep the most affected sow or boar available for examination.
firstSteps: Watch your pigs for a few minutes and note which ones scratch, rub or shake their heads, and check inside the ears of sows and boars for crusts.
Separate the worst-affected pigs into a clean pen if you can, and stop buying, selling or lending pigs and boars until the vet has seen the herd.
Remove and burn or bury dirty bedding, scrape and clean pen floors and walls, and allow pens to dry in the sun where possible.
Make sure all pigs have clean drinking water, shade, and a balanced feed, because well-fed pigs cope better with skin damage and heal faster.
Wear gloves and wash your hands and arms with soap after handling itchy pigs, and wash your clothes, since the mite can cause a temporary itchy rash in people.
Do not apply engine oil, paraffin, diesel or other home mixtures to the skin; they can burn the skin, poison pigs and contaminate meat.
Write down how many pigs are affected, their ages, and any recent new pigs or boar visits, then call your vet or County Veterinary Officer to plan treatment.
detail.vetTreatment: Mange is treated with acaricides, which are medicines that kill mites, and these must be prescribed by a vet who will choose the right product and timing for your farm. Commonly used options include the avermectin group (such as ivermectin or doramectin), given by injection or sometimes in feed, and sprays or pour-ons such as amitraz; which products are registered and available varies, so your vet will advise. The key point is that the whole herd must be treated together, including sows, boars, growers and piglets, because untreated carriers quickly reinfect everyone. Many products do not kill mite eggs, so a repeat treatment is often needed after a set interval, and sows are usually treated before farrowing so they do not pass mites to their new litter. Boars, which spread mites widely, are often treated more frequently. If scratching has caused infected wounds, the vet may decide other treatment is needed, but antibiotics do nothing against the mites themselves and should only be used when the vet prescribes them, to avoid wasting money and building antibiotic resistance. All these medicines have a meat withdrawal period, which is the time after treatment during which the pig must not be slaughtered for food; for some injectable products this can be several weeks, so always follow the label and your vet's advice, especially for pigs close to market weight. Expect the itching to ease over one to a few weeks, but thick crusts and skin take longer to heal, and allergic itching can continue for a while even after the mites are dead.
prevention: Check every new pig before it joins your herd, especially inside the ears, and keep new arrivals in a separate pen for a few weeks; ask your vet about treating them for mange during this time.
Buy breeding stock from farms that are known to be free of mange and willing to tell you their health status.
Avoid using boars from other farms unless you know their health status, and ask the owner whether the boar is regularly treated for mange.
Work with your vet on a planned whole-herd control programme, with sows treated before farrowing and boars treated regularly; some farms can eventually eradicate mange completely.
Clean pens between batches by removing bedding, scraping and washing floors and walls, and leaving them empty and dry for some days before restocking.
Avoid overcrowding, so pigs are not lying on top of each other, and give dry bedding, especially during the cold and wet seasons.
Feed a balanced ration with adequate protein, vitamins and minerals, and control worms and lice, because healthy pigs resist skin damage better.
Check ears and skin of sows and boars regularly and act early when you see head shaking or rubbing, instead of waiting until the whole herd is affected.
detail.impact: Mange is rarely a killer, but it quietly eats into a pig farmer's profit. Itchy pigs spend energy scratching instead of growing, so they take longer to reach market weight and eat more feed for every kilo they gain. In Kenya, where feed is the biggest cost of keeping pigs, this lost feed efficiency hurts. Pens of uneven pigs are harder to sell as one batch, and buyers and butchers may offer less for scrubby, scabby pigs or for carcasses with damaged skin. In sows, restlessness can lead to more piglets being crushed, and poor body condition can affect milk and the next breeding. Boars that are itchy and uncomfortable may serve poorly. Repeated spending on treatments that fail because only some pigs were treated also adds up. A farm with mange can also lose sales of breeding stock, because other farmers will not want to buy infested pigs.
detail.humanHealth: The pig mange mite can occasionally cause an itchy rash of small red bumps on people who handle infested pigs a lot, usually on the arms, hands and body where they touch the pigs. This rash is normally temporary because the pig mite cannot complete its life cycle on humans, and it usually fades once contact with infested pigs stops. Wear gloves or long sleeves when handling itchy pigs, wash with soap afterwards, and wash work clothes. See a health worker if a rash is very itchy, spreads or becomes infected. Also respect the meat withdrawal period of any mange medicine your vet uses, so that drug residues do not end up in pork that your family or customers eat.
detail.outlook: The outlook for mange is good when it is handled properly. Most pigs recover well once the mites are killed, although thick skin and ear crusts can take weeks to clear and allergic itching may linger for a while. Success depends mostly on treating every pig on the farm at the same time, repeating treatment when the vet advises, cleaning pens, and stopping reinfection from new pigs or visiting boars. Farms that only treat the pigs that look sick usually find that mange comes back within weeks. Pigs with badly infected skin, or very thin pigs, recover more slowly. With a planned programme and good biosecurity, many farms can get rid of mange entirely.

faqs.q: Can I use used engine oil or diesel to treat mange, like my neighbours do?
faqs.a: This is a common practice, but it is not recommended. Engine oil and diesel can burn and dry out the skin, cause more irritation, be absorbed into the body and poison pigs, and contaminate the meat. They also do not reliably kill all mites, so the problem returns. Your vet can give you a proper acaricide that is safe for pigs, with a known meat withdrawal period.

faqs.q: I treated my pigs once and the itching came back. Why?
faqs.a: There are usually three reasons. First, many mange medicines do not kill the eggs, so new mites hatch later unless a repeat treatment is given at the right interval. Second, if only the itchy pigs were treated, the sows and boars carrying mites in their ears reinfect everyone. Third, dirty pens and new pigs can bring mites back. Ask your vet to plan whole-herd treatment with a repeat, and clean the pens at the same time.

faqs.q: Do I need to treat piglets and sows that look healthy?
faqs.a: Yes. Older sows and boars can carry many mites in their ear crusts with little itching, and they are the main source of infection for each new litter. Piglets usually pick up mites from their mother within their first weeks. Treating only the pigs that scratch leaves the source untouched, so your vet will usually advise treating all pigs on the farm together.

faqs.q: Can my dogs, goats or cattle catch mange from my pigs?
faqs.a: The pig mange mite is adapted to pigs and does not normally set up lasting infection in other animals. Dogs, goats and cattle have their own types of mange mite. They may get a brief irritation from close contact, but they are not usually the source of pig mange. The main risk to your pigs is other pigs.

faqs.q: Can I sell or slaughter pigs that have been treated for mange?
faqs.a: Only after the meat withdrawal period has passed. Every mange medicine has a set time after treatment when the pig must not be slaughtered for food, and for some injections this is several weeks. Check the label and ask your vet, especially if pigs are near market weight, so you can plan treatment and sale dates together.

faqs.q: Is mange dangerous enough to kill my pigs?
faqs.a: Mange very rarely kills pigs directly, which is why it is easy to ignore. The real damage is slow growth, wasted feed, skin infections, crushed piglets and lower prices. Treating it early and properly usually pays back through faster growth and better pigs.

products.role: Vitamins A and E help maintain healthy skin and support the body's natural defences, so AD3E can be used, on your vet's advice, to support skin repair and recovery in pigs with damaged skin from mange. It does not kill mites and must be used alongside vet-prescribed mange treatment, pen cleaning and good feeding.
