card.headline: Thin, pot-bellied pig with rough coat
card.look: Young pigs grow slowly and look thin over the back but round in the belly, with a dull, rough hair coat. Some cough or have loose, sometimes mucus-streaked dung, even though they are eating.
card.action: Collect fresh dung from several pigs and ask your vet or agrovet to arrange a worm egg test so the right dewormer can be chosen.

detail.summary: Internal worms are parasites that live in a pig's gut, liver and lungs. The three most important in East Africa are the large roundworm (Ascaris suum), the whipworm (Trichuris suis) and the nodular worm (Oesophagostomum species). They rarely kill pigs quickly, but they quietly steal growth, waste feed, cause coughing and diarrhoea, and lead to livers being condemned at slaughter. On most smallholder pig farms, worms are one of the main hidden reasons pigs take longer and cost more to reach market weight.
detail.cause: Worms are spread by eggs passed in the dung of infected pigs. The large roundworm egg is swallowed with soil, dung or dirty feed, hatches in the gut, and the young larva (immature worm) burrows through the gut wall and travels to the liver. There it causes small areas of inflammation that heal as white scars, known as 'milk spots'. The larvae then move to the lungs, where they cause irritation and coughing, are coughed up, swallowed, and grow into long, white, pencil-thick adult worms in the small intestine. Adults compete for nutrients and, in heavy infections, can block the gut or the bile duct. Whipworms live in the large intestine (caecum and colon); they bury their thin front end into the gut lining, causing inflammation, diarrhoea with mucus and sometimes blood, and poor absorption of water and nutrients. Nodular worm larvae burrow into the wall of the large intestine and form small lumps (nodules), which damage the gut and reduce growth; in sows this shows as poor body condition and lighter litters. Worm damage also weakens the pig's defences, so pigs with heavy worm burdens often suffer more from pneumonia and other gut infections.
spread: Pigs swallow worm eggs from dung-contaminated floors, soil, bedding, feed troughs and water, which is why dirty pens are the main source of infection.
Roundworm and whipworm eggs have a tough shell and can stay alive in soil, cracks in floors and old pens for several years, so a pen can stay infective long after the original pigs have left.
Sows that carry worms shed eggs into the farrowing pen, and piglets become infected from the sow's udder, skin and the floor soon after birth.
Free-range, tethered and scavenging pigs pick up eggs from soil around homesteads, rubbish areas and where pig manure has been spread.
New pigs bought from markets or other farms can bring worms in, and so can boots, wheelbarrows and tools moved from dirty pens to clean ones.
Warm, wet conditions during the long and short rains help eggs develop and survive, and muddy pens and wallows increase contact with them.
Earth floors, cracked concrete and pens that are not cleaned daily allow eggs to build up to very high levels.
detail.atRisk: All pigs can carry worms, but the damage is greatest in weaners and growers, roughly from weaning to about six months of age, because they have not yet built up immunity and are growing fast. Roundworms cause most trouble in weaners and growers, whipworm mainly in growers on dirty or earth floors, and nodular worms are more often a problem in sows and older pigs. Pigs kept free-range, tethered or on earth floors, as is common in western Kenya, the Lake Victoria region and many rural homesteads, are at high risk. Confined pigs on concrete are not safe either if floors are cracked, dung is left lying, or the same pens are used batch after batch without thorough cleaning. Farms that buy weaners from markets, mix pigs from different sources, or have no regular deworming routine tend to have heavier burdens. Risk is higher in and after the rainy seasons.

early: Pigs grow more slowly than expected and take longer to reach market weight, even though they are eating normally.
Uneven growth within a litter or pen, with some pigs clearly smaller and thinner than their pen-mates.
A dull, rough or staring hair coat instead of a smooth, shiny one.
A dry cough in weaners and young growers, often heard when they get up or start moving, about one to two weeks after they first meet heavy egg contamination.
Soft or pasty dung, sometimes on and off, in growers.
Feed seems to 'disappear' without the pigs gaining weight, meaning poorer feed conversion.
advanced: Thin pigs with a visible backbone and hips but a swollen, rounded 'pot belly'.
Long, white, round worms the thickness of a pencil seen in dung or vomited.
Watery diarrhoea with mucus and sometimes streaks of blood, especially with heavy whipworm infection, leading to dehydration (sunken eyes, dry skin that stays tented when pinched).
Laboured breathing or persistent coughing, and more cases of pneumonia in the pen.
Yellow colour of the gums, whites of the eyes or skin (jaundice) if worms block the bile duct, which is uncommon but serious.
Sudden belly pain, straining, swollen belly or death in rare cases where a mass of roundworms blocks the intestine.
Sows in poor body condition that produce fewer or lighter piglets and less milk.
At slaughter, livers covered in white 'milk spots' are trimmed or condemned.

lookalikes.name: Swine dysentery (Brachyspira infection)
lookalikes.howToTell: Both cause mucus and blood in the dung of growers, but swine dysentery usually spreads quickly through a pen, the dung is often grey, jelly-like and blood-stained, and pigs can lose condition fast. Whipworm diarrhoea tends to build more slowly on dirty or earth floors. A vet needs dung samples or a post-mortem to tell them apart, and the two can occur together.

lookalikes.name: Enzootic pneumonia and other respiratory disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Enzootic pneumonia (caused by Mycoplasma) also gives a dry cough and slow growth in growers, but the cough continues for weeks and is worse in dusty, crowded, poorly ventilated houses. Roundworm coughing tends to come and go as batches of larvae pass through the lungs, and the farm usually also has worms in dung or milk spots at slaughter. Worms make pneumonia worse, so both may be present.

lookalikes.name: Sarcoptic mange
lookalikes.howToTell: Mange also causes poor growth and rough skin, but pigs rub and scratch constantly against walls and posts, and the skin becomes crusty and thickened, especially around the ears, neck and legs. Worms do not cause intense itching.

lookalikes.name: African swine fever
lookalikes.howToTell: African swine fever causes high fever, pigs refusing feed, red or purple blotches on ears and belly, weakness and many sudden deaths within days. Worms cause slow, chronic problems, not sudden deaths across the herd. If pigs are dying suddenly, treat it as an emergency: stop all movement and report to the County Veterinary Officer immediately, because African swine fever is notifiable.

detail.diagnosis: A vet or animal health officer usually begins with the pigs' history: age, growth rates, deworming record, floor type and whether pigs are free-range. The most useful test is a faecal egg count, where fresh dung is examined under a microscope to find and count worm eggs; this shows which worms are present and roughly how heavy the burden is. Keep in mind that young worms migrating through the liver and lungs do not yet lay eggs, so pigs that are coughing can still have a negative dung test, and whipworm eggs can be shed on and off. Post-mortem examination of a pig that has died or been culled can show adult worms in the gut, nodules in the large intestine wall and milk spots on the liver. Slaughterhouse feedback on milk-spot livers is a very valuable sign that roundworms are circulating on the farm. To help, collect fresh dung (straight from the pig or just passed) from several pigs of different ages into clean, labelled containers, keep them cool and get them to the lab the same day if possible. Write down ages, weights or growth, which pigs are coughing or scouring, what dewormer was last used and when.
firstSteps: Separate pigs that are very thin, scouring heavily or coughing badly so they are not pushed off feed and water by stronger pen-mates.
Make sure all pigs have constant access to clean, fresh drinking water, especially those with diarrhoea, which lose water fast.
Clean out dung from the pen every day and keep floors as dry as possible, so pigs are not swallowing more eggs while you wait for the vet.
Collect fresh dung samples from several pigs and label them by pen and age for a worm egg test.
Wear gloves or wash your hands well with soap after handling pigs, dung or bedding, and keep children away from pig manure.
Record which pigs are affected, their signs, their approximate weight or growth and your past deworming dates and products.
Do not buy and give dewormers by guesswork; ask your vet or a qualified animal health officer which product and programme suit your farm.
If any pig becomes yellow, has a swollen painful belly, stops eating or dies, call the vet urgently and keep the body for examination if possible.
detail.vetTreatment: Worms are treated with anthelmintics (dewormers), which must be chosen and prescribed by a vet or qualified animal health professional who will set the product, dose and timing for your pigs. Common drug groups used in pigs include benzimidazoles (such as fenbendazole, flubendazole or albendazole), macrocyclic lactones (such as ivermectin or doramectin), levamisole and, in some places, piperazine. Not all dewormers work equally well against all worms: whipworm in particular is harder to kill, and some products that work well against roundworms are weaker against whipworm, which is why knowing which worms you have matters. Some dewormers are given in feed or water over several days, others by injection or by mouth. Because roundworm and whipworm eggs survive in pens for years, the vet will usually advise a repeat treatment and a cleaning plan, otherwise pigs are simply reinfected. Pigs with severe diarrhoea may also need rehydration and supportive care, and pigs with pneumonia may need separate treatment for the lung infection; antibiotics do not kill worms and should only be used when a vet diagnoses a bacterial infection, because careless antibiotic use drives antimicrobial resistance. Every dewormer has a meat withdrawal period, the time that must pass after treatment before the pig can be slaughtered for food; follow it strictly. Using the same dewormer over and over, or underdosing by guessing weights, can lead to worms becoming resistant to the drug, so weigh or measure pigs and follow your vet's advice on rotating products. After effective treatment, coughing and diarrhoea usually settle and growth picks up, but lost growth is not fully regained and liver scars take time to fade.
prevention: Follow a regular deworming programme agreed with your vet; a common pattern is to deworm sows before farrowing, boars at regular intervals, and piglets around weaning and again before moving to growing pens, adjusted to your farm's worm test results.
Wash sows with soap and water, especially the udder and belly, before moving them into a clean farrowing pen, so piglets are not born into a load of worm eggs.
Clean pens daily by scraping out dung and wet bedding; worm eggs resist most disinfectants, so physical removal, then washing and letting the pen dry, is the most effective step.
Use solid, smooth concrete floors with a good slope for drainage, and repair cracks where eggs collect; earth floors are very difficult to keep worm-free.
Run pens 'all in, all out' where possible: empty, scrub, wash and dry a pen completely before bringing in a new batch.
Quarantine newly bought pigs for two to three weeks in a separate pen, deworm them as advised by your vet, and only then mix them with your herd.
For free-range or tethered pigs, move them to fresh ground regularly, avoid ground where pig manure was recently spread, and keep them away from rubbish dumps and latrines.
Compost pig manure well before spreading it, and do not put fresh pig manure on vegetable gardens, pig grazing areas or near water sources.
Keep feed and water troughs raised or cleaned daily so they are not contaminated with dung, and use boots and tools dedicated to each pen or cleaned between pens.
Feed a balanced diet with enough protein, minerals and vitamins, because well-fed pigs cope better with worms and recover faster after treatment.
detail.impact: Worms are rarely dramatic, which is why they are often ignored, but they cost Kenyan pig farmers money every day. Wormy pigs eat the same expensive feed but convert less of it into meat, so they take longer to reach market weight and each kilogram of pork costs more to produce. Uneven growth means pigs in a batch do not all reach selling weight together, which complicates marketing. Livers with milk spots are trimmed or condemned at slaughter, and buyers or abattoirs may pay less for pigs from farms with repeated problems. Worms make pneumonia and gut infections worse, increasing vet bills and losses among weaners. In sows, nodular worms and heavy burdens reduce body condition, milk yield and litter weights. Because the eggs build up in pens over years, a farm that ignores worms usually sees its problems slowly get worse with every batch.
detail.humanHealth: The pig roundworm, Ascaris suum, can infect people who accidentally swallow its eggs from soil, pig manure, unwashed hands or vegetables grown with fresh pig manure. In people, the migrating larvae can cause coughing, wheezing or stomach upset, and occasionally adult worms develop; children who play around pig pens are most at risk. Wash hands with soap after handling pigs, dung or bedding, wear gloves and boots when cleaning pens, compost manure well before using it on crops, and wash vegetables thoroughly. Separately, free-range pigs that eat human faeces can pick up the pork tapeworm (Taenia solium), which forms cysts in pork and can cause serious disease, including epilepsy, in people; use latrines, keep pigs confined, have pork inspected and always cook pork thoroughly. Finally, respect dewormer withdrawal periods so that drug residues do not end up in pork sold to your family or customers.
detail.outlook: The outlook for pigs with internal worms is good when the problem is recognised and treated properly. Most pigs respond well to the right dewormer, with coughing and diarrhoea easing and appetite and growth improving afterwards. However, growth lost during heavy infection is not fully made up, and pigs that were badly stunted as weaners may never reach the size of their healthy pen-mates. The biggest risk is reinfection: if pens are not cleaned and the deworming programme is not continued, pigs pick up new worms within weeks. Rare complications such as intestinal or bile duct blockage can be fatal. Long-term success depends on combining correct deworming with clean, dry housing and good feeding.

faqs.q: I saw long white worms in my pig's dung. Is it too late?
faqs.a: No. Seeing adult roundworms tells you the burden is significant, but most pigs recover well after correct deworming. Ask your vet to recommend a suitable product and dose for the pig's weight, clean the pen thoroughly to remove eggs, and check the rest of the herd, because if one pig has worms the others almost certainly do too.

faqs.q: How often should I deworm my pigs?
faqs.a: There is no single schedule that suits every farm. Many farms deworm sows before farrowing, boars every few months, and piglets around weaning and again before moving to growing pens. Free-range pigs and farms with earth floors usually need more frequent treatment than pigs on clean concrete. A worm egg test and your vet's advice will help you set the right programme and avoid wasting money or encouraging drug resistance.

faqs.q: What are the white spots on my pig's liver at the slaughterhouse?
faqs.a: These are 'milk spots', scars left where young roundworm larvae travelled through the liver. They show that pigs were picking up roundworm eggs, often in the weeks before slaughter. The liver is usually trimmed or condemned. It is a useful warning that your pens hold roundworm eggs and your deworming and cleaning routine needs improving.

faqs.q: I dewormed my pigs but they still look thin and cough. Why?
faqs.a: There are several possible reasons. The product may not work well against the worms you have, especially whipworm; the dose may have been too low because the pig's weight was guessed; the pigs may have been reinfected straight away from a dirty pen; or the worms may be resistant to that drug. The cough or poor growth may also come from another problem such as pneumonia, mange or poor feeding. Ask your vet to test dung and examine the pigs before treating again.

faqs.q: Can I sell or slaughter a pig right after deworming?
faqs.a: Not immediately. Every dewormer has a meat withdrawal period written on its label or given by your vet, and you must wait until it has passed before the pig is slaughtered for food. Selling earlier risks leaving drug residues in pork, which is unsafe and can lead to rejection by buyers and abattoirs.

faqs.q: Will cleaning with disinfectant kill worm eggs in my pens?
faqs.a: Most common disinfectants do not reliably kill roundworm and whipworm eggs, which have very tough shells. The most effective approach is to scrape out all dung and bedding, scrub and wash the floor and walls, and then let the pen dry fully, ideally in the sun, before restocking. Repairing cracks in floors removes hiding places for eggs.

products.role: Can be used as supportive care alongside vet-prescribed deworming, to support liver function and digestion in growers recovering from roundworm liver damage and worm-related digestive stress. It does not kill worms or replace a dewormer.

An oral rehydration solution that helps replace fluids and salts lost by pigs with worm-related diarrhoea, especially heavy whipworm cases, while the vet's treatment takes effect. It supports hydration only and does not treat the worms.

card.headline: Small white cysts under the tongue
card.look: Most infected pigs look completely healthy. You may feel or see small, whitish, rice-grain to pea-sized fluid-filled bumps under the tongue, and at slaughter the meat is dotted with similar cysts, often called 'measly pork'.
card.action: Do not eat, sell or give away pork from a suspect pig until a vet or meat inspector has checked it, and keep all pigs confined away from human faeces.

detail.summary: Pork tapeworm is caused by a parasite called Taenia solium that passes between people and pigs. Pigs get small cysts in their tongue and meat after eating human faeces that contain tapeworm eggs, and people get the adult tapeworm by eating undercooked infected pork. The disease rarely makes pigs sick, but it is one of the most serious meat-borne parasites for people, because the eggs can also cause cysts in the human brain that lead to seizures and epilepsy. Infected carcasses can also be condemned at inspection, which costs the farmer money.
detail.cause: The adult pork tapeworm lives only in the human gut. It can grow to several metres long and releases segments full of eggs into the person's stool. When pigs roam freely or are kept where people use open fields, bushes or broken latrines, they eat this faeces and swallow the eggs. Inside the pig, the eggs hatch and the tiny larvae pass through the gut wall into the blood. They settle in muscle, especially the tongue, jaw (chewing) muscles, heart, diaphragm, shoulders and thighs, and sometimes the brain. There each larva forms a cyst, called a cysticercus: a small bladder of clear fluid with a white dot inside, which is the head of a future tapeworm. The cysts usually cause little harm to the pig because it is slaughtered young. When a person eats raw or undercooked pork containing living cysts, the head attaches to their gut wall and grows into a new adult tapeworm, and the cycle continues. A person can also swallow the eggs directly, through unwashed hands, contaminated water or vegetables, or from a tapeworm carrier in the household. The eggs then form cysts in the person's muscles, eyes and brain, which is called human cysticercosis.
spread: Pigs become infected by eating human faeces, or soil, water and feed contaminated with faeces from a person who carries the adult tapeworm.
Free-range, scavenging or loosely tethered pigs in villages without good toilets are the main way the cycle is kept going.
One tapeworm carrier can pass huge numbers of eggs, so a single person using the open bush near pigs can infect many animals.
People get the adult tapeworm by eating raw, undercooked or lightly roasted pork that contains living cysts, including home-slaughtered pork that was never inspected.
People get cysts in their own bodies (cysticercosis) by swallowing tapeworm eggs through dirty hands, contaminated drinking water or raw vegetables, or from food handled by a carrier.
Selling uninspected pork at markets, roadside joints and ceremonies spreads the tapeworm to new households and areas.
Using untreated human waste or latrine contents on gardens or pig feed crops can spread eggs to both pigs and people.
detail.atRisk: Pigs of any age can be infected, but the problem is most common in free-range and tethered pigs kept by smallholders, especially where many homes lack latrines or where latrines are open, shallow or broken. In Kenya, pork tapeworm has been reported most often in pig-keeping areas of western Kenya and around Lake Victoria, but it can occur anywhere pigs can reach human faeces. Pigs kept in confinement with good housing, clean feed and clean water, and fed by people who use proper toilets, are at much lower risk. Local and crossbred pigs sold through informal markets, and pigs slaughtered at home or in unlicensed slabs without meat inspection, carry the greatest risk to consumers. Risk can rise in the rains, when faeces and eggs are washed into water sources and feeding areas, though infection happens all year.

early: In almost all cases there are no signs at all: the pig eats, grows and behaves normally.
On gently lifting and checking the underside of the tongue, you may see or feel small, firm, round, whitish bumps the size of a rice grain to a pea.
Some cysts may be seen on the inside of the lips or under the eyelids in more heavily infected pigs.
A pig that you know has roamed freely near open defecation sites should be treated as at risk even if it looks perfectly well.
advanced: Heavily infected pigs may show many cysts across the tongue and inside the mouth.
Rarely, cysts in the brain can cause nervous signs such as fits, circling, walking in a strange way, or unusual sensitivity of the snout.
Rarely, very heavy infection of the jaw and tongue muscles can make chewing or swallowing difficult.
At slaughter, the cut muscle (especially the tongue, jaw muscles, heart, diaphragm, shoulder and thigh) shows many small clear or white cysts, giving the 'measly' look.
Older cysts may become cloudy, gritty or chalky (calcified) and look like small hard white spots in the meat.

lookalikes.name: Cysticercus tenuicollis (cysts from the dog tapeworm Taenia hydatigena)
lookalikes.howToTell: These cysts come from dogs, not people. They are usually larger, thin-walled, watery bladders hanging from the liver surface, the fat in the belly (omentum) or the abdominal lining, not scattered through the muscle and tongue. A meat inspector can tell them apart.

lookalikes.name: Hydatid cysts (Echinococcus, also from dogs)
lookalikes.howToTell: Hydatid cysts are usually much bigger, often from a marble to an orange in size, and are found mainly in the liver and lungs, not in the tongue or muscle meat. They are a sign that dogs are being fed raw offal and are a separate human health risk.

lookalikes.name: Small abscesses or injection-site lumps
lookalikes.howToTell: Abscesses contain thick pus, not clear fluid with a white dot, and are often near old injection sites or wounds. Injection lumps are usually single and in the neck or thigh where drugs were given.

lookalikes.name: Sarcocystis and other tiny muscle parasites
lookalikes.howToTell: These are usually so small they are hard to see with the naked eye, or appear as thin pale streaks along the muscle fibres rather than round fluid-filled cysts. A lab test or experienced inspector is needed to confirm.

detail.diagnosis: In the live pig, a vet or experienced inspector may restrain the pig, open its mouth and look at and feel the underside of the tongue for cysts. Finding cysts on the tongue is a strong sign of infection, but many infected pigs have no tongue cysts, so a clean tongue does not prove the pig is free. Blood tests, such as tests that detect parasite proteins (antigen tests) or the pig's antibodies, can be done in some laboratories, including research and university labs, and are used mainly in surveys. The most common way the infection is found in Kenya is routine meat inspection at a licensed slaughterhouse, where the inspector looks at and cuts into the tongue, jaw muscles, heart, diaphragm and other muscles. The inspector decides whether the carcass can be passed, must be treated (for example by approved freezing where facilities exist), or must be condemned, depending on how many cysts are found. To help, the farmer can share where the pig was raised, whether it was free-range or tethered, whether other pigs from the same home or village had cysts, and the toilet situation around the home. Always slaughter pigs at a licensed slaughterhouse or slab where an inspector can check the meat.
firstSteps: Do not eat, sell, give away or feed to dogs any pork from a pig you suspect has cysts until a vet or meat inspector has examined it.
Confine all your pigs at once in a clean pen or sty so they can no longer scavenge around homes, bushes, fields or latrines.
Give clean feed and clean drinking water from a protected source, and make sure nobody uses the pig pen or feeding area as a toilet.
Wash your hands well with soap and water after handling pigs, raw pork or soil, and before eating or preparing food.
Record which pigs were affected, where they came from, where they grazed, and when, so the vet can trace the source.
Call your vet, the nearest meat inspector or the Sub-County or County Veterinary Office for advice on examining, treating or slaughtering the pigs.
If pork from a suspect pig has already been eaten, especially undercooked, advise the family to visit a health facility for advice and possible tapeworm testing.
Check that every household member has access to and uses a proper, covered latrine, and repair or dig one if needed.
detail.vetTreatment: Because infected pigs are rarely sick, treatment is mainly about stopping the cysts from reaching people. A vet may treat at-risk or infected pigs with an anti-parasite drug from the benzimidazole group; oxfendazole is the drug most studied and used for killing cysts in pigs, while other related drugs are considered less reliable for this purpose. Availability and registration of these products for this use in Kenya can vary, so the vet will decide what is suitable and legal. All treatment must be prescribed and supervised by a vet; do not guess doses or use human medicines on pigs. The drug kills the cysts, but dead cysts take several weeks to break down and can leave small scars in the meat, so the vet will advise how long to wait before the pig is slaughtered. There is also a meat withdrawal period after treatment, during which the pork must not be eaten or sold, and you must follow it strictly. A vaccine for pigs against pork tapeworm has been developed and is used in some countries, but it is not widely available in Kenya at present; ask your County Veterinary Office about any local programmes. In control programmes, treating pigs works best when people in the community are also tested and treated for tapeworm by health workers, latrines are improved and pigs are confined. Deworming of people is done only by medical clinicians, not vets or farmers.
prevention: Build and use a proper, covered latrine for every household, and make sure workers and visitors use it too; this is the single most important step to break the cycle.
Keep pigs confined in a pen, sty or fenced area at all times so they cannot scavenge human faeces, and never let them roam near bushes, fields or broken latrines.
Give pigs clean feed and clean water from a protected source, and never use human waste or latrine contents as manure on pig feed crops or near pig pens.
Always slaughter pigs at a licensed slaughterhouse or slab where a meat inspector checks the carcass, and do not buy or sell uninspected pork.
Cook pork thoroughly all the way through until no pink meat remains and juices run clear; avoid lightly roasted, rare or raw pork, including at nyama choma joints.
Practise good hand hygiene with soap and water after using the toilet, after handling pigs or soil, and before preparing or eating food, and wash raw vegetables in clean water.
Ask your vet about strategic treatment of pigs in high-risk areas, and ask health workers about tapeworm testing and treatment for people in your household and village.
Work with neighbours, extension officers and community health volunteers, because pork tapeworm is controlled best when the whole village improves toilets and confines pigs together.
detail.impact: For a Kenyan pig farmer, the biggest direct cost comes at slaughter. A carcass with cysts may be condemned or downgraded by the meat inspector, meaning the farmer loses most or all of the value of a pig that took months to raise. Buyers and butchers who check tongues often refuse or pay much less for pigs with visible cysts, and some farmers then sell such pigs cheaply through informal channels, which spreads the disease to consumers. Once an area is known for measly pork, prices and trust in local pork can fall for every farmer there. The largest cost, however, falls on families and communities: human cysticercosis of the brain causes seizures, lost work and school days, medical bills and stigma. Confining pigs does mean more spending on feed and housing, but it also improves growth, reduces other diseases and protects the family's health and the farm's reputation.
detail.humanHealth: Pork tapeworm is a serious zoonosis, meaning it passes between animals and people. There are two forms in people. First, eating raw or undercooked pork with living cysts gives a person the adult tapeworm in the gut (taeniasis). This often causes few signs, perhaps mild stomach upset, but the person may notice small white flat segments in their stool, and they pass eggs that can infect pigs and other people. Second, swallowing the eggs themselves, through dirty hands, contaminated water or food, or from a household member who carries the tapeworm, causes cysts in the person's own body (cysticercosis). When cysts form in the brain (neurocysticercosis), they can cause seizures, epilepsy, severe headaches and other serious problems, and this is a recognised major preventable cause of epilepsy in areas where the parasite is common. Note that eating infected pork gives the gut tapeworm, while brain cysts come from swallowing eggs, so both good cooking and good hygiene and toilets are needed. To protect your family, cook pork thoroughly, buy only inspected pork, wash hands with soap after the toilet and before food, drink safe water, wash vegetables, and use a proper latrine. Anyone who sees tapeworm segments in their stool, or has new seizures or persistent severe headaches, should go to a health facility promptly. Treatment for people must be given by medical health workers.
detail.outlook: For the pig, the outlook is usually good in terms of health, because most infected pigs never show illness. The problem is the meat: once cysts are present, the carcass may be condemned or downgraded, and even after vet treatment the dead cysts and scars can take weeks to clear, so meat quality and value may still be affected. Pigs that are confined and protected from human faeces after treatment are unlikely to be reinfected. On a farm and village level, the outlook depends on breaking the cycle: where every household uses latrines, pigs are confined and all pork is inspected and well cooked, the disease can be greatly reduced over time. Where pigs keep roaming and open defecation continues, pigs will keep getting reinfected no matter how often they are treated.

faqs.q: My pig looks healthy. Can it still have pork tapeworm?
faqs.a: Yes. Most infected pigs look and grow completely normally. The cysts sit quietly in the muscle and are usually only found when the tongue is checked or the meat is inspected after slaughter. That is why prevention, confinement and meat inspection matter so much, and why you cannot judge a pig as safe just by how it looks.

faqs.q: If the tongue has no cysts, is the pork safe?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Checking the tongue can catch many heavily infected pigs, but lightly infected pigs often have no tongue cysts at all while still having cysts in the meat. The only reliable checks are proper meat inspection at a licensed slaughter point and cooking all pork thoroughly before eating.

faqs.q: Can I eat the pork if I cut out the cysts?
faqs.a: No. Cysts are spread through the muscle, and many are too small or deep to see, so cutting out the visible ones does not make the meat safe. Let the meat inspector decide whether the carcass can be passed, treated or must be condemned. Never sell or give away measly pork, as this puts other families at risk.

faqs.q: Does cooking or freezing kill the cysts?
faqs.a: Thorough cooking, so that the meat is cooked all the way through with no pink parts and the juices run clear, kills the cysts. Deep freezing for several days can also kill them, but home freezers vary and may not get cold enough, so do not rely on freezing alone. Lightly roasted or rare pork, and pork that is still pink in the middle, can still pass the tapeworm.

faqs.q: Can I get brain cysts from eating infected pork?
faqs.a: Eating infected pork gives you the tapeworm in your gut, not brain cysts directly. Brain cysts come from swallowing the tapeworm eggs, which are found in the faeces of a person carrying the worm. However, once you carry the tapeworm, you can pass eggs to yourself and your family through poor hand washing. So both cooking pork well and using toilets and washing hands are needed to stay safe.

faqs.q: Will deworming my pigs regularly solve the problem?
faqs.a: Ordinary routine dewormers may not reliably kill pork tapeworm cysts, and even the right drug only works if the pig stops eating human faeces afterwards. Any treatment must be chosen and prescribed by a vet, with the correct withdrawal time before slaughter. Lasting control comes from confining pigs, using latrines, inspecting meat and cooking pork well, with treatment of pigs and people as part of a wider plan.

card.headline: Hungry squealing piglets, sow off feed
card.look: In the first one to three days after farrowing, the sow lies on her belly hiding her teats, refuses feed and feels hot. Her udder is hard, hot or swollen, there may be a smelly discharge from the vulva, and the piglets squeal, fight at the udder and look hollow and thin.
card.action: Take the sow's temperature, keep the piglets warm and fed with colostrum or milk replacer, and call your vet the same day, because both the sow and her litter can go downhill within hours.

aka: Milk fever of sows (not the same as milk fever in cows)
detail.summary: MMA is a group of problems in sows that appear soon after farrowing (giving birth): infection or inflammation of the udder (mastitis), infection of the womb (metritis), and little or no milk (agalactia). Not every sow shows all three, which is why vets now often call it postpartum dysgalactia syndrome, meaning 'poor milk after birth'. It matters because piglets depend completely on the sow's milk in their first days. Without quick action, piglets starve, get chilled, are crushed or die of scours, and the sow herself can become seriously ill.
detail.cause: MMA has no single cause. It usually starts when bacteria that live in the sow's environment and gut, especially coliforms such as E. coli and Klebsiella, enter the udder through the teats or the womb during and after farrowing. These bacteria release poisons called endotoxins. Endotoxins cause fever, make the sow feel ill and lose appetite, and block the hormones (especially oxytocin and prolactin) that make and release milk. So even a sow with only mild infection can suddenly stop letting her milk down. Many things make this more likely: a long or difficult farrowing, a retained piglet or afterbirth, constipation around farrowing (which lets more endotoxins pass from the gut into the blood), overfeeding or a sudden change of feed just before farrowing, a fat sow, not drinking enough water, hot and stuffy farrowing pens, dirty wet floors, and mouldy feed. Some moulds produce mycotoxins (poisons made by fungi) that can upset hormones and reduce milk. Stress from moving the sow late into an unfamiliar pen also plays a part. The result is inflamed, painful udder glands that feel hard and hot, a womb that may hold infected fluid, and a sow that cannot feed her litter.
spread: MMA is not a contagious disease that jumps from pig to pig like a virus; it develops in individual sows when bacteria from the environment meet a sow whose defences are lowered.
Dirty, wet farrowing pens and bedding contaminated with dung put large numbers of coliform bacteria in direct contact with the teats and vulva.
Unclean hands or equipment used to help a sow during a difficult farrowing can carry bacteria into the womb.
Constipation in the days before and after farrowing allows bacterial toxins from the gut to enter the bloodstream and trigger the syndrome.
Not enough clean water, especially from blocked or slow nipple drinkers, reduces milk production and makes constipation worse.
Heat stress in hot, poorly ventilated pigsties lowers feed and water intake and is a common trigger during the hot dry months.
Mouldy feed, for example damp maize germ, maize bran or poorly stored brewers' waste, can add mycotoxins that weaken the sow and her milk supply.
Piglet injuries to the teats from uncut sharp teeth can open a route for bacteria into the udder.
detail.atRisk: Any sow can be affected in the first three days after farrowing, with most cases starting within 12 to 72 hours. Older sows with many litters, fat sows, and first-time gilts with long farrowings are at higher risk. Sows that farrow large litters or have a long farrowing, a retained piglet or retained afterbirth are especially vulnerable. In Kenya, the problem is common on smallholder units where farrowing pens are hard to keep dry, water is carried by bucket and runs out, and feed is mixed at home from maize germ, bran and brewers' by-products that can go mouldy, particularly during the long and short rains. Hot months raise the risk in tin-roofed, poorly ventilated sties. Farms that move sows into the farrowing pen only a day or two before birth, or change their feed suddenly at that time, also see more cases.

early: The sow's rectal temperature rises above about 39.5°C; note that a slight rise just after farrowing can be normal, so a reading that keeps climbing or stays high needs a vet.
She eats less or refuses feed and drinks little, often from the first or second day after farrowing.
She lies flat on her belly (on her udder) and will not roll over to let piglets suckle.
One or more udder glands feel hard, hot, swollen or painful, and she may flinch or bite when touched.
Piglets squeal, fight at the udder, move from teat to teat and keep trying to suckle without settling.
Her dung becomes dry, hard and small, or she passes none, showing constipation.
advanced: Piglets look hollow in the flanks, thin and weak, with rough coats, and some lie away from the sow, chilled or sleepy.
More piglets are crushed because they crowd the sow looking for milk, and some develop scours (diarrhoea) or die.
A thick, white, yellow or bloody discharge with a bad smell comes from the vulva, often more than the small, clear discharge that is normal in the first days.
The udder skin may turn reddish-purple and very hard, and almost no milk can be squeezed from the teats.
The sow becomes dull, breathes fast, may stand reluctantly or not at all, and her ears and skin may feel cold or show bluish colour in severe toxic cases.
In the worst cases the sow collapses and can die from the bacterial toxins if not treated quickly.

lookalikes.name: Normal recovery after farrowing
lookalikes.howToTell: A healthy sow may have a small rise in temperature and a small amount of clear or slightly cloudy discharge for a few days. But she keeps eating, lies on her side to show her teats, and her piglets suckle and then sleep quietly together. In MMA the sow stops eating, hides her udder, and the piglets stay noisy and hungry.

lookalikes.name: Retained piglet or difficult farrowing (dystocia)
lookalikes.howToTell: If the sow strains without producing piglets, or farrowing stopped suddenly with fewer piglets than expected, a piglet may be stuck. This can lead to MMA, so call the vet; only a vet or trained person with clean, lubricated gloved hands should examine inside.

lookalikes.name: Swine erysipelas
lookalikes.howToTell: Erysipelas also causes high fever and refusal of feed, but often shows raised, diamond-shaped or square red patches on the skin and can affect pigs that have not just farrowed. MMA is tied to the days just after farrowing and centres on the udder, womb and milk supply.

lookalikes.name: African swine fever (ASF)
lookalikes.howToTell: ASF causes very high fever, red or purple blotches on ears, belly and legs, and often sudden deaths in several pigs of any age, not just a sow that has farrowed. ASF is notifiable in Kenya: if more than one pig is sick or dying, stop all movement and report to your County Veterinary Officer immediately.

detail.diagnosis: A vet usually diagnoses MMA from the timing (soon after farrowing) and a careful examination. They will take the sow's rectal temperature, feel each udder gland for heat, hardness and pain, try to squeeze milk from the teats, look at any vulval discharge, check her dung and hydration, and watch how the piglets behave and how full their bellies look. They may do a gentle internal examination to check for a retained piglet or afterbirth. In some herds with repeated cases, the vet may take milk or discharge samples to grow the bacteria in a laboratory and test which antibiotics work, and may test feed for mycotoxins. If a sow dies, a post-mortem can confirm the problem and rule out other diseases. To help the vet, have ready: the farrowing date and time, how long farrowing took, the number of piglets born alive and dead, the sow's temperature readings, what and how much she has eaten and drunk, when she last passed dung, any recent change of feed, and whether other sows have had similar problems.
firstSteps: Take the sow's rectal temperature with a clean thermometer and write it down with the time; repeat morning and evening for the first three days after every farrowing.

Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer the same day you notice fever, a hard hot udder, smelly discharge or hungry piglets, because early treatment gives the best chance of saving milk and piglets.
Make sure the sow has plenty of clean, cool water at all times; check that nipple drinkers are flowing well or offer water in a heavy bucket she cannot tip over.
Keep the piglets warm in a dry, draught-free creep area with a heat source such as a covered lamp or warm bedding, because hungry piglets chill quickly and chilled piglets stop trying to feed.

Feed weak piglets: make sure every piglet got colostrum in the first hours, and where milk is short use a piglet milk replacer from a clean cup or shallow dish, or foster some piglets onto another sow that farrowed within a day or two.
Keep the farrowing pen clean and dry by removing wet bedding and dung, and reduce heat with good ventilation, shade over the roof or wetting the floor around (not under) the sow on hot days.
Encourage the sow to stand and move a little and to eat a small amount of moist, fresh feed with some bran or fibre to help prevent constipation, without forcing her.
Wear gloves and wash your hands with soap after handling the sow, her discharge or dead piglets, and do not give any injections or medicines unless your vet has prescribed them.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be prescribed and supervised by a vet, and usually combines several approaches. Anti-inflammatory and pain-relief drugs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatories such as meloxicam, flunixin or ketoprofen) are often the most important part, because they bring the fever down, ease pain and help the sow eat and let down her milk. Where the vet believes bacterial infection is involved, an antibiotic may be given, for example amoxicillin, oxytetracycline or a trimethoprim-sulfonamide combination, ideally chosen on the basis of the vet's experience on your farm or a laboratory test. The vet may also give oxytocin, a hormone that helps the udder release milk and helps the womb empty, and may remove a retained piglet or afterbirth. Fluids may be needed for a dehydrated sow. Expect the vet to also advise on caring for the piglets, including fostering and milk replacer. Many sows begin eating and producing milk again within one to two days if treated early. Always follow the exact product, dose and course length the vet gives, finish the course, and respect the meat withdrawal period printed on the label and explained by the vet before any treated sow is sold or slaughtered. Using antibiotics only when needed and exactly as prescribed helps slow antimicrobial resistance, where bacteria stop responding to medicines on your farm and in your community.
prevention: Feed sows correctly in pregnancy so they are in good body condition, not too fat or too thin, and avoid sudden feed changes in the last week before farrowing; many vets advise reducing the amount slightly just before farrowing and increasing it gradually afterwards.
Include enough fibre, such as wheat bran or good-quality forage, in late pregnancy and early lactation to keep dung soft and prevent constipation.
Provide unlimited clean water; a lactating sow needs a lot of water every day, so check drinker flow regularly and never let buckets run dry, especially during hot months.
Move the sow into a clean, washed, disinfected and dried farrowing pen about five to seven days before her due date so she settles and gets used to the pen.
Wash the sow, especially her udder and back end, before moving her into the farrowing pen, and keep the pen dry by removing dung and wet bedding daily.
Keep farrowing houses cool and well ventilated, with shade, roof insulation or extra air openings where tin roofs make sties hot.

Store feed ingredients such as maize germ, bran and brewers' waste dry and off the floor, throw away any feed that smells musty or looks mouldy, and consider a mycotoxin binder in sow feed when feed quality is uncertain.

Watch every farrowing, help only with clean gloved and lubricated hands when truly needed, record each sow's temperature for three days afterwards, and discuss culling with your vet for sows that get MMA repeatedly.
detail.impact: MMA is one of the most costly problems in the farrowing pen because it hits the litter at its weakest point. Piglets that do not get enough colostrum and milk in the first days grow slowly, are more likely to get scours, are crushed more often and may die, so the number of piglets weaned per sow falls. Survivors are often lighter at weaning and take longer to reach market weight, which means more feed and more time before you can sell them. The farmer also pays for vet visits, medicines and milk replacer, and spends many hours hand-feeding piglets. Affected sows may lose condition, come back on heat later and sometimes have to be culled early, which is a big loss on a smallholder unit with only one or two breeding sows. On farms where MMA keeps returning, it is a strong sign that farrowing hygiene, water supply, feed quality or sow feeding need to be improved.
detail.humanHealth: MMA is not considered a disease that passes to people in the usual way, but the bacteria in the discharge, dung and infected milk, such as E. coli, can cause illness if they get into the mouth or cuts. Wear gloves when handling the sow's back end, discharge or dead piglets, wash hands well with soap and water afterwards, and keep children away from sick animals. The main human-health concern is drug residues: sows treated with antibiotics or other medicines must not be slaughtered or sold for meat until the full withdrawal period on the label and given by your vet has passed. Never slaughter a sick or feverish sow for home use or sale.
detail.outlook: Most sows recover well if the problem is spotted early and treated by a vet within the first day, and many return to good milk production within one to two days. The outlook is poorer when treatment is delayed, when the sow has a very high fever or has already collapsed, when a retained piglet or severe womb infection is present, or when several udder glands are badly damaged. Glands that become very hard and scarred may never produce milk again, which reduces how many piglets that sow can rear in later litters. For the piglets, the outlook depends on how quickly they get colostrum, warmth and replacement milk or foster mothers; with good care, many litters can be saved. Sows that have had MMA more than once are more likely to have it again, and the farmer and vet may decide to cull them.

faqs.q: Is some discharge after farrowing normal?
faqs.a: Yes. A small amount of clear, slightly cloudy or reddish discharge in the first two or three days after farrowing is normal as the womb cleans itself. Worry when the discharge is thick, yellow, white or brown, smells bad, keeps increasing, or comes with fever, loss of appetite or hungry piglets. That suggests infection, and the vet should see the sow.

faqs.q: How can I tell if my piglets are getting enough milk?
faqs.a: Well-fed piglets suckle in quiet, regular sessions, then fall asleep together in a heap with round, full bellies. Hungry piglets squeal, fight at the udder, keep moving from teat to teat, look thin with sunken flanks, and may wander away from the sow or lie chilled. If you see these signs, check the sow's temperature and udder and call your vet.

faqs.q: Can I give my sow an antibiotic from the agrovet to save time?
faqs.a: Please do not treat on your own. MMA often needs pain relief and anti-inflammatory drugs and sometimes a hormone to release milk, not only an antibiotic, and the vet needs to check for a retained piglet. Using antibiotics without a vet's advice can mean the wrong drug, the wrong amount or the wrong length of treatment, which wastes money, may leave residues in the meat and helps create resistant bacteria. Call your vet and use only what they prescribe.

faqs.q: What do I feed the piglets if the sow has no milk?
faqs.a: First make sure each piglet got colostrum in its first 12 to 24 hours, from the sow or from a sow that farrowed at the same time. If another sow farrowed within a day or two and has spare teats, you can foster some piglets onto her. Otherwise use a commercial piglet milk replacer from the agrovet, mixed as the label says and fed little and often from clean cups or shallow dishes. Do not feed plain cow's milk alone for long, and keep everything very clean to avoid scours.

faqs.q: Why do my sows keep getting MMA after every farrowing?
faqs.a: Repeated cases usually point to something on the farm rather than bad luck. Common causes are dirty or wet farrowing pens, not enough water, constipation from low-fibre feed, fat sows, sudden feed changes near farrowing, hot sties and mouldy feed. Ask your vet to visit and look at your whole farrowing routine. Recording temperatures, feed and water for every sow helps find the pattern, and sows that get it repeatedly may need to be culled.

faqs.q: Will the sow's udder recover for her next litter?
faqs.a: Often yes, if treatment was early and the glands softened again. But glands that stayed very hard for a long time may be permanently damaged and produce little or no milk in future litters. At weaning, feel each gland; ask your vet to help judge whether the sow still has enough working teats to rear a full litter.

products.role: An oral rehydration and heat-stress relief solution that can be added to the sow's drinking water to encourage her to drink and help replace fluids and electrolytes while she is feverish, off feed or coping with a hot farrowing house. Good water intake supports milk production and helps against constipation. It supports recovery alongside the vet's treatment and does not treat the infection.

A mycotoxin binder that can be mixed into gestation and lactation feed to help protect sows from aflatoxin and ochratoxin in feed ingredients such as damp maize germ or bran, which can weaken sow health. It is a preventive feed-quality aid used together with dry feed storage and throwing away mouldy feed, not a treatment for MMA.

mma.imagePrompt: A realistic photo inside a simple Kenyan farrowing pen showing a large sow lying flat on her belly hiding her udder while a litter of thin, restless piglets crowd and nose around her side trying to suckle, natural daylight, straw bedding, no people.
mma.seoDescription: MMA in sows: spot fever, hard hot udder, foul discharge and hungry piglets after farrowing. First steps, vet treatment and prevention for Kenyan pig farmers.

card.headline: Sow not coming on heat
card.look: The sow or gilt shows no swollen red vulva, does not stand still when pressed on the back, and does not show interest in the boar, or she is mated but comes back on heat about three weeks later. Litters may be small, with few piglets born alive.
card.action: Start writing down every heat, mating, return and litter size for each sow, and check her body condition, feed and housing before calling your vet or extension officer.

aka: Nguruwe kutopata joto (sow not coming on heat)
detail.summary: Poor sow fertility is a group of problems: sows and gilts that do not come on heat, sows that are mated but return to heat, and sows that farrow small litters. It is rarely one disease. Most cases come from feeding, body condition, heat stress, poor boar use or heat detection, and sometimes infection. Every day a sow is not pregnant costs you feed with no piglets to show for it, so fertility is one of the biggest drivers of profit on a pig farm.
detail.cause: A sow's reproduction is controlled by hormones from the brain and ovaries. These hormones only work well when the sow is well fed, cool, healthy and stimulated by a boar. If a sow loses too much weight while suckling, her body switches off breeding to protect itself, so she does not come on heat after weaning. Heat stress has a similar effect: hot sows eat less, have weaker heats, and early embryos are more likely to die. Gilts that are underfed, kept away from boars, or mated too young often have delayed puberty or small litters. On the male side, a boar that is overworked, too young, lame, sick or has been through a hot spell can produce poor semen for several weeks, causing many returns even when the sows are fine. Mistimed mating, when the sow is served too early or too late in her heat, is a very common cause of returns. Mouldy feed can contain toxins (mycotoxins); one of these, zearalenone, acts like a female hormone and can cause false heats, swollen vulvas in young gilts, and returns. Vitamin and mineral shortages, especially vitamins A and E and selenium, can weaken fertility. Infections can also kill embryos or piglets in the womb: porcine parvovirus causes mummified (dried, dark) piglets and small litters, while leptospirosis, brucellosis and erysipelas can cause abortions, returns and weak piglets. Womb or urinary infections after farrowing or a dirty mating can cause discharge and repeat breeding.
spread: Most fertility problems are not spread but triggered by management: underfeeding during lactation, thin sows at weaning, and poor-quality or unbalanced feed.
Hot weather and hot, poorly ventilated pens, especially in the hot dry months before the long rains, reduce heat signs, conception and embryo survival in sows and semen quality in boars.
Lack of daily contact with a mature boar delays puberty in gilts and weakens heat signs after weaning.
Mouldy maize, maize bran or other ingredients stored damp, especially after the rains, can carry mycotoxins that disturb sow hormones.
Infections such as parvovirus, leptospirosis and brucellosis spread between pigs through contact with infected urine, aborted material, afterbirth, and in some cases during mating.
Bringing in new pigs, borrowing a boar from a neighbour, or sharing a boar between farms can bring infections into a clean herd.
Rats, contaminated water and wet, muddy pens can spread leptospirosis.
Inbreeding, by mating closely related pigs over generations, can reduce litter size and piglet vigour.
detail.atRisk: Gilts and first- and second-litter sows are most at risk, because they are still growing and lose condition easily while suckling; many farmers see a poor second litter after a good first one. Sows that farrowed large litters, had long lactations on little feed, or were lame or sick are also at risk. Exotic breeds such as Large White, Landrace and their crosses are productive but sensitive to heat and poor feeding. Sows in iron-roofed pens without shade or ventilation suffer most in hot months and in hot areas such as the Coast, Lake region and lowlands. Smallholders who have no boar of their own, rely on a borrowed boar, or keep sows on kitchen waste and maize bran only often see delayed heats and returns. Herds that buy in pigs without quarantine or keep pigs in wet, rat-infested pens are at higher risk of infectious causes.

early: A gilt older than about 7–8 months that has never shown a heat, even though she looks healthy.
A sow that has not come on heat within about a week after weaning, when most sows show heat 4–7 days after weaning.
Weak or very short heats: only a slightly pink vulva, little mucus, and the sow does not stand firmly for the boar or for pressure on her back.
A sow that comes back on heat roughly 18–24 days after mating, which usually means she did not conceive.
A sow that comes back on heat at an irregular time, around 25–38 days or longer after mating, which often means the embryos died after conception.
Sows getting thin, with hip bones and backbone easy to see or feel, especially at weaning.
Several sows returning to heat after being served by the same boar.
advanced: Repeated returns to service over two or more matings, with the sow eating feed but producing nothing.
Litters smaller than usual for the herd, or many piglets born dead.
Mummified piglets: small, dark, dried foetuses of different sizes born with live piglets, a classic sign of parvovirus.
Abortions, with expelled foetuses or afterbirth found in the pen.
A white, yellow or bloody discharge from the vulva some days after mating or between heats.
Swollen, red vulvas in young gilts or even piglets, with no real heat, which suggests mycotoxins in the feed.
A sow that seemed pregnant but has a large belly and no piglets at the expected farrowing date (pseudo-pregnancy).

lookalikes.name: The sow is actually pregnant
lookalikes.howToTell: A pregnant sow will not come on heat, so 'no heat' after mating is often good news. Count the days: farrowing is about 114 days (three months, three weeks and three days) after a successful mating. Ask your vet to confirm with an ultrasound scan from about four weeks after mating before giving any treatment to bring her on heat.

lookalikes.name: Silent heat or poor heat detection
lookalikes.howToTell: The sow is cycling normally but the farmer misses the heat, often because no boar is present or the sow is checked only once a day. Checking twice daily with a boar nearby, pressing on her back and watching for a red swollen vulva usually reveals heats that were being missed.

lookalikes.name: Boar infertility
lookalikes.howToTell: If many different sows return after mating with the same boar, while sows served by another boar or by artificial insemination conceive, the boar is the likely problem. Recent heat stress, fever, lameness, overuse or a very young boar point the same way. A vet can check his semen.

lookalikes.name: African swine fever (ASF) causing abortion
lookalikes.howToTell: ASF is a serious notifiable disease. Abortions come with high fever, pigs going off feed, red or purple skin on ears and belly, and sudden deaths in several pigs. Simple fertility problems do not make pigs sick or kill them. If you see sick or dying pigs together with abortions, stop all movement and report to the County Veterinary Officer at once.

detail.diagnosis: A vet or animal health officer starts with your records: ages of gilts, weaning dates, heat dates, mating dates and which boar was used, returns, litter sizes, piglets born dead and mummies. Without records, finding the cause is guesswork, so keep a simple card for each sow. The vet will look at body condition, feed, water, housing temperature, ventilation and lameness, and will examine the sow, the vulva and any discharge. An ultrasound scan can show whether a sow is pregnant and sometimes whether the ovaries are abnormal. If infection is suspected, blood samples can be tested for antibodies to parvovirus, leptospirosis, brucellosis and other diseases, and aborted foetuses, mummies and afterbirth can be sent to a laboratory such as the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete or a regional veterinary lab. Feed samples can be tested for mycotoxins. The boar's semen may be examined. To prepare, have your records ready, keep any aborted material cool in a sealed bag (handled with gloves), keep a sample of the current feed, and note recent weather, feed changes and new pigs.
firstSteps: Confirm the sow is not pregnant: count days from her last mating and do not try to bring a possibly pregnant sow on heat.
Start or update a record card for every sow and gilt, noting heats, matings, boar used, returns, litter size, dead piglets and mummies.
Check body condition: if you can easily see or feel the backbone and hip bones, she is too thin and needs better feeding before she will breed well.
Check heats twice a day, ideally with a mature boar in a nearby pen or walked past the sows, and press firmly on her back to see if she stands.
Cool the pens: give shade, open the sides for airflow, wet the floor or provide a wallow or mister in hot weather, and make sure clean water is always available.
Inspect the feed store and throw away any mouldy, caked, musty-smelling or damp feed or maize bran.
Wear gloves when handling aborted foetuses, afterbirth or discharge, bury or burn them safely, and wash your hands well afterwards.
Call your vet or extension officer if several sows are affected, if there are abortions or mummies, or if any pigs are sick, feverish or dying.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on the cause, so a vet must first find out why the sow is not breeding. For most herds the main 'treatment' is management: correcting feeding in lactation and before mating, improving body condition, cooling pens, using a fertile boar properly, and timing mating correctly. For sows or gilts that stay without heat, a vet may prescribe hormone products, such as gonadotrophin combinations that stimulate the ovaries, or a progestagen (altrenogest) to synchronise gilts; prostaglandins may be used in specific situations, but they can cause abortion, so they are only given once pregnancy is ruled out. Hormones do not fix an underfed or overheated sow, and results vary. Where a womb or urinary infection, leptospirosis or erysipelas is diagnosed, the vet may prescribe antibiotics; these must be used exactly as prescribed, and milk and meat withdrawal periods must be followed before any pig is slaughtered. Using antibiotics without a diagnosis does not fix nutritional or heat problems and adds to antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to drugs. Viral causes such as parvovirus cannot be cured by antibiotics; they are controlled by vaccination, where available, and by managing gilts. Sows that keep failing after the causes have been corrected are usually best culled. All drugs, hormones and doses must be prescribed by a vet.
prevention: Feed lactating sows well and let them eat as much as they want, so they do not lose too much condition before weaning; ask a nutritionist or extension officer for a balanced sow ration.
Aim to wean sows in moderate condition, and feed them well between weaning and mating ('flushing') to support heat and ovulation.
Grow gilts steadily and mate them at their second or third heat, at around 7–8 months and a good body weight for exotic breeds, rather than at the very first heat.
Give gilts and weaned sows daily contact with a mature boar to bring on heats and make them easier to see.
Mate sows when they stand firmly, and serve them twice about 12–24 hours apart, so that sperm is present when eggs are released.
Keep boars cool, well fed and not overused, rest them after illness or a hot spell, and have a back-up boar or artificial insemination available.
Keep pens shaded and well ventilated, with wallows, misters or wet floors in hot weather, and always provide clean water.
Store feed dry and off the floor, buy from reliable suppliers, and never feed mouldy maize, bran or brewers' waste.
Ask your vet about vaccination against parvovirus, erysipelas and leptospirosis where vaccines are available, giving gilts protection before their first mating.
Quarantine new pigs for at least a month, avoid sharing boars with farms of unknown health, control rats, and keep pens clean and dry.
detail.impact: Every day a sow is empty, she eats feed and takes up space without producing piglets. Returns add about three weeks of lost time each, and a sow that takes months to get back in pig may produce one litter less per year. Small litters mean fewer weaners to sell, and for a smallholder with one to five sows this can turn a profitable venture into a loss. Farmers then often cull or sell sows cheaply, and must spend money raising or buying replacement gilts. Infectious causes such as parvovirus or leptospirosis can affect many sows at once, while a single infertile boar can quietly spoil a whole round of matings. Good records and simple changes in feeding, cooling and boar use often give the best return on any pig farm.
detail.humanHealth: Most causes of poor fertility pose no risk to people, but some infections that cause abortion and returns in pigs, such as leptospirosis and brucellosis (Brucella suis), can infect humans and cause fever, joint pain and serious illness. People can be infected through contact with aborted foetuses, afterbirth, discharges and urine, or through cuts and splashes into the eyes or mouth. Always wear gloves and, if possible, boots when handling aborted material or assisting at farrowing, wash hands well with soap, cover cuts, and keep children away. Control rats and avoid wading in pig urine and mud. Do not eat aborted or dead piglets. If you develop a fever after contact with aborting pigs, tell your doctor you work with pigs. If any drugs are prescribed, observe the meat withdrawal period before slaughter.
detail.outlook: The outlook is usually good when the cause is feeding, body condition, heat stress, mistimed mating or boar management, because these can be corrected. Thin sows often come back on heat once they regain condition, and heat-stress problems usually improve when the weather cools and pens are made cooler, though it can take several weeks. Problems caused by a boar's poor semen after heat or illness may take around six weeks or more to clear, because new sperm takes time to develop. Infectious causes can be controlled with vaccination where available, testing and hygiene, but losses already suffered cannot be reversed. Old sows, sows with long-term womb damage, and sows that keep returning despite good care often do not recover their fertility and are better culled.

faqs.q: How long after weaning should my sow come on heat?
faqs.a: Most healthy sows show heat within about 4–7 days after weaning. If a sow has not shown heat within 10 days, check her body condition, feed and housing, and make sure a boar is close by. Thin first-litter sows commonly take longer. If she still shows no heat, talk to your vet.

faqs.q: How do I know my sow is truly on heat?
faqs.a: Look for a swollen, red vulva, sometimes with clear mucus, restlessness, mounting other pigs and grunting. The best test is to press firmly on her back or sit on her with a boar nearby: if she stands still with her ears pricked, she is in standing heat and ready to mate. Check twice a day, because heats can be short.

faqs.q: My sow was mated but came back on heat. Is she sick?
faqs.a: Not usually. A return about 18–24 days after mating usually means the eggs were not fertilised, often because of mating at the wrong time or a boar with poor semen. Returns at irregular times, later than this, more often point to embryo loss from heat stress, poor feeding, mycotoxins or infection. Check your records: if many sows return after the same boar, suspect the boar.

faqs.q: Can mouldy maize or bran really affect my sows?
faqs.a: Yes. Mould can produce toxins called mycotoxins. One of them acts like a female hormone and can cause swollen vulvas in young gilts, false heats, returns and small litters, and other mycotoxins harm the liver and immunity. Mouldy feed is common after the rains when grain is stored damp. Never feed mouldy or musty feed, and store feed dry and off the floor.

faqs.q: Should I buy an injection to bring my sow on heat?
faqs.a: Hormone treatments do exist, but they must be prescribed by a vet after confirming the sow is not pregnant, because some hormones cause abortion. They also do not work well on thin, overheated or sick sows. Fix feeding, body condition, cooling and boar contact first. Your vet can advise whether hormones make sense for your situation.

faqs.q: Why was my sow's second litter smaller than her first?
faqs.a: This is common and is often called second-litter syndrome. The young sow is still growing and loses a lot of condition suckling her first litter, so she has fewer eggs at the next mating. Feeding her generously in lactation, not weaning her too thin, and feeding her well before mating usually helps. Waiting for her second heat after weaning may also help in some cases; ask your vet or extension officer.

products.role: A breeding-sow supplement that can help top up the nutrients sows need for fertility and lactation, used alongside a properly balanced ration, good body condition management, cooling and correct boar use. It supports nutrition only and will not fix heat stress, poor mating timing, boar problems or infections, which need management changes and vet advice.

Provides vitamins A, D3 and E, which support normal reproduction and immunity, so it may help where the diet is short of these vitamins, such as sows fed mainly maize bran or kitchen waste. It is not a fertility treatment; ask your vet or nutritionist whether the ration is deficient, and use it alongside better feeding and good management.
