card.headline: Fast panting, lying flat and spread out
card.look: Pigs breathe fast through an open mouth and lie stretched out on their sides, apart from each other, often on wet floors or in their own dung and urine to cool down. They eat less, move little and may look dull or wobbly.
card.action: Move the pigs into shade, wet their skin with cool (not ice-cold) water, give plenty of fresh drinking water and call your vet if any pig is collapsing or breathing very hard.

detail.summary: Heat stress happens when a pig gains more heat than it can lose. Pigs have very few working sweat glands, a thick fat layer and lungs that are small for their body size, so hot weather, crowding and poor housing quickly overwhelm them. It reduces feed intake and growth, damages sow and boar fertility, and can kill pigs suddenly, especially heavy finishers, pregnant sows and pigs being transported.
detail.cause: A pig's body works best within a narrow temperature range, and its normal rectal temperature is about 38.5 to 39.5°C. Unlike cattle or people, pigs cannot sweat to cool themselves. They lose heat mainly by panting, by lying on cool, wet surfaces and by wallowing in mud or water so that evaporation cools the skin. When the air is hot and humid, the roof is hot iron sheeting, there is no breeze, or pigs are packed tightly, these cooling methods fail. Body temperature rises, the heart beats faster and blood is pushed to the skin, leaving less for the gut and other organs. The pig eats less to avoid the heat produced by digestion, so growth and milk production fall. In the reproductive system, heat harms eggs, early embryos and sperm, so sows return to heat, lose litters early or produce small litters, and boars become less fertile for several weeks after a hot spell. If body temperature keeps rising, the pig develops heat stroke: organs, brain and muscles are damaged, the blood becomes acidic, and the pig collapses and can die within a short time. Large, fat pigs and sows in late pregnancy produce the most body heat, so they are in the greatest danger.
spread: Heat stress is not infectious and does not pass from pig to pig; it is triggered by the environment and management.
Hot, sunny afternoons, especially during the hot dry months before the long and short rains, are the most common trigger.
High humidity makes things worse because wet air slows evaporation from the skin and lungs, so hot, humid weather at the Coast, around Lake Victoria and in Western Kenya is especially risky.
Low iron-sheet roofs without a ceiling or insulation radiate heat down onto the pigs, turning the pen into an oven by midday.
Overcrowding, poor airflow, closed walls and few openings trap body heat and moisture inside the pen.
Running out of drinking water, or nipple drinkers with weak flow, quickly turns mild heat stress into a dangerous situation.
Chasing, loading, transport in the heat of the day, mixing and fighting all increase body heat, which is why many deaths happen in lorries and at markets.
Feeding a large meal in the hottest part of the day adds heat from digestion at the worst possible time.
detail.atRisk: All pigs can suffer, but the most at risk are heavy finishing pigs close to market weight, fat pigs, sows in late pregnancy and lactating sows eating large amounts of feed, and working boars. Pigs with existing lung problems such as pneumonia struggle more because they cannot pant efficiently. Some improved breeds and lines carrying the stress gene (porcine stress syndrome) can collapse and die suddenly when heated or excited. Piglets are less at risk from heat because they need warmth, but they suffer when the sow stops eating and her milk drops. Risk is highest in hot lowland areas such as the Coast, Lake Basin, lower Eastern and parts of the Rift Valley floor, during the hot dry season and on hot, still afternoons in any area. Smallholder pigs kept in small, low, iron-roofed pens with no shade or wallow are at high risk, and so are commercial units with high stocking and poor ventilation. Pigs being transported to market or the slaughterhouse are among the most vulnerable.

early: Faster breathing than normal while resting, with the flanks moving more quickly.
Pigs lie flat on their sides, stretched out and spaced apart rather than huddled together.
Pigs seek out wet areas, lie in the dunging area or wallow in dung and urine to cool their skin, so they become dirtier than usual.
Eating less, especially in the afternoon, and leaving feed in the trough.
Drinking much more water and playing with or crowding around drinkers.
Reduced activity, dullness and reluctance to get up or move.
Sows lying on their bellies to keep the udder away from piglets, or stopping nursing.
advanced: Open-mouth panting with rapid, shallow breathing, sometimes with drooling or foam at the mouth.
Skin turns red or blotchy purple, particularly on the ears, belly and legs, and feels hot to touch.
Weakness, staggering, trembling or muscle stiffness when made to move.
Vomiting, or the pig lies down and will not get up even when encouraged.
Collapse, convulsions or loss of consciousness, which is heat stroke and an emergency.
Sudden deaths, often of the biggest pigs or heavily pregnant sows, on a hot day or during or shortly after transport.

Later effects in the herd: sows returning to heat, abortions, small litters, more stillborn piglets, sows taking longer to come on heat after weaning, and poor conception from a boar used in hot weather.

lookalikes.name: African swine fever (ASF)
lookalikes.howToTell: ASF causes high fever, red or blue-purple skin on ears and belly, loss of appetite and many deaths, which can look like heat stroke. But in ASF pigs stay feverish and sick even after they are cooled and the weather is cool, deaths spread through the herd over days, and there may be bloody diarrhoea, vomiting or abortions in cool weather. ASF is notifiable in Kenya; if you suspect it, stop all movement and report to the County Veterinary Officer immediately.

lookalikes.name: Pneumonia and other lung infections
lookalikes.howToTell: Pigs with pneumonia breathe fast and may pant, but they also cough, have a fever, and breathe hard even in the cool morning or at night. Heat-stressed pigs usually breathe more normally once the day cools down.

lookalikes.name: Swine erysipelas
lookalikes.howToTell: Erysipelas causes fever, dullness and red skin, but often shows raised, diamond-shaped pink-purple patches on the skin, lameness from painful joints, and can occur in any weather. Heat stress does not produce these diamond-shaped patches.

lookalikes.name: Salt poisoning (water deprivation)
lookalikes.howToTell: When pigs run out of water, especially in hot weather, they become thirsty and then show nervous signs: wandering, pressing the head against walls, blindness, and fits that start a day or more after water returns. Always check water supply first. A vet should guide how water is reintroduced, as giving unlimited water too fast can make these pigs worse.

detail.diagnosis: Heat stress is usually diagnosed from the situation and the signs: hot weather or a hot pen, fast panting, pigs lying stretched out and wet, poor appetite, and improvement once they are cooled. A vet will take the rectal temperature, listen to the heart and lungs, and check the pen's roof, ventilation, stocking density and water flow. Because heat stroke can look like serious infections such as African swine fever, erysipelas or pneumonia, the vet may take blood samples or perform a post-mortem on any pig that dies to rule these out. At post-mortem, heat stroke shows congestion of organs and fast decay of the carcass but no specific infection. For fertility problems after hot months, the vet will look at breeding records, returns to heat and litter sizes, and may check boar semen. Before the vet arrives, write down when signs started, the time of day and weather, which pigs are affected (age, weight, pregnant or not), how many have died, how much they are eating and drinking, whether water ever ran out, and any recent moving, mixing or transport. Do not open dead pigs yourself; keep the carcass covered and away from other animals in case an infectious disease is involved.
firstSteps: Move affected pigs gently into the coolest shaded place available, without chasing, hitting or rushing them, because excitement adds more body heat.

Wet the skin with cool, clean water using a hosepipe on a gentle spray, a watering can or wet sacks, starting with the legs, belly and neck and then the rest of the body; do not use ice or ice-cold water, which can shock the pig.

Keep air moving over the wet skin by opening doors, windows and curtains, removing sacks or barriers that block breeze, and using a fan if you have one, so the water can evaporate and carry heat away.
Make sure every pig has easy access to plenty of fresh, cool drinking water; check that nipple drinkers flow well and add extra buckets or troughs that cannot easily be tipped over.
Wet the floor or create a shallow wallow so pigs can lie on a cool, wet surface, and reduce crowding by moving some pigs to another pen if possible.
Do not force-feed or drench a pig that is collapsed or struggling to breathe, because it may choke; stop feeding in the heat of the day and offer feed in the cool early morning and evening instead.
Postpone any moving, mixing, loading, castration or other handling until the cool part of the day.

Record which pigs are affected, their signs, how many die and the weather, and call your vet urgently if any pig is collapsed, fitting, foaming at the mouth, or if pigs keep dying, or if they stay sick after cooling, as this could be an infection such as African swine fever.
detail.vetTreatment: For pigs in heat stroke, the vet's first priority is controlled cooling and keeping the pig calm, because cooling quickly enough is what saves most animals. The vet monitors rectal temperature and stops active cooling once it approaches normal, to avoid the pig becoming too cold. Depending on the case, the vet may give fluids into a vein or under the skin to correct dehydration and blood chemistry, and may prescribe anti-inflammatory and pain-relief drugs such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (for example meloxicam or flunixin) to reduce inflammation and support recovery. Sedatives are used only with great care, since they can interfere with breathing. Oral rehydration and electrolyte solutions are often recommended for the herd during and after a hot spell. Antibiotics do not treat heat stress; they are only used if the vet finds a bacterial infection such as pneumonia, and should never be given just in case, because unnecessary use builds antimicrobial resistance. All drugs must be prescribed by a vet, who will tell you the meat withdrawal period, the time you must wait after treatment before a pig can be slaughtered for food. Mildly affected pigs often recover within hours of cooling, while pigs that collapsed may need close nursing for a day or two and should be watched for lasting weakness. For herd fertility problems, the vet will advise on breeding management, boar use and cooling sows rather than a single drug.
prevention: Provide good shade for every pig: plant trees around the pigsty, extend roof overhangs, and never keep pigs in an open yard with no shelter from the midday sun.

Improve the roof by raising it high, placing a ceiling or a layer of grass thatch, makuti, or other insulation under iron sheets, and painting the top of the roof white or a light colour to reflect sunlight.
Build or orient pens to catch the breeze, usually with the long side running east to west, and use open sides with wire mesh or curtains that can be rolled up on hot days.
Give pigs a way to cool their skin, such as a clean wallow, a wet floor area, drip coolers for sows in farrowing pens, or a hosepipe or sprinkler run in short bursts during the hottest hours.
Ensure unlimited fresh, clean, cool water at all times; pigs drink far more in hot weather, so check nipple flow daily, shade water tanks and pipes, and have a backup supply in case water runs out.
Reduce stocking density during the hot season and avoid mixing unfamiliar pigs, which leads to fighting and extra heat.

Feed in the cool early morning and late evening, split the daily ration into smaller meals, and ask a nutritionist about feed formulation for hot weather, such as adjusting fibre and energy sources to reduce digestive heat, and feeding wet mash where practical.

Plan transport for the cool hours of early morning or night, avoid feeding a large meal just before loading, do not overload the vehicle, provide ventilation and shade on the truck, and never leave a loaded vehicle parked in the sun.

Protect breeding stock by giving sows and boars the coolest, best-ventilated pens, using boars mainly in the cool part of the day, and expecting lower fertility after hot spells so you can plan matings and replacement gilts accordingly.

Treat and prevent lung disease, keep pigs at a healthy body condition rather than overly fat, and when buying breeding stock ask your supplier about stress-resistant lines suited to your local climate.
detail.impact: Heat stress costs Kenyan pig farmers money in several ways, even when no pigs die. Growing pigs eat less, so they grow slowly and take longer to reach market weight, which means more days of feeding and housing per pig. Lactating sows produce less milk, so piglets are weaned lighter and weaker, and sows lose body condition. Breeding suffers most of all: sows return to heat, have smaller litters, abort or take longer to come back on heat after weaning, and a boar used during a hot spell may sire few piglets for several weeks afterwards. This seasonal infertility can leave gaps in production months later. Sudden deaths of heavy finishers or pregnant sows are a direct and painful loss, because these are the most valuable animals on the farm. Deaths and bruising during transport reduce the price farmers get at market or the slaughterhouse, and stressed carcasses may give poorer quality pork. For smallholders who depend on selling a few pigs to pay school fees or other bills, a single hot-season loss can be a serious setback.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good for pigs with mild to moderate heat stress that are cooled promptly and given water; most recover within hours once the temperature drops. Pigs that have collapsed, are fitting or have very high body temperatures are in danger, and some die even with fast cooling and vet care, especially heavy pigs and those with lung disease or the stress gene. Some survivors may have lasting weakness or reduced performance. The effects on fertility are usually temporary and improve once the weather cools, but because sperm and eggs take weeks to develop, poor results can continue for some time after the hot period ends. The best results come from preventing heat stress through good housing, shade, water and careful timing of feeding and transport, rather than treating it after it happens.

faqs.q: Why do my pigs lie in their own dung and urine when it is hot? Are they dirty pigs?
faqs.a: No, this is a sign they are trying to cool down. Pigs cannot sweat, so they lie on wet surfaces and wallow to let moisture evaporate from their skin. If there is no clean water or wallow, they use dung and urine instead. When you see this, it means the pen is too hot. Provide shade, a wet floor area or a clean wallow, and better airflow, and the pigs will usually keep their dunging area separate again once they are comfortable.

faqs.q: Can I just pour a bucket of very cold water over a pig that has collapsed in the heat?
faqs.a: Sudden ice-cold water can shock the pig and cause blood vessels in the skin to tighten, which may trap heat inside the body. It is better to use cool, clean water, wet the legs, belly and neck first and then the whole body, and keep air moving so the water evaporates. Keep the pig calm, do not force water into its mouth if it is struggling to breathe, and call your vet immediately.

faqs.q: My sows were fine but after the hot season many came back on heat or had small litters. Could heat be the reason?
faqs.a: Yes, this is common and is often called seasonal infertility. Heat harms eggs and early embryos in sows and reduces sperm quality in boars. Because sperm takes several weeks to form, a boar can stay less fertile for weeks after a hot spell. Ask your vet to review your breeding records, rule out infections that cause abortions or returns, and help you plan cooler housing for sows and boars before the next hot season.

faqs.q: Will antibiotics help my pigs with heat stress?
faqs.a: No. Heat stress is caused by too much heat, not by germs, so antibiotics do nothing for it. Using them without a reason wastes money, leaves drug residues in pork and helps germs become resistant to treatment, a problem called antimicrobial resistance. Your vet may prescribe antibiotics only if they find a real bacterial infection, such as pneumonia, alongside the heat stress.

faqs.q: How can I take pigs to market without losing them on the way?
faqs.a: Transport in the cool early morning or at night, not in the afternoon heat. Do not give a large meal just before loading, as a full stomach makes the pig hotter. Load calmly without beating or chasing, do not overcrowd the vehicle, make sure it has shade and airflow, and avoid stopping in the sun. Wetting the pigs and the floor of the truck before departure on a warm day can help. Heavy, fat pigs need the most care.

faqs.q: How do I know if it is heat stress or African swine fever?
faqs.a: Heat-stressed pigs usually improve once the day cools or once they are wetted and shaded, and problems match hot weather. African swine fever keeps pigs feverish and sick even in cool weather, often causes red or purple skin, bloody diarrhoea or abortions, and deaths spread through the herd over days. If pigs stay sick after cooling or keep dying, stop all pig movement and contact your vet or County Veterinary Officer immediately, because African swine fever is notifiable and must be reported.

products.role: RE-COVER is an oral rehydration and heat-stress relief solution that can be added to drinking water during hot spells and after transport to help pigs replace water and electrolytes lost through panting and reduced eating. It supports hydration and recovery alongside shade, cooling, good housing and vet care; it does not replace cooling a collapsed pig or calling the vet.

AGRIPIG-SOW is a breeding sow supplement that can help support fertility and lactation in sows whose feed intake and body condition drop during the hot season. It is an aid to good nutrition alongside cooling the sow house, sound breeding management and vet advice, and it cannot overcome fertility losses if sows are kept in hot, poorly ventilated pens.

card.headline: Bitten, bleeding or shortened pig tails
card.look: One or more pigs have wet, chewed, red or bleeding tails, and pen-mates keep following them and nibbling. Pigs at risk often hold their tails tucked low between the back legs instead of curled up.
card.action: Remove the bitten pig and the main biter from the pen at once, then find and fix the stress, such as crowding, heat, water or feed.

detail.summary: Tail biting is when pigs chew and bite the tails of pen-mates. It is not a germ but a behaviour problem caused by stress, boredom and unmet needs. Once a tail bleeds, the taste of blood attracts other pigs and an outbreak can spread through the whole pen in a day or two. Bitten tails can become infected, and the infection can travel up the spine and into the body, causing lameness, paralysis, poor growth, condemned carcasses and deaths.
detail.cause: Pigs are naturally curious animals that spend much of their day rooting, chewing and exploring with their snouts. When they are kept in bare, crowded or uncomfortable pens with nothing to root in, that natural urge gets redirected onto the nearest thing that moves and can be chewed, which is often a pen-mate's tail. Stress makes this much worse. Common triggers include too many pigs in a pen, hot and stuffy housing, poor airflow or ammonia smell, too few feeders or drinkers so pigs fight for access, empty or blocked drinkers, sudden feed changes, and diets short in protein, especially the amino acid lysine (an essential building block of protein that pigs must get from feed), or short in salt and minerals. Sick pigs, pigs with worms or mange, and mixing of strange pigs also raise stress. The bite itself starts as gentle chewing, but once the skin breaks and blood appears, biting often becomes more forceful. The open wound lets bacteria in from the floor and mouths of other pigs. Infection can spread along the tail into the spine, forming abscesses (pockets of pus) around the backbone that press on the nerves and cause weakness or paralysis of the back legs. Bacteria can also travel in the blood to the joints, lungs, kidneys and other organs, which is why badly bitten pigs may later be found to have abscesses throughout the carcass at slaughter.
spread: It is not passed from pig to pig like a germ, but the behaviour spreads quickly because other pigs copy the biter and are attracted by the smell and taste of blood.
Overcrowding, where pigs cannot all lie down, eat or drink comfortably at the same time, is one of the most common triggers.
Heat stress during hot months, in iron-roofed pens with poor ventilation, makes pigs restless and irritable and increases biting.
Boredom in bare concrete pens with no straw, grass, soil or chewable objects to root in leaves pigs with nothing to do.
Shortage of water, from blocked nipple drinkers, dry troughs or too few drinking points, causes frustration and competition.
Poor or unbalanced feed, including sudden diet changes, too little protein or lysine, too little salt, or mouldy feed, is linked to outbreaks.
Mixing unfamiliar pigs, moving pigs, rough handling and other stress events can set off biting.
Illness in the group, such as worms, mange, diarrhoea or coughing, adds stress and can trigger biting.
detail.atRisk: Growing and fattening pigs (weaners and growers, roughly from weaning to market weight) are most often affected, because they are active, competitive and often kept in groups. Fast-growing improved breeds such as Large White and Landrace crosses kept intensively are commonly affected, but any pig can bite or be bitten. Pigs in zero-grazing style concrete pens with no bedding or rooting material are at highest risk, while free-range and pigs with access to soil and forage bite less often. Risk rises in the hot, dry months before the long and short rains, when iron-roofed sties become very hot, and whenever feed is scarce, expensive or suddenly changed. Farmers who buy pigs from several sources and mix them, or who keep more pigs than the space allows as the pigs grow, see more cases. Tail-bitten pigs, small or weak pigs, and pigs lying in corners are the usual victims.

early: Pigs hold their tails down or tucked between the back legs instead of curled up; this is one of the best early warnings that biting has started or is about to start.
Pigs follow one another and take tails into their mouths, chewing gently, often while the victim does not react much.
Tails look wet, slimy or slightly swollen from chewing, sometimes with small bite marks or hair rubbed off.
The group seems restless, with more nosing, fighting and squealing than usual, especially at feeding time or in the heat.
One or two pigs spend a lot of time chasing and biting, and the same victims keep moving away or hiding in corners.
Pigs may also start chewing ears, flanks or the pen fittings, a sign that they are frustrated or bored.
advanced: Tails are raw, red and bleeding, and blood may be seen on the victim's back legs, the floor or the faces of other pigs.
Parts of the tail are missing, leaving a short stump, and several pigs may be chasing the bleeding pig.
The tail stump becomes swollen, hot, smelly and crusted with pus or black dead tissue, showing infection.
The bitten pig eats less, loses weight, grows slowly and may have a fever (feels hot and lies dull).
Lameness, swollen joints, a hunched back, dragging or wobbling back legs, or inability to stand, which can mean an abscess near the spine pressing on the nerves.
Severely affected pigs may become very weak and die, and at slaughter the carcass may be partly or fully condemned because of abscesses.

lookalikes.name: Fighting injuries after mixing
lookalikes.howToTell: When strange pigs are mixed they fight to sort out who is boss. The scratches and bites are mainly on the head, ears, neck and shoulders, and they usually calm down within a few days. Tail biting focuses on the tail and keeps getting worse rather than settling.

lookalikes.name: Mange (Sarcoptic mange)
lookalikes.howToTell: Mange is caused by tiny mites in the skin. Pigs scratch and rub themselves on walls constantly, and the skin becomes crusty, thick and scaly, especially on the ears, face and legs. The tail is not bitten off by other pigs. A vet can confirm mange with a skin scraping.

lookalikes.name: Tail and ear necrosis
lookalikes.howToTell: In some piglets and weaners the tail tip or ear edges turn dark, dry and die off, sometimes linked to infection, poor circulation or mouldy feed. There are no clear bite wounds and pen-mates may not be chasing the pig. A vet can help tell the two apart and look for the cause.

lookalikes.name: Hind-leg weakness from other causes
lookalikes.howToTell: Back-leg weakness can also come from calcium and phosphorus deficiency, injuries, joint infections or some diseases. If the weak pig has a bitten or infected tail, a spinal abscess is likely, but if the tail is normal, the vet will look for other causes.

detail.diagnosis: Tail biting itself is usually easy to recognise from the wounds and the behaviour you can see in the pen. What the vet adds is an assessment of how serious the damage is and whether infection has spread. The vet will examine the tail stump for swelling, heat, pus and dead tissue, check temperature, watch the pig walk, and feel the back and joints for pain or swelling. Weakness or paralysis of the back legs suggests an abscess near the spine. The vet will also walk through the housing to find the triggers, checking space per pig, ventilation, temperature, drinkers, feeders, feed quality and bedding. In pigs that die or are slaughtered, a post-mortem examination (opening the carcass to look inside) can show abscesses along the spine and in organs. To help, the farmer should record how many pigs are affected and since when, which pigs seem to be the biters, the number of pigs in the pen and its size, recent feed changes, any mixing or moving of pigs, how much water they get, and any treatments already given.
firstSteps: Remove the bitten pig at once to a clean, dry, quiet hospital pen so it is not attacked again, and keep it alone or with calm pigs until the wound heals.
Watch the pen for a few minutes to identify the main biter or biters and move them out too, because one persistent biter can keep an outbreak going.
Check every drinker immediately: make sure water is clean, flowing well and that there are enough drinking points so all pigs can drink without fighting.
Cool the pens in hot weather by improving airflow, giving shade, wetting the roof or providing a wallow or sprinkler area, and avoid handling pigs in the midday heat.
Give the remaining pigs something safe to root and chew straight away, such as fresh straw, dry grass, hay, maize stalks, sisal-free ropes, fresh soil or untreated wooden blocks.
Reduce crowding if you can by moving some pigs to another pen, and make sure all pigs can reach the feeder at the same time.
Gently rinse a bleeding tail with clean water only if it is easy and safe, wear gloves, and do not use harsh chemicals, engine oil or home remedies on the wound.
Call your vet or animal health officer, especially if tails are infected, pigs are lame or weak, or more than one or two pigs are affected; do not give any drugs without their advice.
detail.vetTreatment: For a mild bite, the vet may simply clean the wound and apply an antiseptic or wound spray, some of which also contain a bitter or coloured repellent that discourages other pigs from biting. Infected tails may need the dead tissue removed and the wound cleaned properly. Where infection has set in, the vet may prescribe an antibiotic, often from the penicillin or tetracycline groups or others chosen to suit the likely bacteria, and may give an anti-inflammatory painkiller such as meloxicam to reduce pain and swelling. Only a vet should decide which drug is needed, how much and for how long, because antibiotics used wrongly help bacteria become resistant (antimicrobial resistance), making future infections harder to treat on your farm and for people. Every drug has a meat withdrawal period, which is the number of days after the last treatment before a pig can be slaughtered for food; you must respect it and record it. Pigs with abscesses along the spine and paralysis respond poorly to treatment, because antibiotics struggle to reach pus pockets, and the vet may advise humane culling to end suffering. Such pigs should not be sent for slaughter while sick or within a withdrawal period. Most importantly, the vet will help you fix the cause, because treating wounds without changing the housing, feeding or water usually leads to new cases.
prevention: Give pigs enough space as they grow so all can lie down together, move freely and avoid each other; reduce numbers or split groups before pens become crowded rather than after biting starts.

Provide rooting and chewing material every day, such as straw, hay, dry grass, maize stover, fresh soil, or hanging ropes and untreated wood, and refresh it often because pigs lose interest in the same object.
Make sure clean water is always available, with enough drinkers for the group, drinkers checked and cleaned daily, and nipple flow tested, especially in hot weather.
Keep pens cool and well ventilated, with shade, good roof height, insulation or wetting of iron roofs, and a wallow or sprinkler where possible during the hot months.
Feed a balanced diet with enough protein, especially lysine, plus salt and minerals; buy feed from reliable suppliers, avoid mouldy feed and change diets gradually over several days.
Provide enough feeder space so pigs do not fight to eat, and feed at regular times so pigs are not hungry and frustrated.
Avoid unnecessary mixing and moving, keep groups stable, handle pigs calmly and quarantine new stock before adding them to the herd.
Control worms and mange with a regular programme agreed with your vet, keep pens clean and dry to cut ammonia smell, and check pigs' tail posture daily so you act at the first tucked tails.
detail.impact: Tail biting costs Kenyan pig farmers money in several ways. Bitten pigs eat less and grow slowly, so they take longer to reach market weight and eat more feed per kilo gained. Treatment and vet costs add up, and some pigs become lame or paralysed and must be culled. At the slaughterhouse, abscesses found in the spine or carcass can lead to parts of the carcass or the whole carcass being condemned, and buyers may pay less for scarred or poor-condition pigs. Outbreaks also take a lot of the farmer's time and cause stress in the whole herd, which can slow growth of pigs that were not even bitten. Because the triggers are often things like crowding, heat and water, the same problems usually reduce performance across the farm, so fixing them pays back beyond tail biting alone.
detail.humanHealth: Tail biting itself does not spread to people, but infected tail wounds and abscesses can contain bacteria such as Streptococcus suis and Erysipelothrix (the cause of swine erysipelas), which can infect people through cuts or scratches on the hands. Wear gloves when handling bitten tails, wash hands with soap afterwards, and cover any cuts on your skin. Meat from pigs with abscesses should be inspected at a licensed slaughterhouse and not eaten from home slaughter of sick pigs. Always respect the meat withdrawal period after any antibiotic or other drug, so that residues do not end up in pork eaten by your family or customers.
detail.outlook: Pigs with mild, fresh bites usually heal well once they are removed from the biters and the wound is kept clean, although the tail may end up shorter. The outlook becomes poorer once infection spreads; pigs with swollen, pus-filled stumps can recover with vet care but often grow more slowly. Pigs with back-leg weakness or paralysis from spinal abscesses rarely recover fully, and humane culling is often the kindest option. The outlook for the herd depends mostly on whether the farmer finds and fixes the cause. Outbreaks that are caught early, at the stage of tucked tails and gentle chewing, can often be stopped within days by improving space, water, cooling, feed and rooting material.

faqs.q: Is tail biting a disease I can vaccinate against?
faqs.a: No. Tail biting is a behaviour caused by stress, boredom and unmet needs, not by a single germ, so there is no vaccine. Prevention means good housing, enough space, constant water, cool pens, balanced feed and things for pigs to root and chew. Vaccines against other diseases can still help indirectly, because healthy pigs are less stressed.

faqs.q: Should I cut my piglets' tails to stop biting?
faqs.a: Tail docking, which is cutting off part of the tail in young piglets, is practised on some farms and can reduce the damage, but it does not remove the cause, and docked pigs can still bite tails, ears and flanks. It is painful and should only be done, if at all, by a trained person with advice from a vet on pain relief and hygiene. Many countries now discourage routine docking for welfare reasons. Fixing space, water, heat, feed and boredom is the better long-term answer.

faqs.q: What should I do with the pig that is doing the biting?
faqs.a: Move it out of the group into a separate pen. Some biters calm down once given space, bedding and chewing material, and can later be kept with a smaller, calm group. If a pig keeps biting wherever it goes, many farmers choose to fatten and sell it separately once any withdrawal period is finished. Remember that a biter is usually a sign the pen has a problem, so check conditions for the rest of the group too.

faqs.q: Can I put engine oil, ash or pepper on the tail to stop other pigs biting?
faqs.a: It is better not to. Engine oil and harsh chemicals damage the wound, can poison pigs that lick it, and can leave residues in meat. Ash and pepper may irritate the wound and introduce dirt. Ask your vet or agrovet for a proper wound spray, some of which contain a safe bitter or coloured repellent, and focus on removing the injured pig and fixing the cause.

faqs.q: Why did my pig become paralysed weeks after its tail healed?
faqs.a: Bacteria from an infected tail can travel up the tail bones into the spine and form an abscess, a pocket of pus, that presses on the nerves to the back legs. This can happen even after the tail itself looks better. Call your vet, but be prepared that these pigs often do not recover and humane culling may be recommended. Early cleaning and vet care for infected tails reduces this risk.

faqs.q: Can the type of feed really cause tail biting?
faqs.a: Yes, feed is an important trigger. Diets short in protein, especially the amino acid lysine, or short in salt and minerals, are linked to more biting, as are sudden diet changes, mouldy feed and too little feeder space. Buy feed from reliable suppliers, follow formulation advice for each stage of growth, change feeds gradually and make sure every pig can eat without fighting.

products.role: Where a vet or nutritionist finds the diet is short in lysine, adding this amino acid helps balance the protein in the feed, which supports growth and removes one known dietary trigger for tail biting; it works alongside enough space, water, cooling and rooting material, not instead of them.

During hot weather or after an outbreak, this oral rehydration and heat-stress relief solution added to clean drinking water can help pigs stay hydrated and cope with heat, reducing a common stress behind biting; it supports recovery but does not heal wounds or replace vet treatment and better ventilation.

card.headline: Grey to bloody, slimy diarrhoea in growers
card.look: Growing pigs pass soft grey or yellow dung full of jelly-like mucus, which often turns bloody with dark red streaks. The pigs' tails and back legs become stained and they lose condition quickly.
card.action: Separate the scouring pigs, stop all pig movement on and off the farm, and call your vet for a diagnosis before giving any medicine.

aka: Kuhara damu kwa nguruwe (Swahili description: bloody diarrhoea in pigs)
detail.summary: Swine dysentery is a bacterial infection of the large intestine, the last part of the gut, in pigs. It mainly hits weaners, growers and finishers and causes grey, slimy diarrhoea that often becomes bloody. Few pigs die when it is treated early, but sick pigs grow slowly, waste feed and need costly treatment. Once it enters a farm it tends to stay through carrier pigs, rats and dirty pens, so prevention and biosecurity matter as much as treatment.
detail.cause: The disease is caused by Brachyspira hyodysenteriae, a spiral-shaped bacterium called a spirochaete. A few related Brachyspira species can cause a similar disease. The pig swallows the bacteria in dung-contaminated feed, water or soil. The bacteria pass through the stomach and small intestine and settle in the caecum and colon, which together form the large intestine. There they burrow into the mucus layer and the gut lining and produce toxins. The lining becomes inflamed, swollen and damaged. It produces large amounts of mucus and starts to bleed in small spots. A healthy large intestine takes back water and salts from the gut contents. A damaged one cannot, so the pig loses water, salts and blood in its dung. This causes dehydration (loss of body water), weakness and weight loss. The small intestine, where most feed is digested, usually stays healthy. That is why many pigs keep eating at first, even though they are scouring. The time from infection to signs is usually one to two weeks, but it can be shorter or much longer. Stress, sudden feed changes and some diets can trigger an outbreak in pigs already carrying the bacteria.
spread: The main route is through dung: sick pigs and recovered carrier pigs shed huge numbers of bacteria, and other pigs pick them up by rooting, licking floors or eating soiled feed.
Buying in weaners or breeding stock from an infected farm or a pig trader is the most common way the disease reaches a new farm, because carrier pigs often look completely healthy.
Recovered pigs can keep shedding the bacteria for weeks to months, so the disease can flare up again in each new batch of growers.
Rats and mice carry the bacteria in their gut for a long time and spread it around and between pig houses; dogs, flies and some birds can also carry it.
Boots, clothes, wheelbarrows, spades, feed sacks and vehicles carry infected dung from pen to pen and from farm to farm, including pig traders' trucks and shared boars.
The bacteria survive for weeks in wet, cool dung and slurry, so dirty pens, blocked drains and muddy runs keep the infection alive, especially during the long and short rains.
Stress from mixing, moving, overcrowding, cold, wet bedding or a sudden change in feed can turn a hidden infection into an outbreak.
detail.atRisk: Pigs from about six weeks of age up to slaughter weight are most often affected, especially growers and finishers. Suckling piglets are rarely affected, and adult sows and boars usually carry the bacteria without showing signs, although they can scour. All breeds can get it, including Large White, Landrace, Camborough crosses and local pigs. Risk is highest on farms that buy weaners from many sources or from markets and traders, mix pigs from different litters or farms, and have poor drainage. Wet, cold weather during the long and short rains raises the risk because dung stays moist and pens are hard to dry. Housed pigs on solid concrete floors that are not cleaned daily, pigs kept on muddy ground, and farms with many rats are at greater risk. Farms that have had the disease before, or that have relied on in-feed antibiotics, often see it return.

early: Soft, grey, yellow or brown dung that looks like porridge or cement, often with shiny clear or white mucus (slime) mixed in.
Dung stuck to the tail, around the anus and down the back legs, and wet patches of slimy dung on the pen floor.
A few pigs in one pen affected first, then more pigs in the same and nearby pens over the following days.
Slightly reduced appetite in some pigs, though many keep eating at first.
Mild fever in some pigs at the start; the ears and body may feel a little warmer than pen mates.
Pigs looking a bit dull, with rough hair and hollow flanks.
advanced: Watery dung containing jelly-like mucus, flecks of fresh red blood or dark red to black streaks, and sometimes shreds of grey tissue-like material.
Rapid loss of weight and condition, with a visible backbone and hips and a tucked-up belly.
Sunken eyes, dry skin that stays tented when pinched, and pigs drinking a lot or too weak to drink, all signs of dehydration.
Weakness, staggering and lying down, with dung-stained, wet back ends and a bad smell in the pen.
Pigs that stay small and uneven in the batch even after the diarrhoea stops.
Occasional sudden death in a pig that was scouring heavily, usually from dehydration and salt loss.
Repeated outbreaks every few weeks in the same unit, or when medication is stopped.

lookalikes.name: African swine fever (ASF)
lookalikes.howToTell: ASF is a deadly viral disease that must be reported. It often causes high fever, red or purple blotches on the ears, belly and legs, pigs that stop eating and huddle, and many deaths across all ages within days. Swine dysentery mostly affects growers, usually without high fever or skin colour changes, and few pigs die. If pigs of all ages are dying or the skin turns red-purple, treat it as possible ASF: lock down the farm and call the County Veterinary Officer at once.

lookalikes.name: Ileitis (porcine proliferative enteropathy, caused by Lawsonia intracellularis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Ileitis affects the end of the small intestine. In growers it often causes grey, loose dung without much mucus and poor growth. In older finishers and young breeding pigs it can cause black, tarry dung, pale skin and sudden death. Swine dysentery dung is typically slimy with fresh red blood streaks. A vet can tell them apart at post-mortem, because dysentery damages only the large intestine and ileitis thickens the small intestine, and with laboratory tests.

lookalikes.name: Whipworm infection (Trichuris suis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Heavy whipworm burdens also cause mucoid, sometimes bloody diarrhoea and wasting in growers, especially on dirty ground or deep litter. A faecal egg count can show whipworm eggs, though eggs may not appear early in the infection. At post-mortem, thin white whip-shaped worms are seen attached to the lining of the large intestine. A vet may check for worms before concluding it is swine dysentery.

lookalikes.name: Salmonellosis (Salmonella infection)
lookalikes.howToTell: Salmonella usually causes a higher fever, yellow watery diarrhoea that may contain blood, loss of appetite and sometimes purple ears and sudden deaths. It can also damage the small intestine and spread through the blood. It is also a risk to people. Only laboratory testing of dung or tissues can reliably separate it from swine dysentery.

detail.diagnosis: A vet first examines the sick pigs and the pens. The vet looks at the dung, checks temperature and hydration, and asks about pig ages, recent purchases, feed changes and any medicines used. Slimy, bloody dung in growers with little fever strongly suggests swine dysentery. The vet will also rule out notifiable diseases such as African swine fever. To confirm it, the vet sends fresh dung samples or rectal swabs from untreated, recently sick pigs to a laboratory, for example a county or regional veterinary laboratory or the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete. The lab can grow the bacteria (culture) or detect its genetic material using a test called PCR. Culture also allows a sensitivity test, which shows which antibiotics still work against your farm's strain. A post-mortem on a pig that has just died, or a sick pig put down humanely, is often the quickest and most useful test. In swine dysentery the walls of the caecum and colon are swollen and red, covered in mucus, blood and sometimes a grey crust, while the small intestine looks normal. To help, keep a record of how many pigs are sick, their ages, when signs started and any medicine already given. Keep a fresh carcass cool and covered for the vet, and do not treat all the pigs before samples are taken, because medication can make the lab tests negative.
firstSteps: Move scouring pigs into a separate, clean, dry pen away from healthy pigs, and handle and feed them last each day.
Make sure every pig, especially sick ones, has constant access to clean, fresh drinking water, because dehydration is what weakens and kills scouring pigs.
Keep sick pigs warm, dry and out of draughts and rain, with clean dry bedding such as wood shavings or dry grass, and change soiled bedding daily.
Stop buying, selling, mixing or moving pigs, and do not lend or borrow boars until the vet has assessed the farm.
Scrape out wet dung from all pens every day, and keep the dung heap or slurry away from pig pens and water sources.
Wear gumboots and an overall or apron used only in the pig unit, and use a footbath with disinfectant at the entrance; wash your hands with soap after handling pigs.
Write down the number of pigs affected, their ages, dates signs began and any deaths, and photograph the dung to show the vet.

Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer promptly, and do not give antibiotics or other medicines from the agrovet before a diagnosis, because wrong or incomplete treatment fuels drug resistance and hides the cause.
detail.vetTreatment: Swine dysentery is treated with antibiotics, and these must be prescribed by a vet. The drugs most commonly used belong to the pleuromutilin group, such as tiamulin and valnemulin. Lincomycin and tylosin are also used, though many strains are now resistant to tylosin and some to lincomycin. Very sick pigs that cannot eat or drink well are usually treated first by injection. The rest of the group is often treated through the drinking water or feed, because many pigs in a pen are usually infected even if they look normal. The vet chooses the drug based on lab results where possible and on what has worked on the farm before. The full course must be finished. Badly dehydrated pigs may need fluids and salts, and the vet will advise on supportive care. Most pigs improve within a few days of the right treatment, but the disease often returns when medication stops unless dung, rats and carrier pigs are dealt with at the same time. Some farms work with their vet on an eradication plan. This combines medicating the whole herd, deep cleaning and disinfecting, rodent control and sometimes emptying and restocking with clean pigs. All these antibiotics have meat withdrawal periods. Treated pigs must not be slaughtered or sold for meat until the withdrawal time on the product label, as confirmed by your vet, has passed. Using antibiotics only when needed and exactly as prescribed helps slow antimicrobial resistance, which is already a real problem with this bacterium.
prevention: Buy weaners and breeding pigs only from known farms with no history of bloody scours. Ask the seller directly, and avoid mixing pigs from several sources or from markets.
Quarantine every new pig in a separate pen for at least three to four weeks. Watch it for diarrhoea before mixing, and ask your vet about testing new stock.
Run an all-in, all-out system where possible. Fill a pen with one batch, empty it completely at sale, then clean, disinfect and dry it before the next batch.
Remove dung from pens daily, keep floors sloped and drains open, and let pens dry out. The bacteria survive in wet dung but die in dry, sunny conditions and with good disinfectants.
Control rats and mice seriously with bait stations, sealed feed stores and removal of rubbish and long grass around the unit, because rodents keep the infection on the farm.
Keep dogs, poultry, wild birds and visitors out of pig houses. Use dedicated boots and a footbath, and keep pig traders and their vehicles away from your pens.
Change feed gradually over about a week, avoid overcrowding, and keep pigs warm and dry during the rains to reduce the stress that triggers outbreaks.

Deworm on a schedule agreed with your vet to control whipworm, which damages the large intestine and can make dysentery worse. Feed a balanced diet stored dry so it does not grow mould. There is no widely available vaccine against swine dysentery in Kenya, so management is the main protection.
detail.impact: Swine dysentery rarely wipes out a herd, but it quietly eats into profit. Affected growers eat but do not convert feed into meat well. They take weeks longer to reach market weight, and the batch becomes uneven, so some pigs sell at lower weights or prices. Feed is the biggest cost in Kenyan pig farming, so slow growth directly cuts margins. Antibiotic treatment, vet visits, lab tests and extra labour for cleaning add costs. Treated pigs cannot be sold until withdrawal periods end, which delays income. Some pigs die, especially if treatment is late. On farms that sell weaners, a reputation for scours can lose buyers. Because the disease keeps returning in each new batch unless controlled, the losses repeat, and long-term reliance on antibiotics raises costs and drives resistance.
detail.humanHealth: Brachyspira hyodysenteriae is not considered a risk to people, so swine dysentery itself is not known to infect humans. However, other germs that cause bloody diarrhoea in pigs, such as Salmonella, can infect people, so always wash hands with soap after handling pigs or dung and keep children away from sick pens. The bigger human risk comes from the antibiotics used to treat it: meat from treated pigs can contain drug residues if pigs are slaughtered before the withdrawal period ends. Always keep treatment records and respect withdrawal times.
detail.outlook: With early diagnosis and the right antibiotic, most affected pigs recover and few die. However, growth is often set back, and some pigs never fully catch up. Pigs that were very dehydrated, thin or treated late do worse. The disease is hard to remove from a farm, and outbreaks commonly return when medication stops, when new pigs arrive or during stressful periods. Farms that combine vet-guided treatment with strict cleaning, all-in all-out batches, rodent control and careful buying usually bring it under control, and some can eradicate it with a planned programme. Resistance to some antibiotics means results vary between farms, so lab testing matters.

faqs.q: Can I just buy an antibiotic from the agrovet and put it in the water?
faqs.a: It is better not to. Bloody diarrhoea in pigs has several causes, including African swine fever, which antibiotics cannot help and which must be reported. Swine dysentery strains are often resistant to common drugs, so the wrong product wastes money and makes resistance worse. Starting medicine before samples are taken can also hide the cause from the lab. Let a vet confirm the diagnosis and prescribe the right drug, course length and withdrawal period.

faqs.q: My pigs got better after treatment but the scours came back. Why?
faqs.a: This is very common with swine dysentery. Recovered pigs can carry and shed the bacteria for weeks to months. Rats and mice carry it too, and it survives in wet dung in pens and drains. When the medicine stops, the bacteria multiply again, especially in new young pigs. Lasting control needs treatment plus daily dung removal, cleaning and drying pens between batches, rat control and careful buying of new stock, planned with your vet.

faqs.q: Can I sell or eat pigs that have swine dysentery?
faqs.a: The disease is not known to infect people. Still, sick, thin pigs should not be slaughtered, and any pig treated with antibiotics must not be slaughtered or sold for meat until the full withdrawal period has passed. Ask your vet for the exact withdrawal time of the drug used and keep written records. Selling live sick or recovering pigs to other farmers spreads the disease, so avoid it.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine for swine dysentery?
faqs.a: There is no widely available, proven vaccine for swine dysentery in Kenya at present. Prevention depends on good management: buying clean stock, quarantine, all-in all-out batches, daily cleaning, dry pens, rodent control and avoiding stress and sudden feed changes. Ask your vet or County Veterinary Officer if anything new becomes available.

faqs.q: How do I know whether it is swine dysentery or African swine fever?
faqs.a: You cannot be fully sure by looking, which is why a vet is needed. Swine dysentery mainly affects growers, with slimy, bloody dung, little fever and few deaths. ASF often causes high fever, pigs refusing feed, red or purple skin on the ears and belly, and many deaths among pigs of all ages within days. If you see sudden deaths or purple skin, stop all movement and report to the County Veterinary Officer immediately.

faqs.q: What disinfectant should I use, and is cleaning really that important?
faqs.a: Cleaning is one of the most important steps. Disinfectants do not work well on dung, so first scrape and wash away all dung and bedding with water and detergent. Then apply a disinfectant recommended by your vet or agrovet for pig units, following the label. Most importantly, let the pen dry completely before restocking, because the bacteria survive in wet conditions but die when pens are dry and exposed to sunlight.

products.role: An oral rehydration solution that can be offered in drinking water to help scouring pigs replace lost water and salts and stay drinking while vet-prescribed treatment works. It supports hydration only and does not kill the bacteria or replace antibiotics prescribed by the vet.

Can be used during recovery to support digestion and liver function after the gut has been damaged and the pigs have been through antibiotic treatment, helping them get back to eating and growing. It is a supportive aid alongside vet care, cleaning and good management, not a treatment for swine dysentery.

card.headline: Swollen red vulva in young gilts
card.look: Young gilts, and sometimes even piglets, have a swollen, red vulva and enlarged teats, while growers eat less, grow slowly and look rough. These signs often appear across many pigs at once after a new batch of maize, bran or brewers' waste.
card.action: Stop feeding the suspect feed straight away, keep a sample of it, and call your vet.

detail.summary: Mycotoxin poisoning happens when pigs eat feed contaminated with poisons made by moulds (fungi). The best-known ones are aflatoxin, which damages the liver, and zearalenone, which acts like a female hormone and upsets breeding. Pigs are among the most sensitive farm animals to these poisons. The damage is often slow and hidden: poor growth, failed breeding and weak immunity can cost a farm a lot before anyone suspects the feed.
detail.cause: Moulds such as Aspergillus and Fusarium grow on maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cotton and sunflower seed cake, maize bran and wet by-products like brewers' waste (machicha). Some moulds grow in the field during wet or drought-stressed seasons, and others grow later in damp, poorly ventilated stores. As they grow, they produce mycotoxins, which are chemical poisons. These poisons are not killed by cooking, boiling or drying, and feed can carry dangerous levels even when it does not look very mouldy. Each toxin harms the body in its own way. Aflatoxin damages the liver, the organ that cleans the blood and processes nutrients, so pigs grow poorly, may turn yellow (jaundice) and lose their resistance to infection. Zearalenone copies the female hormone oestrogen, so it makes the vulva swell, causes false heat and disturbs pregnancy. Deoxynivalenol, also called vomitoxin, makes pigs refuse feed and sometimes vomit. Fumonisins can cause fluid in the lungs (porcine pulmonary oedema) and liver damage. Ochratoxin damages the kidneys. A single feed often contains several toxins at once, and together they can do more harm than any one alone.
spread: Mycotoxin poisoning is not contagious and does not pass from pig to pig; every affected animal ate the contaminated feed.
Maize harvested wet or left on the ground during the long or short rains is a major source, especially if it was not dried properly before storage.
Grain and bran stored in sacks on the floor or against damp walls, or in leaking stores, can grow mould and build up toxins over weeks.
Wet by-products such as brewers' waste, spent grains and kitchen leftovers can go mouldy within a few days in warm weather if not used quickly.
Cheap, rejected or 'second-grade' maize, maize germ and bran from posho mills can carry high levels, because damaged and broken grain grows mould more easily.
Seed cakes such as groundnut, cotton and sunflower cake are known carriers of aflatoxin if stored or processed badly.
Feeders and troughs that are not cleaned let wet, old feed cake and go mouldy, mixing toxins into fresh feed.
Sows pass some toxins, especially aflatoxin and zearalenone, into their milk, so suckling piglets can be affected even though they eat little feed.
detail.atRisk: All pigs can be affected, but young growing pigs, weaners and breeding animals suffer most. Prepubertal gilts (young females that have not yet come on heat) show the most obvious zearalenone signs, and sows and boars can lose fertility. Suckling piglets are at risk through the sow's milk. Risk rises during and after the long and short rains, when grain is hard to dry, and in hot humid conditions that favour mould. Farms in areas with known aflatoxin problems in maize, such as parts of Eastern and Lower Eastern Kenya, need extra care. Smallholders who mix their own feed from bran, local maize and by-products, or who buy cheap feed without knowing its source, face higher risk than those using tested commercial feed. Zero-grazing style pig units and free-ranging pigs fed on swill and leftovers can both be affected.

early: Pigs eat less than usual, leave feed in the trough, or sniff and walk away from a new batch of feed.
Growers and finishers grow slowly and uneven, with some pigs falling behind their penmates despite eating.
Coats look rough and dull, and pigs seem less lively than normal.
Young gilts develop a swollen, red vulva, sometimes with a little discharge, even though they are too young to be on heat.
Teats and udders swell in young gilts and sometimes in piglets, and boars or male piglets may show a swollen sheath.
Sows show false heat, irregular heat, no heat at all, or keep returning to the boar after service.
Some pigs vomit soon after eating, which points strongly to vomitoxin in the feed.
More pigs than usual fall sick with ordinary infections such as diarrhoea or coughs, because their immunity is weakened.
advanced: Yellowing of the gums, eyes or pale skin (jaundice), showing serious liver damage from aflatoxin.
Straining and prolapse, where the vagina or rectum pushes out of the body, especially in gilts affected by zearalenone.
Small litters, weak or splay-legged piglets, mummified or stillborn piglets, early pregnancy loss and sometimes abortion.
Severe weight loss, dark or bloody dung, and bleeding or bruising under the skin caused by liver failure.
Sudden breathing difficulty, open-mouth breathing and purple skin, which can follow high fumonisin levels and may end in death within hours.
Drinking and urinating much more than usual, which can signal kidney damage from ochratoxin.
Sudden deaths of several pigs after a heavily contaminated batch of feed.

lookalikes.name: African swine fever (ASF)
lookalikes.howToTell: ASF is a notifiable viral disease that spreads between pigs and farms. It usually causes high fever, red or purple blotches on the ears, belly and legs, and many sudden deaths over a few days, including in pigs that were not eating the same feed. Mycotoxin poisoning does not spread and is linked to a feed batch. If pigs are dying quickly with red-purple skin, treat it as possible ASF and report to the County Veterinary Officer immediately.

lookalikes.name: Normal heat in a mature gilt
lookalikes.howToTell: A gilt coming on true heat, usually from around 5 to 7 months old, has a swollen red vulva for only a few days and stands still when pressed on the back or when near a boar. Zearalenone causes swelling in gilts that are too young, lasts longer, affects many gilts at once and is often seen with swollen teats and swelling in piglets or male pigs.

lookalikes.name: Infectious causes of abortion and poor litters
lookalikes.howToTell: Infections such as leptospirosis, brucellosis and porcine parvovirus can also cause abortion, stillbirths or mummified piglets. These often come with fever, follow the introduction of new animals, or affect gilts more than older sows. Mycotoxin problems usually line up with a change of feed and come with other feed signs such as reduced eating and poor growth. Only lab tests on blood, aborted foetuses and feed can separate them for sure.

lookalikes.name: Heavy worm burden or poor nutrition
lookalikes.howToTell: Worms and an unbalanced diet also cause slow growth and rough coats. Worms are often seen in dung, pigs may cough, and the problem improves after a vet-advised deworming. Poor growth from mycotoxins improves when the feed is changed, and is often seen together with breeding signs or jaundice.

detail.diagnosis: There is no simple quick test on the live pig, so a vet puts together several clues. They will ask about the feed, when the problem started and whether a new batch of maize, bran or by-product was brought in. They examine the pigs for jaundice, vulva and teat swelling, prolapses and body condition. If a pig dies, a post-mortem (examining the body after death) can show a pale, yellow, firm or enlarged liver, kidney changes or fluid in the lungs, and tissue samples can be sent to a lab. The most important step is testing the feed itself at a laboratory, such as government, university or private feed-testing labs, which can measure aflatoxin, zearalenone and other toxins. Mycotoxins sit in patches within a bag or store, so one handful can give a false clean result. To help, keep the suspect feed and do not throw it all away. Take small amounts from the top, middle and bottom of several bags, mix them, and store about a kilogram in a clean, dry, labelled paper or cloth bag. Write down the feed source, date bought, when signs began, how many pigs are affected, ages, breeding records and any deaths.
firstSteps: Stop feeding the suspect feed immediately and switch to fresh, clean feed from a trusted source, ideally from a different batch or supplier.
Keep a well-mixed sample of the suspect feed in a dry, labelled bag for the vet and laboratory, and record where and when you bought it.
Empty, scrub and dry all feeders and troughs to remove caked or old feed, and do not mix leftover suspect feed into the new ration.
Give plenty of clean, fresh water at all times, because sick pigs with liver or kidney damage need it and may drink more.
Separate gilts or sows with prolapses into a clean, dry, well-bedded pen where other pigs cannot bite them, and keep the prolapsed tissue clean and moist with clean wet cloth until the vet arrives.
Keep sick pigs cool, shaded and calm, and avoid moving, mixing or stressing them.
Wear a dust mask and gloves when handling mouldy grain or bran, and wash your hands afterwards.
Do not give antibiotics, hormones or other drugs without your vet's advice, and call the vet promptly, especially if pigs are jaundiced, struggling to breathe or dying.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no antidote that removes mycotoxins once a pig has eaten them. Treatment is mainly about stopping more poison going in and helping the body recover. The vet will confirm the feed change and may advise adding a mycotoxin binder to the clean feed while the farm sorts out its feed supply. They may recommend better-quality protein and extra vitamins such as vitamins A and E with selenium, which help the liver and immune system. Pigs with weakened immunity often pick up secondary infections, and the vet may prescribe antibiotics for these. Antibiotics do not remove the toxin, so they should only be used when there is a real infection, exactly as prescribed, to reduce antimicrobial resistance. Any drug a vet gives has a meat withdrawal period, the time you must wait before the pig can be slaughtered for food, and you must keep to it. Prolapses need a vet to clean, replace and secure the tissue, and some badly affected animals may be best culled. In gilts with zearalenone signs, the swelling usually settles over a few weeks once clean feed is given, but breeding may be delayed. Pigs with severe liver damage may not recover fully, and the vet may advise early slaughter or culling if the animal is suffering or will never grow well. Treatment must be prescribed and guided by a vet.
prevention: Buy maize, bran and seed cakes only when they are dry, clean and free of mould, musty smell, insect damage and broken grain, and ask suppliers whether the feed has been tested for aflatoxin.

Dry home-grown maize thoroughly before storage, to around 13 percent moisture or below; well-dried grain rattles and breaks cleanly when bitten, and a cheap moisture meter or the salt-in-a-jar test can help.
Store feed in a dry, cool, well-ventilated store, with sacks raised on pallets off the floor and away from walls, and use older stock first.
Consider hermetic storage bags or airtight containers for grain, which slow mould and insect damage.
Buy wet by-products such as brewers' waste in small amounts and use them within a day or two, or ensile them properly; never feed smelly, heated or mouldy machicha or kitchen waste.
Clean feeders and troughs every day so no wet feed cakes and rots in corners.
Sort out and burn or bury visibly mouldy, discoloured or shrivelled grain rather than feeding it to pigs, poultry or people.
Use a mycotoxin binder in the ration during high-risk periods, such as after the rains or when feed quality is uncertain, as an extra layer of protection alongside good storage, not instead of it.
Feed breeding gilts and sows the best-quality grain on the farm, because they are the most sensitive to zearalenone and the cost of lost litters is high.
Keep breeding, growth and feed-batch records so you can quickly link a problem to a particular feed delivery.
detail.impact: Mycotoxins are a hidden drain on many Kenyan pig farms. Pigs that eat less and convert feed poorly take longer to reach market weight, so the farmer spends more on feed for each kilo of pork sold. Breeding losses are often the most expensive: gilts that come on false heat or fail to conceive, sows that return to service, small litters, weak piglets and abortions all mean fewer pigs to sell. Weakened immunity leads to more illness, more vet costs and sometimes vaccine failure. Prolapses and severe liver damage can force early culling. Buyers and slaughterhouses may reject jaundiced carcasses or condemn livers. Because the signs develop slowly, farmers often keep using the same contaminated feed for weeks, so losses grow before the cause is found.
detail.humanHealth: Mycotoxins in pig feed are not an infection and do not spread from pigs to people, but they are a real health concern. Aflatoxin is a recognised cause of liver cancer in people, and heavy exposure has caused serious illness and deaths in Kenya when people ate badly contaminated maize. Mouldy maize that is unsafe for pigs is also unsafe for your family, so never eat it, sell it to others or pass it to other farmers. Small amounts of aflatoxin and its breakdown products can remain in the liver and kidneys of exposed pigs, so avoid eating organs from pigs known to have eaten heavily contaminated feed, and follow the meat inspector's decision on condemned livers. Breathing in dust from mouldy grain can irritate the lungs and may cause fungal lung infection in some people, so wear a dust mask and gloves when handling it. If a vet treats your pigs with drugs, keep strictly to the meat withdrawal period before slaughter.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends on which toxin was involved, how much the pigs ate and for how long. Mild cases, such as feed refusal from vomitoxin or vulva swelling from zearalenone, usually improve within days to a few weeks after switching to clean feed. Breeding animals may take longer to return to normal cycles, and pregnancies already lost cannot be saved. Pigs with mild liver damage can recover slowly with good feed, but growth may stay behind their penmates. Pigs with jaundice, bleeding or severe weight loss have a poorer outlook, and some do not recover. Sudden breathing problems from fumonisins can kill quickly. Acting fast, removing the feed and fixing storage give the best chance of limiting losses.

faqs.q: If I dry mouldy maize in the sun or cook it, is it safe for my pigs?
faqs.a: No. Drying stops more mould from growing, but the toxins already made stay in the grain. Mycotoxins are not destroyed by normal cooking, boiling or sun-drying. Mouldy or musty grain should be removed and destroyed, not fed to pigs, chickens or people.

faqs.q: Will a mycotoxin binder make mouldy feed safe?
faqs.a: A binder can reduce how much toxin the pig absorbs from the gut, and it is useful as protection when feed quality is uncertain. But no binder removes all toxins, and many binders work better on aflatoxin than on zearalenone, vomitoxin or fumonisins. It is not a licence to feed visibly mouldy feed. Clean, dry feed always comes first.

faqs.q: My young gilts have swollen red vulvas. Will they still breed?
faqs.a: In most cases the swelling goes down over a few weeks after the contaminated feed is removed, and many gilts go on to breed normally. Some may have delayed or irregular heats for a while. Gilts that suffered prolapses or severe problems may have lasting damage, so ask your vet whether to keep them for breeding.

faqs.q: Which feeds are most likely to carry mycotoxins in Kenya?
faqs.a: Maize and maize products such as bran and germ are the biggest risk, especially after wet harvests. Groundnut, cotton and sunflower seed cakes, sorghum, brewers' waste and old kitchen leftovers can also be contaminated. Feed that smells musty, feels warm or damp, has clumps, or shows green, grey, black or pink patches should be treated as suspect.

faqs.q: Can I sell or eat pigs that ate mouldy feed?
faqs.a: Pigs that ate contaminated feed and recovered are usually acceptable for slaughter once they are healthy and any drug withdrawal periods have passed. The meat inspector may condemn yellow or damaged livers, and you should not eat organs from pigs known to have eaten heavily contaminated feed. Talk to your vet before selling pigs that are jaundiced or unwell.

faqs.q: How do I know for sure that the feed is the problem?
faqs.a: The surest way is a laboratory test of a properly mixed feed sample, which your vet or County Veterinary Office can help you arrange. Clues on the farm include many pigs affected at once, signs starting after a new feed batch, no fever, and improvement after switching to clean feed. Because some serious infections like African swine fever can look similar at first, always involve your vet.

products.role: A mycotoxin binder that can be mixed into clean feed to help reduce absorption of aflatoxin and ochratoxin from the gut, useful during high-risk seasons or while the farm changes feed supply. It supports good storage and the removal of mouldy feed but does not replace them, and protection against zearalenone and other Fusarium toxins may be more limited.

Supports liver function and digestion in pigs recovering from aflatoxin exposure once the contaminated feed has been removed, as an aid alongside clean feed and the vet's treatment plan, not as a cure for liver damage.
